Identification of total phosphate, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size thresholds for success of biomanipulation in peri-urban eutrophic ponds Sylvia De Backer · Samuel Teissier · Ludwig Triest Received: 23 November 2012 / Accepted: 27 October 2013 / Published online: 8 November 2013 © Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2013 Abstract In small shallow lakes and ponds, the clear-water state can generally be maintained at higher nutrient concentrations compared to larger shallow lakes. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for total phosphorus (TP), submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size that determine biomanipulation success in peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationship between transparency and TP is discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Using classification trees, a threshold TP concentration of 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) was determined below which a clear-water state was generally maintained after biomanipulation. When the average TP concentration was >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of the clear-water state largely depended on the presence of sufficiently large zooplankton (>0.87 mm) or a submerged vegetation cover of >82% at some point during the year. This threshold TP concentration is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) which is generally suggested for longer-term success of biomanipulation in shallow lakes. Such threshold nutrient concentration is important when restoring ecological quality in eutrophic small lakes and ponds. Extended follow-up of biomanipulation success in eutrophic ponds could provide more insight into the feasibility of these thresholds on the longer term. Keywords Ponds · Shallow lakes · Eutrophic · Clear-water state · Restoration · Turbid Introduction During the past decades, ecological quality of shallow lakes and ponds has often been degraded as a result of eutrophication due to human activities, causing a transition to a turbid, phytoplankton-dominated state, often associated with severe blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria (Willame et al., 2005; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Nutrient reduction alone as a method to restore such lakes and ponds is often expensive and inefficient, as recovery is often delayed by internal phosphorus loading or biological resistances (Søndergaard et al., 2005a; Jeppesen et al., 2007). Internal loading was found to be a significant part of total P loading during the productive summer period in eutrophic Danish lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2013). Next to nutrient reduction measures, biomanipulation, through complete or partial fish removal, is often performed to improve ecological quality of shallow lakes (Meijer et al., 1994; Lammens, 1999; Jyväsjärvi et al., 2013). In shallow lakes, a short-term response to biomanipulation is generally dependent on the ability of large zooplankton, once released from its predation pressure, to control phytoplankton sufficiently to create a clear-water state, irrespective of the nutrient levels (van Donk et al., 1990; Meijer et al., 1999). In eutrophic ponds, zooplankton grazing was shown to be a first important mechanism for obtaining a clear-water state (Peretyatko et al., 2009). Once a clear-water state is obtained, the increased water transparency could promote the growth of macrophytes (Bakker et al., 2013) which, in turn, could stabilize the clear-water state on the longer term by a series of mechanisms (Van den Berg et al., 1997; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002; Peretyatko et al., 2007a). On the longer term, however, the success of biomanipulation is more speculative and has often been related to elevated nutrient concentrations (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2008; Hobbs et al., 2012). The negative relationship between nutrient loading and water transparency in shallow lakes is generally well recognized. Scheffer et al. (1993) already suggested a stepwise rather than a gradual shift from a macrophyte-dominated to a phytoplankton-dominated state when nutrients are gradually increased. Although the theory of only two alternative states has been nuanced lately, the general idea remains that once a certain threshold nutrient concentration is surpassed, a more dramatic increase in turbidity can occur and a return to a clear-water state will be very difficult (Scheffer & van Nes, 2007; Hobbs et al., 2012). Another important factor influencing biomanipulation success in shallow lakes and ponds is the level of nutrients. It is often suggested that the clear-water state in ponds and small lakes is generally less dependent on nutrients compared to larger shallow lakes (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2005b). In small shallow lakes and ponds, a lower Chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) yield per unit of nitrogen or phosphorus is generally observed (Søndergaard et al., 2005b). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that ponds (<3 ha) deviated considerably from the overall relationship between water transparency and total phosphorus (TP) in Danish shallow lakes, because both a high transparency and submerged vegetation were still found at higher TP concentrations than for larger lakes. This phenomenon has several possible explanations. Jeppesen et al. (1990) already mentioned that conditions are more favourable for macrophytes in small lakes. Additionally, in smaller lakes and ponds, macrophytes suffer less from wind stress and wind-induced resuspension of the sediment. Also, a reduced depth provides a better light availability for macrophytes at a given water transparency and as such, macrophytes can colonize larger parts of the lake area (Scheffer and van Nes, 2007; Van Geest et al., 2007). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that for a given shallow lake, transparency was higher when an average submerged vegetation cover of >30% was present, compared to cases with a cover <30%, confirming the positive effect of submerged vegetation on transparency (Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002). Favourable conditions for macrophytes in ponds thus could contribute to an increased transparency, despite high nutrient concentrations. Also, in ponds, some piscivorous fish, such as northern pike (Esox lucius L.), benefit from an abundant vegetation and a higher shore to total area ratio (Grimm, 1989). Winter fish kill due to oxygen depletion could also play a major role, increasing zooplankton grazing during summer, resulting in a more efficient control of phytoplankton (Søndergaard et al., 2005b), which can favour the growth of submerged macrophytes. When biomanipulation is performed on shallow lakes or ponds, it can be useful to determine above which nutrient level a clear-water state can no longer be achieved. When nutrient concentrations (mainly phosphorus) are above a certain threshold, a shift back to the turbid state after biomanipulation might be inevitable and in such cases a nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation is performed. According to Jeppesen et al. (1990), a long-term effect of biomanipulation can only be achieved when the average TP concentration is below 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) in shallow lakes larger than 3 ha. Hosper & Jagtman (1990) came to similar conclusions and suggested 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) as a threshold for a stable clear-water state after biomanipulation of shallow lakes. In shallow lakes with a TP concentration higher than 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\), only short-term effects can be expected. We hypothesize that, taking into account that phytoplankton biomass is less affected by nutrients in small lakes and ponds compared to larger shallow lakes, the threshold nutrient level at which both alternative states can exist is higher for ponds than for Table 1 General characteristics and applied restoration measures of the studied ponds

Higher nutrient threshold levels could be an advantage for deciding and attempting a restoration of eutrophic ponds through biomanipulation. Nevertheless, even for ponds, beyond a certain threshold, nutrient levels might be too high to obtain a stable clear-water state after fish removal on the longer term. For management purposes, it is crucial to determine the threshold nutrient concentrations above which biomanipulation will no longer be successful in highly eutrophicated ponds. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for key factors (TP concentration, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size) that are known to strongly determine the outcome of biomanipulation in a series of peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationships between transparency and TP, and the obtained thresholds for eutrophic ponds are discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Materials and methods Study area For this study, 13 ponds, located in the Brussels Capital Region (Belgium), were biomanipulated and monitored during 2004–2010. All ponds are located within the same catchment (Woluwe river catchment) in a close proximity of each other (<10 km) and their connectivity is rather high. All the ponds were man-made and created more than a century ago by the damming of small low-order streams (Marlier, 1971). They are shallow (maximum depth 3 m), flat-bottomed and range in surface area from 0.2 to 6 ha and are mainly fed by small rivulets and ground water seepage. Fish communities in the Brussels Capital Region generally consist of species that are typical for Western European fresh waters, such as common carp (Cyprinus carpio carpio L.), northern pike (Esox lucius L.), perch (Perca fluviatilis L.), roach (Rutilus rutilus L.) and tench (Tinca tinca L.) (De Backer et al., 2010). More detailed characteristics of the studied ponds, including an overview of the applied restoration measures for each pond, are given in Table 1. Restoration measures Biomanipulation was performed in 13 ponds during 2005–2009 by water drawdown and complete fish removal (Table 1). This was generally done in winter or early spring to avoid the presence of numerous juvenile fish which could easily escape or survive in the mud for some time. In most ponds, the water level could be lowered manually, due to their artificial nature. During water drawdown, fishermen removed all or as much fish as possible using fishing nets. More than 500 kg of fish per ha was removed in each pond, confirming that all ponds were overstocked with fish before biomanipulation. A few weeks to several months after fish removal, the ponds were slowly refilled through overflow of neighbouring ponds, groundwater seepage or inflow of small rivulets. In a second phase, northern pike (Esox lucius L.) were added in an attempt to stabilize the clear-water state. Addition of piscivores is often performed in an attempt to control planktivorous fish after biomanipulation, allowing large zooplankton to increase grazing pressure on phytoplankton and, as such, further stabilizes the clear-water state (Lammens, 1999; Ha et al., 2013). The individuals that were added in the studied ponds were larger than the 0+ pike that are generally used for this purpose, as the result of 0+ pike additions is often not just temporary (Søndergaard et al., 1997) or the added pike lack piscivory (Skov et al., 2003). In February 2008, only 1+ pikes were added to 10 biomanipulated ponds (Table 1). In February 2010, various densities of 1+, 2+ and 3+ pike (with a size of 20, 30 and 45 cm, respectively) were added into 7 biomanipulated ponds. Sampling and sample processing Samples were taken 1 year before and 1–5 years after biomanipulation during the warm season (May–September) on 3–5 occasions per year. A detailed overview of all sampling occasions is given in Table 2. Except for very small ponds, all samples were taken from a boat. Secchi depth was measured using a 30-cm-diameter disc. In case the Secchi disc was still visible when reaching the pond bottom, Secchi depth was estimated as the actual pond depth plus 1 m in case the disc was still clearly visible or plus 0.1 m in case it was only partially visible. This approach is similar to the method of Cottenie et al. (2001) and was used to obtain a more realistic Secchi depth when the disc was still visible at the pond bottom. Quantitative phytoplankton, Chl \( a \), main nutrient (TP, soluble reactive phosphorus—SRP, and dissolved inorganic nitrogen i.e. \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) and \( \mathrm{NO}_x \) (NO\(_2^-\) and NO\(_3^-\))) and zooplankton samples were collected on each occasion. Mixed water samples based on 10 random subsamples were taken from each pond (including vegetated parts) with a plastic tube sampler of 4.5 cm diameter and 70 cm length that closes in the lower part. An extension was fixed to the sampler to reach the deeper parts of the ponds when appropriate. In case of deeper ponds (depth >1 m), subsamples were taken alternately from shallower and deeper parts of the pond in order to obtain a sample representative of the whole water column. After stirring the collected water, 500 ml was taken for phytoplankton identification and quantification, 1 l for chemical analyses and 1 l for Chl \( a \) determination. Samples for Chl \( a \) analysis were filtered onto Whatman GF/C filters and stored at −18 °C for a maximum of 7 days before analysis. Pigments were extracted in 90% acetone in the dark for 8 h. Pigment concentrations were measured spectrophotometrically. Nutrient concentrations were measured according to standard methods (APHA-AWWA-WEF, 1995). Phytoplankton samples were fixed in the field with alkaline lugol, sodium thiosulphate and buffered formalin (Sherr & Sherr, 1993) and stored in the dark before identification and enumeration to genus level using inverted microscopy. Biovolumes were calculated using the approximations of cell shapes to simple geometrical forms (Wetzel & Likens, 2000). Total phytoplankton biovolume was mainly used as a proxy for turbidity of the water column. Eight phytoplankton groups were differentiated: Cyanobacteria, Bacillariophyta, Euglenophyta, Chlorophyta, Cryptophyta, Dinophyta, Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta. In order to assess the zooplankton community structure, 10 subsamples of 1 l were collected with the same sampler used for phytoplankton and nutrients. (2003), Daphnia spp., Diaphanosoma spp., Eurycercus spp., Sida spp., and Simocephalus spp. were considered as large (non-predatory) cladocerans. At least 10 individuals were measured per sample. Direct effects of northern pike were not studied, as it was beyond the scope of this paper. However, since the effect of pike additions is mainly to release zooplankton from predation pressure by planktivorous fish (Lammens, 1999), zooplankton density and size can be indicative of the indirect effect of pike additions. Submerged vegetation cover was estimated from a boat during each field visit, visually and by the use of a rake, along transects throughout the whole pond. Macrophytes were identified to species level, except for filamentous algae that were identified to genus level. Statistical data analyses To identify the factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. ‘failure’ or ‘success’), it is essential to define exactly what ‘failure’ is or what can be considered as ‘success’. In terms of phytoplankton biovolume and composition, ‘failure’ of biomanipulation is essentially a return to a situation that is comparable to the phytoplankton composition and biomass before biomanipulation. Therefore, a hierarchical cluster analysis was performed on averaged per year phytoplankton data (division level). All data were log-transformed to obtain normality if needed. By arranging the data into different clusters, we could study how the situation before biomanipulation was related to the situation after biomanipulation for each pond, in each year. The cluster analysis was performed using PC-ORD (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Sørensen distance was used as a dissimilarity measure and the farthest neighbour linkage as group linkage method. One-way clustering was carried out on both samples and phytoplankton groups. For the latter, data were relativised (i.e. each value divided by the maximum value observed per phytoplankton group). This is generally done to avoid separation of more common species into separate groups from rare species (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Based on previous field observations and the nature of the data, we expect a clustering into two main groups, corresponding to clear with low phytoplankton biomass and to turbid with high phytoplankton biomass conditions. Based on the position of each data point within the cluster, successfully biomanipulated ponds (situation 1), situated inside a low phytoplankton biomass group, could be further subdivided into two categories: before (1b) and after (1a) biomanipulation. Ponds where biomanipulation failed (situation 2) were defined as ponds where data of at least 1 year after biomanipulation were situated inside a high phytoplankton biomass group within the cluster. Situation 2 could be further subdivided into three categories: before biomanipulation (2b), after biomanipulation but before failure (2a, situated in the low phytoplankton subcluster) and after biomanipulation when it failed (2f, data with high phytoplankton biovolume). Essentially, the cluster analysis based on phytoplankton data was performed to assign each data point to one of the 5 predefined categories (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a or 2f). Differences between these 5 categories were analyzed further using One-way ANOVA. A Tukey HSD test, modified for unequal sample size, was used as a post hoc comparison test to compare mean values between individual groups. The one-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to investigate the data for normality and the Brown–Forsythe test was used to check for homogeneity of variance. When one of both assumptions was not met (as was the case for SRP and submerged vegetation cover), a non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test was used to investigate differences between the groups. For all analyses, averaged per year per pond data were used. Three repeated-measures ANOVA were carried out on the considered variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, length of large Cladocera and %SVmax) with time (year) as factor because biomanipulations were not carried out in the same year for every pond. ANOVA was done for the years ‘before biomanipulation’, for the first year following biomanipulation and for all follow-up years after biomanipulation. An additional repeated measure ANOVA was done for the same variables for all ponds in 2010 but using pike addition as a factor in three classes, namely no addition, pikes added in 2008 and pikes added in 2010. Previous research indicated that the impact of total phosphorus concentration (TP), large Cladocera length (LCL) and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) on phytoplankton biovolume in these ponds did not show a linear but a threshold relationship (De Backer, 2011). Therefore, classification trees (Breiman et al., 1984) were used to estimate the thresholds of different environmental factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. phytoplankton biovolume). This type of analysis could allow us to identify threshold values for each predictor (TP, LCL and SV_{max}), below or above which biomanipulation will most likely fail or be successful. All classification tree analyses were performed with Statistica version 8 (Statsoft Inc., Tulsa, OK, USA). The goodness of fit of each split was estimated by the Chi square statistic. Only the best fitting option was shown in the resulting graph. The ‘prune on deviance’ option was used as a stopping rule with a minimum of 10% of the total number of cases needed to allow a subsequent split. For all classification tree analyses, averaged per year per pond values of post-biomanipulation data were used. A series of classification trees was performed to explore the relationships between phytoplankton biovolume and the three predictors (all together or each predictor individually). Since submerged vegetation can affect phytoplankton, phytoplankton can also affect submerged vegetation cover, using average submerged vegetation cover (SV_{av}) as a predictor of phytoplankton biovolume seems irrelevant, as the percentage of cover might be negatively influenced by phytoplankton itself. Use of SV_{max} as a predictor variable of phytoplankton biovolume, rather than SV_{av}, allows us to identify the threshold cover of submerged vegetation above which an increased phytoplankton growth is prevented. Finally, the relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}), LCL and TP concentration was studied using Pearson product-moment correlations. Results Classification of biomanipulated ponds Hierarchical cluster analysis of averaged per year phytoplankton biovolume (per division) of biomanipulated ponds constructed two main groups (Fig. 1). In Group A, as indicated by relative abundances and percentiles of each phytoplankton group, phytoplankton biovolume was generally lower when compared to Group B. For all phytoplankton groups (with the exception of Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta that clustered separately from all other groups), the highest phytoplankton biovolume values were found in pond samples of Group B. All pre-biomanipulation samples aggregated into Group B, except for two cases (VKn1 and WtMl). For 8 ponds (Beml, Dens, PRB1, Sbsk, Fig. 1 Hierarchical cluster analysis based on averaged per year phytoplankton data (2004–2010) for all biomanipulated ponds using Sørensen distance as a dissimilarity measure and the farthest neighbour linkage as group linkage method. Years are indicated by the number before the pond name, for example: 8Beml = Beml in 2008. Asterisks indicate situations before biomanipulation. A colour gradient ranging from white to black was used to colour the matrix based on percentiles (left group of squares) and on relative abundance (right group of squares) per phytoplankton group (vertically). Symbols indicate biomanipulation status: 1b, 1a—successfully biomanipulated ponds before and after biomanipulation; 2b, 2a, 2f—unsuccessfully biomanipulated ponds before biomanipulation, after biomanipulation but before failure, and after biomanipulation failure VKn1, VKn2, WPk1 and WtMI), all post-biomanipulation samples were situated in Group A. These 8 clear-water ponds, therefore, were considered as successfully biomanipulated (named ‘situation 1’). For the remaining five ponds, several (for Leyb-a, Leyb-b and MIKI) or all (for NrPd1 and PRB2) post-biomanipulation samples remained situated in Group B, indicating that phytoplankton composition in these ponds during some years after biomanipulation was more similar to the situation before biomanipulation when compared to other succeeded post-biomanipulation situations. These five ponds were considered as ponds where biomanipulation failed (named ‘situation 2’). Based on this cluster analysis, we split up ‘situation 1’ for the successfully biomanipulated ponds (i.e. ponds of which all post-biomanipulation samples were a part of Group A) into their before (1b) and after (1a) biomanipulation conditions. For ponds where biomanipulation failed (i.e. ponds of which some or all post-biomanipulation samples were classified under Group B), this ‘situation 2’ was split up into three conditions, namely pond samples before biomanipulation (2b), samples of those ponds that temporarily turned into clear water during at least 1 year (2a) and finally samples of these ponds after failure i.e. in turbid conditions (2f). There was only a marginal effect of time on the variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, LCL and SV_{max}) when considering the year before biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 2.32, P = 0.058 \)) due to a higher TP and phytoplankton biovolume in 1 out of 13 ponds (PRB1 in 2008). There was no effect of time when considering all ponds just 1 year following biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 1.22, P = 0.319 \)) or all years after biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 0.59, P = 0.910 \)). There was no effect of pike addition on the variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, LCL and SV_{max}) in the years after biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 1.23, P = 0.348 \)). Features of ponds before and after biomanipulation All the ponds studied were rich in nutrients with a mean TP >0.1 mg, before and after biomanipulation. Nutrient levels were generally higher in situations where biomanipulation failed, as TP concentrations were significantly lower in clear-water situations after biomanipulation (1a) when compared to turbid ponds following a failure (2f) (Fig. 2; Table 3). All other TP concentrations were intermediate between those of 1a and 2f. SRP concentrations did not differ significantly between before and after biomanipulation but this is only in cases where biomanipulation was successful (1b and 1a). On the other hand, dissolved nutrients (SRP, NH_4^+ and NO_x) often attained more elevated concentrations after biomanipulation (Fig. 2) and this was significantly higher for SRP in ponds where biomanipulation failed (2f). The five status groups (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a and 2f) showed significant differences in total phytoplankton biovolume, relative cyanobacterial biovolume, Secchi depth, large Cladocera length, %SV_{max} cover and SRP, whereas large Cladocera density was only marginally significant (Table 3, Fig. 2). For NH_4^+ and NO_x concentrations, no significant differences were obtained (Table 3; Fig. 2). The three proxies for phytoplankton biomass (averaged total phytoplankton biovolume, Chl a concentrations and Secchi depth) showed a very similar pattern for the distinguishable situations (Fig. 2; Table 3). Phytoplankton biomass was high in all starting conditions prior to biomanipulation and was comparably high for failed situations of subsequent years (1b, 2b and 2f). Significantly low phytoplankton biomass was measured in situations where biomanipulation was immediately (1a) or temporarily successful (2a). In those situations where biomanipulation temporarily kept a clear-water condition before returning to a turbid state (2a), phytoplankton biovolume also did decrease significantly; however, returned in the following year(s) again to failure (2f) up to a level that was comparable to their origin situation before biomanipulation. Although average relative cyanobacterial biovolume did not differ significantly between most of the situations, it varied considerably in those ponds where biomanipulation failed, namely reaching up to 40% prior to biomanipulation (2b) or when the water shifted to a turbid state again (2f). In temporarily successful conditions (2a), the average relative cyanobacterial biovolume (Fig. 2) could reach up to 20% before turning into failure with higher abundances. In ponds where biomanipulation was successful in maintaining clear-water conditions (1a), the relative cyanobacterial biovolume also was <10% in the period prior to biomanipulation (1b). Determining thresholds of TP, LCL and SVmax needed for successful biomanipulation A first classification tree was performed to differentiate between ponds where biomanipulation failed and ponds where biomanipulation succeeded, based on TP, LCL and SVmax. For this purpose, only data after biomanipulation were used. The classes that were determined for different post-biomanipulation situations were used as a categorical, dependent variable: 1a (after biomanipulation when it was successful, \( N = 31 \)), 2a (after biomanipulation but before failure, \( N = 6 \)) and 2f (when biomanipulation failed, \( N = 11 \)). As such, differences between failure and success situations in the level of TP, LCL or SVmax (added as predictors of the categorical variable) could be identified (Fig. 3). The first split of the resulting tree was based on a TP concentration of 0.300 mg L−1 and separated most of the cases in which biomanipulation was successful (1a) from most of the cases in which biomanipulation failed, both before (2a) and after (2f) failure. 27 out of 30 cases (90%) with an average TP concentration below 0.300 mg L−1 were successfully biomanipulated (1a; Fig. 3; ID = 2). Out of the 18 cases with an average TP concentration of >0.300 mg L−1, 14 cases (78%) are from ponds where biomanipulation failed, before (2a) or after failure (2f; Fig. 3; ID = 3). Thus, a threshold of 0.300 mg L−1 of TP was determined below which biomanipulation is generally successful. When TP >0.300 mg L−1, cases in which biomanipulation has not yet failed (2a) are separated from the cases in which biomanipulation failed (2f) by a larger length (>0.99 mm) of large cladocerans (Fig. 3; ID = 15). Thus, when TP is >0.300 mg L−1, failure of biomanipulation can be prevented as long as cladocerans are sufficiently large (except for one case of ‘2f’ in which LCL is also >0.99 mm). Once LCL decreases to ≤0.99 mm, failure is most likely (Fig. 3; ID = 18). Regarding the % cover of submerged macrophytes that restored after biomanipulation, a threshold of failure in highly eutrophic conditions (TP >0.300 mg L−1) could be considered as 87% of submerged vegetation covering the pond surface (Fig. 3; ID = 16). Next, in order to quantify the difference between failure and success situations in terms of phytoplankton biovolume, a threshold of phytoplankton biovolume was estimated that determines success (1a) or failure (2f). For this purpose, a classification tree was used with the ‘post-biomanipulation status’ (‘1a’, ‘2a’ or ‘2f’) as a response variable and averaged phytoplankton biovolume as a predictor. An almost ‘pure’ split was obtained at 10.8 mm3 L−1 of phytoplankton biovolume, separating all clear-water situations (\( N = 38 \) i.e. ‘1a’: after successful biomanipulation and ‘2a’: before failure) with an average phytoplankton biovolume ≤10.8 mm3 L−1 from all failure situations (2f with \( N = 11 \)) with an average phytoplankton biovolume of >10.8 mm3 L−1 (except Fig. 3 Classification tree for three categories of after biomanipulation situations: 1a—successfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation; 2a, 2f—unsuccessfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation: before and after failure, for one case of 2f with a low phytoplankton biovolume). The obtained threshold of 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\) of phytoplankton biovolume was then used in further analyses to differentiate between clear-water and turbid situations. Based on this threshold, 2 categories were created: categories ‘0’ and ‘1’ for cases in which phytoplankton biovolume was \( \leq \) or \( > \) than the threshold biovolume of 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\), respectively. For all remaining analyses, the phytoplankton data were transformed to ‘0’ or ‘1’ values and used as such instead of the original phytoplankton data. These two categories of phytoplankton biovolume were then used in further analyses. Using all three predictors in the same analysis might blur the effect of some predictors individually on phytoplankton biovolume. Therefore, the classification tree analysis based on these two phytoplankton categories was executed with TP, LCL or SV\(_{\text{max}}\) individually as categorical predictors to study the behaviour of phytoplankton depending on each respectively. Averaged per year TP, averaged large Cladocera length (LCL) and maximum submerged vegetation cover (SV) were used as continuous predictors of biomanipulation category. Discussion On the short term, a clear-water state can be established in ponds after biomanipulation, independent of the level of nutrients. The likelihood of obtaining such a clear-water state depends mostly on the development of sufficiently large cladocerans after biomanipulation, irrespective of the nutrient levels present (Peretyatko et al., 2009). On the longer term, nutrients will play a more important role in determining biomanipulation success. Biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) resided in a clear-water state with low phytoplankton biomass, relatively independent of large cladoceran size or the extent of submerged vegetation cover (except for one case without submerged vegetation Fig. 5 Relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and TP, large Cladocera length (LCL) and maximum submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) when TP \leq 0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (left) or >0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (right) in ponds after biomanipulation. Significant Pearson correlations (\( P < 0.05 \)) are indicated by a line; for the lower two graphs, a dotted line corresponds to all cases with LCL \leq 0.87; a full line corresponds to all cases with LCL >0.87. More details concerning the Pearson correlations are given in Table 4 and where large cladoceran length is <0.83 mm). Above 0.300 mg P L^{-1}, the maintenance of the clear-water state mainly depended on large Cladocera size. As long as sufficiently large cladocerans were present (average length >0.87 mm), phytoplankton biomass remained low, even at high TP concentrations. If, however, in such case, large Cladocera size decreased due to predation by recolonizing fish (De Backer et al., 2012), a shift to the turbid state was unavoidable, except for a few cases in which submerged vegetation cover reached >82% and where a clear-water state was maintained despite the lack of sufficiently large cladocerans. Despite the often high cover of submerged vegetation that was often observed in spring, several ponds still developed a high phytoplankton biomass in summer and, nevertheless, returned to a turbid state. Long-term follow-up of these ponds could clarify if this is only a transitional stage to a permanent turbid state where macrophyte cover will eventually be absent, even in spring. Failure of biomanipulation thus appears to be related mainly to a combination of both elevated nutrient concentrations and the lack of large Cladocera grazing, independently of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. After biomanipulation, all ponds remained in a clear-water state below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP, independent of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. It should, however, be noted that in biomanipulated ponds, in most of the ponds with an average TP concentration <0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\), LCL was >0.87 mm, which could have been the main reason for low phytoplankton biomass below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP. Although the positive effect of large zooplankton grazing and the presence of submerged vegetation is generally well recognized (Van den Berg et al., 1997; Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002), few studies have shown the direct impact of these factors on Chl \(a\)--TP relationships in shallow lakes or ponds. Chl \(a\)--TP relationships were studied in the same 13 biomanipulated ponds, showing that after biomanipulation, for a given TP concentration, the yield of Chl \(a\) was lower in ponds with an extensive submerged vegetation cover and high grazing pressure, compared to the same ponds before biomanipulation (Teissier et al., 2012). This directly shows that other factors than nutrients, such as submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing, can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. An additional difference between the situation before biomanipulation and during the first years after biomanipulation is the presence of large benthivorous fish in the former. Benthivorous fish that resuspend the sediment, thereby increasing suspended solids, nutrients and phytoplankton abundance in the water column, can cause a reduction of transparency and prevent macrophyte recolonization (Roozen et al., 2007). Next to the effect of planktivorous fish removal on zooplankton grazing, removal of benthivorous fish also contributes to an increased sedimentation and an improved transparency after biomanipulation (Meijer et al., 1990). This aspect could also have contributed to the lower Chl \(a\)--TP yield in biomanipulated ponds. As in several ponds, fish recolonized after biomanipulation, large benthivorous fish might eventually be present again in these ponds. We did not observe any significant improvement on large zooplankton density or length in 2010 in any of the ponds in which pike were added. Therefore, it is unlikely that the numbers of pike that survived were sufficient to reduce predation pressure on zooplankton in any pond in 2010. In a similar study on non-biomanipulated ponds (De Backer, 2011), no clear-water state is found when TP is >0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\). Therefore, it also is unlikely that biomanipulated ponds with an average TP concentration above this threshold will remain clear in the future (if biomanipulation did not already fail). Consequently, nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation when average TP concentrations exceed the threshold concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg L\(^{-1}\). It is often suggested that in smaller lakes and ponds, phytoplankton is less influenced by nutrients (Jeppesen et al., 1990) and that factors other than nutrients are more important for phytoplankton control (Søndergaard et al., 2005b; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Our results confirm this, although the threshold levels obtained should be interpreted carefully due to limited number of data and additionally need to be validated with an additional training set using non-biomanipulated ponds. The threshold TP concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg P L\(^{-1}\) below which a clear-water state can be maintained is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1–0.125 mg P L\(^{-1}\) that is often suggested for shallow lakes (Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990). As already mentioned, high submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. Possibly, the strong effect of both factors can be the reason for the lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass on nutrients in ponds, compared to shallow lakes. Similar studies on shallow lakes could demonstrate whether the effect of zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation on the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship would be as strong as it is in the case of the pond systems studied here. Conclusions For biomanipulation of eutrophic ponds, our results suggest that, although a clear-water state can be obtained even when TP concentrations are >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of this clear-water state is insufficient and largely depends on the presence of sufficiently large-sized zooplankton or of a nearly full cover of submerged vegetation. Once they disappear, generally through predation or disturbance by recolonizing fish, a shift to the turbid state is very likely. As fish recolonization is almost inevitable at some point in these peri-urban ponds (or at least difficult to avoid in the near proximity of recreational fishing areas), we suggest that nutrient reduction measures should be undertaken before biomanipulation, in case the average TP concentration is >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\). After 2–4 years following biomanipulation, all biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below this threshold showed promising results, as they remained in a clear-water state during the whole study period. Longer term studies on biomanipulated ponds are necessary to see how the situation in these ponds will evolve. The threshold concentration of 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP above which biomanipulation is likely to fail is considerably higher than similar thresholds known for shallow lakes. Such lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass in the studied biomanipulated ponds could be caused by the strong effect of large zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation cover on phytoplankton biomass in eutrophic ponds. Identification of total phosphate, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size thresholds for success of biomanipulation in peri-urban eutrophic ponds Sylvia De Backer · Samuel Teissier · Ludwig Triest Received: 23 November 2012 / Accepted: 27 October 2013 / Published online: 8 November 2013 © Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2013 Abstract In small shallow lakes and ponds, the clear-water state can generally be maintained at higher nutrient concentrations compared to larger shallow lakes. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for total phosphorus (TP), submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size that determine biomanipulation success in peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationship between transparency and TP is discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Using classification trees, a threshold TP concentration of 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) was determined below which a clear-water state was generally maintained after biomanipulation. When the average TP concentration was >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of the clear-water state largely depended on the presence of sufficiently large zooplankton (>0.87 mm) or a submerged vegetation cover of >82% at some point during the year. This threshold TP concentration is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) which is generally suggested for longer-term success of biomanipulation in shallow lakes. Such threshold nutrient concentration is important when restoring ecological quality in eutrophic small lakes and ponds. Extended follow-up of biomanipulation success in eutrophic ponds could provide more insight into the feasibility of these thresholds on the longer term. Keywords Ponds · Shallow lakes · Eutrophic · Clear-water state · Restoration · Turbid Introduction During the past decades, ecological quality of shallow lakes and ponds has often been degraded as a result of eutrophication due to human activities, causing a transition to a turbid, phytoplankton-dominated state, often associated with severe blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria (Willame et al., 2005; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Nutrient reduction alone as a method to restore such lakes and ponds is often expensive and inefficient, as recovery is often delayed by internal phosphorus loading or biological resistances (Søndergaard et al., 2005a; Jeppesen et al., 2007). Internal loading was found to be a significant part of total P loading during the productive summer period in eutrophic Danish lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2013). Next to nutrient reduction measures, biomanipulation, through complete or partial fish removal, is often performed to improve ecological quality of shallow lakes (Meijer et al., 1994; Lammens, 1999; Jyväsjärvi et al., 2013). In shallow lakes, a short-term response to biomanipulation is generally dependent on the ability of large zooplankton, once released from its predation pressure, to control phytoplankton sufficiently to create a clear-water state, irrespective of the nutrient levels (van Donk et al., 1990; Meijer et al., 1999). In eutrophic ponds, zooplankton grazing was shown to be a first important mechanism for obtaining a clear-water state (Peretyatko et al., 2009). Once a clear-water state is obtained, the increased water transparency could promote the growth of macrophytes (Bakker et al., 2013) which, in turn, could stabilize the clear-water state on the longer term by a series of mechanisms (Van den Berg et al., 1997; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002; Peretyatko et al., 2007a). On the longer term, however, the success of biomanipulation is more speculative and has often been related to elevated nutrient concentrations (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2008; Hobbs et al., 2012). The negative relationship between nutrient loading and water transparency in shallow lakes is generally well recognized. Scheffer et al. (1993) already suggested a stepwise rather than a gradual shift from a macrophyte-dominated to a phytoplankton-dominated state when nutrients are gradually increased. Although the theory of only two alternative states has been nuanced lately, the general idea remains that once a certain threshold nutrient concentration is surpassed, a more dramatic increase in turbidity can occur and a return to a clear-water state will be very difficult (Scheffer & van Nes, 2007; Hobbs et al., 2012). Another important factor influencing biomanipulation success in shallow lakes and ponds is the level of nutrients. It is often suggested that the clear-water state in ponds and small lakes is generally less dependent on nutrients compared to larger shallow lakes (Jeppesen et al., 1990; Søndergaard et al., 2005b). In small shallow lakes and ponds, a lower Chlorophyll \( a \) (Chl \( a \)) yield per unit of nitrogen or phosphorus is generally observed (Søndergaard et al., 2005b). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that ponds (<3 ha) deviated considerably from the overall relationship between water transparency and total phosphorus (TP) in Danish shallow lakes, because both a high transparency and submerged vegetation were still found at higher TP concentrations than for larger lakes. This phenomenon has several possible explanations. Jeppesen et al. (1990) already mentioned that conditions are more favourable for macrophytes in small lakes. Additionally, in smaller lakes and ponds, macrophytes suffer less from wind stress and wind-induced resuspension of the sediment. Also, a reduced depth provides a better light availability for macrophytes at a given water transparency and as such, macrophytes can colonize larger parts of the lake area (Scheffer and van Nes, 2007; Van Geest et al., 2007). Jeppesen et al. (1990) found that for a given shallow lake, transparency was higher when an average submerged vegetation cover of >30% was present, compared to cases with a cover <30%, confirming the positive effect of submerged vegetation on transparency (Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002). Favourable conditions for macrophytes in ponds thus could contribute to an increased transparency, despite high nutrient concentrations. Also, in ponds, some piscivorous fish, such as northern pike (Esox lucius L.), benefit from an abundant vegetation and a higher shore to total area ratio (Grimm, 1989). Winter fish kill due to oxygen depletion could also play a major role, increasing zooplankton grazing during summer, resulting in a more efficient control of phytoplankton (Søndergaard et al., 2005b), which can favour the growth of submerged macrophytes. When biomanipulation is performed on shallow lakes or ponds, it can be useful to determine above which nutrient level a clear-water state can no longer be achieved. When nutrient concentrations (mainly phosphorus) are above a certain threshold, a shift back to the turbid state after biomanipulation might be inevitable and in such cases a nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation is performed. According to Jeppesen et al. (1990), a long-term effect of biomanipulation can only be achieved when the average TP concentration is below 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) in shallow lakes larger than 3 ha. Hosper & Jagtman (1990) came to similar conclusions and suggested 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\) as a threshold for a stable clear-water state after biomanipulation of shallow lakes. In shallow lakes with a TP concentration higher than 0.1 mg L\(^{-1}\), only short-term effects can be expected. We hypothesize that, taking into account that phytoplankton biomass is less affected by nutrients in small lakes and ponds compared to larger shallow lakes, the threshold nutrient level at which both alternative states can exist is higher for ponds than for Table 1 General characteristics and applied restoration measures of the studied ponds

Higher nutrient threshold levels could be an advantage for deciding and attempting a restoration of eutrophic ponds through biomanipulation. Nevertheless, even for ponds, beyond a certain threshold, nutrient levels might be too high to obtain a stable clear-water state after fish removal on the longer term. For management purposes, it is crucial to determine the threshold nutrient concentrations above which biomanipulation will no longer be successful in highly eutrophicated ponds. The main objective of this study was to identify thresholds for key factors (TP concentration, submerged vegetation cover and zooplankton size) that are known to strongly determine the outcome of biomanipulation in a series of peri-urban eutrophic ponds. Additionally, the relationships between transparency and TP, and the obtained thresholds for eutrophic ponds are discussed with regard to similar relationships and thresholds reported for shallow lakes. Materials and methods Study area For this study, 13 ponds, located in the Brussels Capital Region (Belgium), were biomanipulated and monitored during 2004–2010. All ponds are located within the same catchment (Woluwe river catchment) in a close proximity of each other (<10 km) and their connectivity is rather high. All the ponds were man-made and created more than a century ago by the damming of small low-order streams (Marlier, 1971). They are shallow (maximum depth 3 m), flat-bottomed and range in surface area from 0.2 to 6 ha and are mainly fed by small rivulets and ground water seepage. Fish communities in the Brussels Capital Region generally consist of species that are typical for Western European fresh waters, such as common carp (Cyprinus carpio carpio L.), northern pike (Esox lucius L.), perch (Perca fluviatilis L.), roach (Rutilus rutilus L.) and tench (Tinca tinca L.) (De Backer et al., 2010). More detailed characteristics of the studied ponds, including an overview of the applied restoration measures for each pond, are given in Table 1. Restoration measures Biomanipulation was performed in 13 ponds during 2005–2009 by water drawdown and complete fish removal (Table 1). This was generally done in winter or early spring to avoid the presence of numerous juvenile fish which could easily escape or survive in the mud for some time. In most ponds, the water level could be lowered manually, due to their artificial nature. During water drawdown, fishermen removed all or as much fish as possible using fishing nets. More than 500 kg of fish per ha was removed in each pond, confirming that all ponds were overstocked with fish before biomanipulation. A few weeks to several months after fish removal, the ponds were slowly refilled through overflow of neighbouring ponds, groundwater seepage or inflow of small rivulets. In a second phase, northern pike (Esox lucius L.) were added in an attempt to stabilize the clear-water state. Addition of piscivores is often performed in an attempt to control planktivorous fish after biomanipulation, allowing large zooplankton to increase grazing pressure on phytoplankton and, as such, further stabilizes the clear-water state (Lammens, 1999; Ha et al., 2013). The individuals that were added in the studied ponds were larger than the 0+ pike that are generally used for this purpose, as the result of 0+ pike additions is often not just temporary (Søndergaard et al., 1997) or the added pike lack piscivory (Skov et al., 2003). In February 2008, only 1+ pikes were added to 10 biomanipulated ponds (Table 1). In February 2010, various densities of 1+, 2+ and 3+ pike (with a size of 20, 30 and 45 cm, respectively) were added into 7 biomanipulated ponds. Sampling and sample processing Samples were taken 1 year before and 1–5 years after biomanipulation during the warm season (May–September) on 3–5 occasions per year. A detailed overview of all sampling occasions is given in Table 2. Except for very small ponds, all samples were taken from a boat. Secchi depth was measured using a 30-cm-diameter disc. In case the Secchi disc was still visible when reaching the pond bottom, Secchi depth was estimated as the actual pond depth plus 1 m in case the disc was still clearly visible or plus 0.1 m in case it was only partially visible. This approach is similar to the method of Cottenie et al. (2001) and was used to obtain a more realistic Secchi depth when the disc was still visible at the pond bottom. Quantitative phytoplankton, Chl \( a \), main nutrient (TP, soluble reactive phosphorus—SRP, and dissolved inorganic nitrogen i.e. \( \mathrm{NH}_4^+ \) and \( \mathrm{NO}_x \) (NO\(_2^-\) and NO\(_3^-\))) and zooplankton samples were collected on each occasion. Mixed water samples based on 10 random subsamples were taken from each pond (including vegetated parts) with a plastic tube sampler of 4.5 cm diameter and 70 cm length that closes in the lower part. An extension was fixed to the sampler to reach the deeper parts of the ponds when appropriate. In case of deeper ponds (depth >1 m), subsamples were taken alternately from shallower and deeper parts of the pond in order to obtain a sample representative of the whole water column. After stirring the collected water, 500 ml was taken for phytoplankton identification and quantification, 1 l for chemical analyses and 1 l for Chl \( a \) determination. Samples for Chl \( a \) analysis were filtered onto Whatman GF/C filters and stored at −18 °C for a maximum of 7 days before analysis. Pigments were extracted in 90% acetone in the dark for 8 h. Pigment concentrations were measured spectrophotometrically. Nutrient concentrations were measured according to standard methods (APHA-AWWA-WEF, 1995). Phytoplankton samples were fixed in the field with alkaline lugol, sodium thiosulphate and buffered formalin (Sherr & Sherr, 1993) and stored in the dark before identification and enumeration to genus level using inverted microscopy. Biovolumes were calculated using the approximations of cell shapes to simple geometrical forms (Wetzel & Likens, 2000). Total phytoplankton biovolume was mainly used as a proxy for turbidity of the water column. Eight phytoplankton groups were differentiated: Cyanobacteria, Bacillariophyta, Euglenophyta, Chlorophyta, Cryptophyta, Dinophyta, Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta. In order to assess the zooplankton community structure, 10 subsamples of 1 l were collected with the same sampler used for phytoplankton and nutrients. Direct effects of northern pike were not studied, as it was beyond the scope of this paper. However, since the effect of pike additions is mainly to release zooplankton from predation pressure by planktivorous fish (Lammens, 1999), zooplankton density and size can be indicative of the indirect effect of pike additions. Submerged vegetation cover was estimated from a boat during each field visit, visually and by the use of a rake, along transects throughout the whole pond. Macrophytes were identified to species level, except for filamentous algae that were identified to genus level. Statistical data analyses To identify the factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. ‘failure’ or ‘success’), it is essential to define exactly what ‘failure’ is or what can be considered as ‘success’. In terms of phytoplankton biovolume and composition, ‘failure’ of biomanipulation is essentially a return to a situation that is comparable to the phytoplankton composition and biomass before biomanipulation. Therefore, a hierarchical cluster analysis was performed on averaged per year phytoplankton data (division level). All data were log-transformed to obtain normality if needed. By arranging the data into different clusters, we could study how the situation before biomanipulation was related to the situation after biomanipulation for each pond, in each year. The cluster analysis was performed using PC-ORD (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Sørensen distance was used as a dissimilarity measure and the farthest neighbour linkage as group linkage method. One-way clustering was carried out on both samples and phytoplankton groups. For the latter, data were relativised (i.e. each value divided by the maximum value observed per phytoplankton group). This is generally done to avoid separation of more common species into separate groups from rare species (McCune & Mefford, 2006). Based on previous field observations and the nature of the data, we expect a clustering into two main groups, corresponding to clear with low phytoplankton biomass and to turbid with high phytoplankton biomass conditions. Based on the position of each data point within the cluster, successfully biomanipulated ponds (situation 1), situated inside a low phytoplankton biomass group, could be further subdivided into two categories: before (1b) and after (1a) biomanipulation. Ponds where biomanipulation failed (situation 2) were defined as ponds where data of at least 1 year after biomanipulation were situated inside a high phytoplankton biomass group within the cluster. Situation 2 could be further subdivided into three categories: before biomanipulation (2b), after biomanipulation but before failure (2a, situated in the low phytoplankton subcluster) and after biomanipulation when it failed (2f, data with high phytoplankton biovolume). Essentially, the cluster analysis based on phytoplankton data was performed to assign each data point to one of the 5 predefined categories (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a or 2f). Differences between these 5 categories were analyzed further using One-way ANOVA. A Tukey HSD test, modified for unequal sample size, was used as a post hoc comparison test to compare mean values between individual groups. The one-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to investigate the data for normality and the Brown–Forsythe test was used to check for homogeneity of variance. When one of both assumptions was not met (as was the case for SRP and submerged vegetation cover), a non-parametric Kruskal–Wallis test was used to investigate differences between the groups. For all analyses, averaged per year per pond data were used. Three repeated-measures ANOVA were carried out on the considered variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, length of large Cladocera and %SVmax) with time (year) as factor because biomanipulations were not carried out in the same year for every pond. ANOVA was done for the years ‘before biomanipulation’, for the first year following biomanipulation and for all follow-up years after biomanipulation. An additional repeated measure ANOVA was done for the same variables for all ponds in 2010 but using pike addition as a factor in three classes, namely no addition, pikes added in 2008 and pikes added in 2010. Previous research indicated that the impact of total phosphorus concentration (TP), large Cladocera length (LCL) and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) on phytoplankton biovolume in these ponds did not show a linear but a threshold relationship (De Backer, 2011). Therefore, classification trees (Breiman et al., 1984) were used to estimate the thresholds of different environmental factors that determine the outcome of biomanipulation (i.e. phytoplankton biovolume). This type of analysis could allow us to identify threshold values for each predictor (TP, LCL and SV_{max}), below or above which biomanipulation will most likely fail or be successful. All classification tree analyses were performed with Statistica version 8 (Statsoft Inc., Tulsa, OK, USA). The goodness of fit of each split was estimated by the Chi square statistic. Only the best fitting option was shown in the resulting graph. The ‘prune on deviance’ option was used as a stopping rule with a minimum of 10% of the total number of cases needed to allow a subsequent split. For all classification tree analyses, averaged per year per pond values of post-biomanipulation data were used. A series of classification trees was performed to explore the relationships between phytoplankton biovolume and the three predictors (all together or each predictor individually). Since submerged vegetation can affect phytoplankton, phytoplankton can also affect submerged vegetation cover, using average submerged vegetation cover (SV_{av}) as a predictor of phytoplankton biovolume seems irrelevant, as the percentage of cover might be negatively influenced by phytoplankton itself. Use of SV_{max} as a predictor variable of phytoplankton biovolume, rather than SV_{av}, allows us to identify the threshold cover of submerged vegetation above which an increased phytoplankton growth is prevented. Finally, the relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}), LCL and TP concentration was studied using Pearson product-moment correlations. Results Classification of biomanipulated ponds Hierarchical cluster analysis of averaged per year phytoplankton biovolume (per division) of biomanipulated ponds constructed two main groups (Fig. 1). In Group A, as indicated by relative abundances and percentiles of each phytoplankton group, phytoplankton biovolume was generally lower when compared to Group B. For all phytoplankton groups (with the exception of Chrysophyta and Xanthophyta that clustered separately from all other groups), the highest phytoplankton biovolume values were found in pond samples of Group B. All pre-biomanipulation samples aggregated into Group B, except for two cases (VKn1 and WtMl). For 8 ponds (Beml, Dens, PRB1, Sbsk, Fig. 1 Hierarchical cluster analysis based on averaged per year phytoplankton data (2004–2010) for all biomanipulated ponds using Sørensen distance as a dissimilarity measure and the farthest neighbour linkage as group linkage method. Years are indicated by the number before the pond name, for example: 8Beml = Beml in 2008. Asterisks indicate situations before biomanipulation. A colour gradient ranging from white to black was used to colour the matrix based on percentiles (left group of squares) and on relative abundance (right group of squares) per phytoplankton group (vertically). Symbols indicate biomanipulation status: 1b, 1a—successfully biomanipulated ponds before and after biomanipulation; 2b, 2a, 2f—unsuccessfully biomanipulated ponds before biomanipulation, after biomanipulation but before failure, and after biomanipulation failure VKn1, VKn2, WPk1 and WtMI), all post-biomanipulation samples were situated in Group A. These 8 clear-water ponds, therefore, were considered as successfully biomanipulated (named ‘situation 1’). For the remaining five ponds, several (for Leyb-a, Leyb-b and MIKI) or all (for NrPd1 and PRB2) post-biomanipulation samples remained situated in Group B, indicating that phytoplankton composition in these ponds during some years after biomanipulation was more similar to the situation before biomanipulation when compared to other succeeded post-biomanipulation situations. These five ponds were considered as ponds where biomanipulation failed (named ‘situation 2’). Based on this cluster analysis, we split up ‘situation 1’ for the successfully biomanipulated ponds (i.e. ponds of which all post-biomanipulation samples were a part of Group A) into their before (1b) and after (1a) biomanipulation conditions. For ponds where biomanipulation failed (i.e. ponds of which some or all post-biomanipulation samples were classified under Group B), this ‘situation 2’ was split up into three conditions, namely pond samples before biomanipulation (2b), samples of those ponds that temporarily turned into clear water during at least 1 year (2a) and finally samples of these ponds after failure i.e. in turbid conditions (2f). There was only a marginal effect of time on the variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, LCL and SV_{max}) when considering the year before biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 2.32, P = 0.058 \)) due to a higher TP and phytoplankton biovolume in 1 out of 13 ponds (PRB1 in 2008). There was no effect of time when considering all ponds just 1 year following biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 1.22, P = 0.319 \)) or all years after biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 0.59, P = 0.910 \)). There was no effect of pike addition on the variables (mean TP, mean phytoplankton biovolume, LCL and SV_{max}) in the years after biomanipulation (ANOVA, \( F = 1.23, P = 0.348 \)). Features of ponds before and after biomanipulation All the ponds studied were rich in nutrients with a mean TP >0.1 mg, before and after biomanipulation. Nutrient levels were generally higher in situations where biomanipulation failed, as TP concentrations were significantly lower in clear-water situations after biomanipulation (1a) when compared to turbid ponds following a failure (2f) (Fig. 2; Table 3). All other TP concentrations were intermediate between those of 1a and 2f. SRP concentrations did not differ significantly between before and after biomanipulation but this is only in cases where biomanipulation was successful (1b and 1a). On the other hand, dissolved nutrients (SRP, NH_4^+ and NO_x) often attained more elevated concentrations after biomanipulation (Fig. 2) and this was significantly higher for SRP in ponds where biomanipulation failed (2f). The five status groups (1b, 1a, 2b, 2a and 2f) showed significant differences in total phytoplankton biovolume, relative cyanobacterial biovolume, Secchi depth, large Cladocera length, %SV_{max} cover and SRP, whereas large Cladocera density was only marginally significant (Table 3, Fig. 2). For NH_4^+ and NO_x concentrations, no significant differences were obtained (Table 3; Fig. 2). The three proxies for phytoplankton biomass (averaged total phytoplankton biovolume, Chl a concentrations and Secchi depth) showed a very similar pattern for the distinguishable situations (Fig. 2; Table 3). Phytoplankton biomass was high in all starting conditions prior to biomanipulation and was comparably high for failed situations of subsequent years (1b, 2b and 2f). Significantly low phytoplankton biomass was measured in situations where biomanipulation was immediately (1a) or temporarily successful (2a). In those situations where biomanipulation temporarily kept a clear-water condition before returning to a turbid state (2a), phytoplankton biovolume also did decrease significantly; however, returned in the following year(s) again to failure (2f) up to a level that was comparable to their origin situation before biomanipulation. Although average relative cyanobacterial biovolume did not differ significantly between most of the situations, it varied considerably in those ponds where biomanipulation failed, namely reaching up to 40% prior to biomanipulation (2b) or when the water shifted to a turbid state again (2f). In temporarily successful conditions (2a), the average relative cyanobacterial biovolume (Fig. 2) could reach up to 20% before turning into failure with higher abundances. In ponds where biomanipulation was successful in maintaining clear-water conditions (1a), the relative cyanobacterial biovolume also was <10% in the period prior to biomanipulation (1b). Determining thresholds of TP, LCL and SVmax needed for successful biomanipulation A first classification tree was performed to differentiate between ponds where biomanipulation failed and ponds where biomanipulation succeeded, based on TP, LCL and SVmax. For this purpose, only data after biomanipulation were used. The classes that were determined for different post-biomanipulation situations were used as a categorical, dependent variable: 1a (after biomanipulation when it was successful, \( N = 31 \)), 2a (after biomanipulation but before failure, \( N = 6 \)) and 2f (when biomanipulation failed, \( N = 11 \)). As such, differences between failure and success situations in the level of TP, LCL or SVmax (added as predictors of the categorical variable) could be identified (Fig. 3). The first split of the resulting tree was based on a TP concentration of 0.300 mg L−1 and separated most of the cases in which biomanipulation was successful (1a) from most of the cases in which biomanipulation failed, both before (2a) and after (2f) failure. 27 out of 30 cases (90%) with an average TP concentration below 0.300 mg L−1 were successfully biomanipulated (1a; Fig. 3; ID = 2). Out of the 18 cases with an average TP concentration of >0.300 mg L−1, 14 cases (78%) are from ponds where biomanipulation failed, before (2a) or after failure (2f; Fig. 3; ID = 3). Thus, a threshold of 0.300 mg L−1 of TP was determined below which biomanipulation is generally successful. When TP >0.300 mg L−1, cases in which biomanipulation has not yet failed (2a) are separated from the cases in which biomanipulation failed (2f) by a larger length (>0.99 mm) of large cladocerans (Fig. 3; ID = 15). Thus, when TP is >0.300 mg L−1, failure of biomanipulation can be prevented as long as cladocerans are sufficiently large (except for one case of ‘2f’ in which LCL is also >0.99 mm). Once LCL decreases to ≤0.99 mm, failure is most likely (Fig. 3; ID = 18). Regarding the % cover of submerged macrophytes that restored after biomanipulation, a threshold of failure in highly eutrophic conditions (TP >0.300 mg L−1) could be considered as 87% of submerged vegetation covering the pond surface (Fig. 3; ID = 16). Next, in order to quantify the difference between failure and success situations in terms of phytoplankton biovolume, a threshold of phytoplankton biovolume was estimated that determines success (1a) or failure (2f). For this purpose, a classification tree was used with the ‘post-biomanipulation status’ (‘1a’, ‘2a’ or ‘2f’) as a response variable and averaged phytoplankton biovolume as a predictor. An almost ‘pure’ split was obtained at 10.8 mm3 L−1 of phytoplankton biovolume, separating all clear-water situations (\( N = 38 \) i.e. ‘1a’: after successful biomanipulation and ‘2a’: before failure) with an average phytoplankton biovolume ≤10.8 mm3 L−1 from all failure situations (2f with \( N = 11 \)) with an average phytoplankton biovolume of >10.8 mm3 L−1 (except Fig. 3 Classification tree for three categories of after biomanipulation situations: 1a—successfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation; 2a, 2f—unsuccessfully biomanipulated ponds after biomanipulation: before and after failure, for one case of 2f with a low phytoplankton biovolume). The obtained threshold of 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\) of phytoplankton biovolume was then used in further analyses to differentiate between clear-water and turbid situations. Based on this threshold, 2 categories were created: categories ‘0’ and ‘1’ for cases in which phytoplankton biovolume was \( \leq \) or \( > \) than the threshold biovolume of 10.8 mm\(^3\) L\(^{-1}\), respectively. For all remaining analyses, the phytoplankton data were transformed to ‘0’ or ‘1’ values and used as such instead of the original phytoplankton data. These two categories of phytoplankton biovolume were then used in further analyses. Using all three predictors in the same analysis might blur the effect of some predictors individually on phytoplankton biovolume. Therefore, the classification tree analysis based on these two phytoplankton categories was executed with TP, LCL or SV\(_{\text{max}}\) individually as categorical predictors to study the behaviour of phytoplankton depending on each respectively. Discussion On the short term, a clear-water state can be established in ponds after biomanipulation, independent of the level of nutrients. The likelihood of obtaining such a clear-water state depends mostly on the development of sufficiently large cladocerans after biomanipulation, irrespective of the nutrient levels present (Peretyatko et al., 2009). On the longer term, nutrients will play a more important role in determining biomanipulation success. Biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below 0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\) resided in a clear-water state with low phytoplankton biomass, relatively independent of large cladoceran size or the extent of submerged vegetation cover (except for one case without submerged vegetation Fig. 5 Relationship between phytoplankton biovolume and TP, large Cladocera length (LCL) and maximum submerged vegetation cover (SV_{max}) when TP \leq 0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (left) or >0.300\ \mathrm{mg\ P\ L}^{-1} (right) in ponds after biomanipulation. Significant Pearson correlations (\( P < 0.05 \)) are indicated by a line; for the lower two graphs, a dotted line corresponds to all cases with LCL \leq 0.87; a full line corresponds to all cases with LCL >0.87. More details concerning the Pearson correlations are given in Table 4 and where large cladoceran length is <0.83 mm). Above 0.300 mg P L^{-1}, the maintenance of the clear-water state mainly depended on large Cladocera size. As long as sufficiently large cladocerans were present (average length >0.87 mm), phytoplankton biomass remained low, even at high TP concentrations. If, however, in such case, large Cladocera size decreased due to predation by recolonizing fish (De Backer et al., 2012), a shift to the turbid state was unavoidable, except for a few cases in which submerged vegetation cover reached >82% and where a clear-water state was maintained despite the lack of sufficiently large cladocerans. Despite the often high cover of submerged vegetation that was often observed in spring, several ponds still developed a high phytoplankton biomass in summer and, nevertheless, returned to a turbid state. Long-term follow-up of these ponds could clarify if this is only a transitional stage to a permanent turbid state where macrophyte cover will eventually be absent, even in spring. Failure of biomanipulation thus appears to be related mainly to a combination of both elevated nutrient concentrations and the lack of large Cladocera grazing, independently of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. After biomanipulation, all ponds remained in a clear-water state below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP, independent of the extent of the submerged vegetation cover. It should, however, be noted that in biomanipulated ponds, in most of the ponds with an average TP concentration <0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\), LCL was >0.87 mm, which could have been the main reason for low phytoplankton biomass below 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP. Although the positive effect of large zooplankton grazing and the presence of submerged vegetation is generally well recognized (Van den Berg et al., 1997; Scheffer, 1998; van Donk and van de Bund, 2002), few studies have shown the direct impact of these factors on Chl \(a\)--TP relationships in shallow lakes or ponds. Chl \(a\)--TP relationships were studied in the same 13 biomanipulated ponds, showing that after biomanipulation, for a given TP concentration, the yield of Chl \(a\) was lower in ponds with an extensive submerged vegetation cover and high grazing pressure, compared to the same ponds before biomanipulation (Teissier et al., 2012). This directly shows that other factors than nutrients, such as submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing, can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. An additional difference between the situation before biomanipulation and during the first years after biomanipulation is the presence of large benthivorous fish in the former. Benthivorous fish that resuspend the sediment, thereby increasing suspended solids, nutrients and phytoplankton abundance in the water column, can cause a reduction of transparency and prevent macrophyte recolonization (Roozen et al., 2007). Next to the effect of planktivorous fish removal on zooplankton grazing, removal of benthivorous fish also contributes to an increased sedimentation and an improved transparency after biomanipulation (Meijer et al., 1990). This aspect could also have contributed to the lower Chl \(a\)--TP yield in biomanipulated ponds. As in several ponds, fish recolonized after biomanipulation, large benthivorous fish might eventually be present again in these ponds. We did not observe any significant improvement on large zooplankton density or length in 2010 in any of the ponds in which pike were added. Therefore, it is unlikely that the numbers of pike that survived were sufficient to reduce predation pressure on zooplankton in any pond in 2010. In a similar study on non-biomanipulated ponds (De Backer, 2011), no clear-water state is found when TP is >0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\). Therefore, it also is unlikely that biomanipulated ponds with an average TP concentration above this threshold will remain clear in the future (if biomanipulation did not already fail). Consequently, nutrient reduction is recommended before biomanipulation when average TP concentrations exceed the threshold concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg L\(^{-1}\). It is often suggested that in smaller lakes and ponds, phytoplankton is less influenced by nutrients (Jeppesen et al., 1990) and that factors other than nutrients are more important for phytoplankton control (Søndergaard et al., 2005b; Peretyatko et al., 2007b). Our results confirm this, although the threshold levels obtained should be interpreted carefully due to limited number of data and additionally need to be validated with an additional training set using non-biomanipulated ponds. The threshold TP concentration of \( \sim 0.300 \) mg P L\(^{-1}\) below which a clear-water state can be maintained is considerably higher than the threshold of 0.1–0.125 mg P L\(^{-1}\) that is often suggested for shallow lakes (Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990). As already mentioned, high submerged vegetation cover and large zooplankton grazing can considerably influence the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship in eutrophic ponds. Possibly, the strong effect of both factors can be the reason for the lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass on nutrients in ponds, compared to shallow lakes. Similar studies on shallow lakes could demonstrate whether the effect of zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation on the Chl \(a\)--TP relationship would be as strong as it is in the case of the pond systems studied here. Conclusions For biomanipulation of eutrophic ponds, our results suggest that, although a clear-water state can be obtained even when TP concentrations are >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\), the stability of this clear-water state is insufficient and largely depends on the presence of sufficiently large-sized zooplankton or of a nearly full cover of submerged vegetation. Once they disappear, generally through predation or disturbance by recolonizing fish, a shift to the turbid state is very likely. As fish recolonization is almost inevitable at some point in these peri-urban ponds (or at least difficult to avoid in the near proximity of recreational fishing areas), we suggest that nutrient reduction measures should be undertaken before biomanipulation, in case the average TP concentration is >0.300 mg P L\(^{-1}\). After 2–4 years following biomanipulation, all biomanipulated ponds with a TP concentration below this threshold showed promising results, as they remained in a clear-water state during the whole study period. Longer term studies on biomanipulated ponds are necessary to see how the situation in these ponds will evolve. The threshold concentration of 0.300 mg L\(^{-1}\) of TP above which biomanipulation is likely to fail is considerably higher than similar thresholds known for shallow lakes. Such lesser dependence of phytoplankton biomass in the studied biomanipulated ponds could be caused by the strong effect of large zooplankton grazing and submerged vegetation cover on phytoplankton biomass in eutrophic ponds.
