Only parameters that fulfilled the required significance of p < 0.05 are shown, n = 25 forest surrounding the lakes (Fee et al. 1996; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Also, small surface areas were, as expected, statistically linked to shallow water and shallow mixing depth (Strasbaska 1980; Duarte and Kalff 1989; Fee et al. 1996). Our findings that small lakes are generally richer in nutrients, algal biomass, dissolved organic matter and CO$_2$ than large lakes located in the same surroundings, likewise agree well with previous broad-scale comparisons (Søndergaard et al. 2005; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007; Hanson et al. 2007; Nøges 2009). Loading of DOC to lakes has previously been associated with the amount of wetlands in the watershed (Gergel et al. 1999), in particular wetlands with coniferous vegetation (Xenopoulos et al. 2003). The catchments of our study lakes had a small share of wetlands (0–7%), and DOC concentration was better related to the proportion of forest in the catchments, suggesting that regional models have limited applicability in predicting DOC in other geographical areas of the world (Xenopoulos et al. 2003). The strong influence of lake area and forest cover on lake DOC (Fig. 3a, b) supports two explanations. Firstly, hydrological input of DOC and nutrients across the terrestrial-aquatic boundary increases when the drainage ratio (catchment area to lake surface area) is high. Secondly, small lakes possess a long shoreline for input of air-born terrestrial organic matter relative to lake surface area and volume and receive significant amounts of organic matter from litter fall (Gasith and Hasler 1976). The implications of higher DOC for physical and biological processes were firstly, shallower surface mixed layers and reduced light penetration (Snucins and Gunn 2000; Houser 2006) secondly, reduced planktonic production and increased planktonic respiration (Del Giorgio and Peters 1994), and finally, increased ecosystem respiration through mineralization of allochthonous organic carbon (Hanson et al. 2003; Staehr et al. 2010a). The fluorescence index (FI) as derived by McKnight et al. (2001) suggested that not only does the amount of DOC vary notably across the studied lakes, but the quality (or origin) of the DOC varies as well (Fig. 3e, f). In agreement with expectations, we found that small lakes tend to contain more terrestrial material, whereas autochthonous production was a more important DOC source in larger lakes. The low FI in algal rich small lakes (Table 2) show that the terrestrial input of DOC is much higher than the input of DOC from degrading or leaking phytoplankton. Although large lakes do receive allochthonous DOC, its signal is overwhelmed by the production of autochthonous DOC and the greater exposure to photochemical and microbial degradation as a result of longer residence times (Lindell et al. 2000). Regulation of ecosystem metabolism by meta-parameters Previous investigations on the influence of lake morphometry and catchment conditions on pelagic productivity of lakes has provided deviating conclusions. A global comparison of 55 shallow to deep lakes (1–730 m) showed that volumetric estimates of primary production decreased with increasing lake size, but was more strongly influenced by light and nutrient availability (Brylinsky and Mann 1973). In agreement with our findings (Fig. 2), studies in small to large lakes (1–3 × 10^6 ha) by Duarte and Kalff (1989) found declining trophy and phytoplankton biomass with increasing area and mean depth. Work by Fee and co-workers on seven mid-sized to very large pristine lakes (30–10^7 ha), however, showed that lake size was a poor predictor of lake trophy and phytoplankton photosynthesis (Fee et al. 1992, 1996; Guildford et al. 1994). This response was explained by a greater turbulence and probability of nutrient regeneration within the mixed layer in very large lakes and greater upward nutrient flux (N and Si, but not P) across the thermocline. Also, in more recent studies of small lakes (0.02–20 ha), nutrients, algal biomass and CO_2 super saturation decreased with lake size, but no apparent scaling was found for pelagic metabolism (Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). Thus, previous studies on the importance of lake morphometry for primary productivity generally support our findings in small to mid-sized lakes (0.1–1,700 ha). However, relationships were weaker or inconsistent for the full range of lake sizes and relationships also depended on methodology. Earlier conclusions on lake metabolism were all based on bottle incubations, which only provide estimates of pelagic productivity. We used open water diel changes in DO to estimate whole-lake metabolism, which offer more reliable results and integrate pelagic and benthic processes under conditions of full vertical mixing (see more in Staehr et al. 2010b). Forest lakes received less light and were expected to receive less easily accessible dissolved nutrients for phytoplankton production compared to lakes in fertilized agricultural landscapes (Larsen et al. 1994; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2009). We therefore expected high forest cover to be associated with lower nutrient status, phytoplankton biomass and GPP in the lakes (Jackson and Hecky 1980). Nutrient levels were, however, similar for our open and forested lakes, and little differences in GPP were found between lakes of the same size but different forest cover. High inputs of organic material in forest lakes, on the other hand, stimulate growth and metabolism of bacteria and zooplankton and enhance community respiration and constrain phytoplankton production due to greater background shading from colored DOC (Christensen et al. 1996; Jonsson et al. 2001; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007). Brown-colored small lakes in forest catchments were therefore significantly more net heterotrophic, in agreement with previous studies (Del Giorgio et al. 1999; Sand-Jensen and Staehr 2007, 2009). The high perimeter to area ratio for small lakes, coupled with high DOC flux and retention (Curtis and Schindler 1997) elevated carbon mineralization and net efflux of CO_2 to the atmosphere. Influence of benthic processes on whole-lake metabolism With increasing lake area, water depth tends to increase and the relative influence of benthic primary production can be expected to decrease as light becomes more limiting (Kemp et al. 1992). Although the importance of benthic primary producers is expected to be higher in shallow systems, poor light conditions associated with eutrophication may switch the dominance from benthic to pelagic processes (Vadeboncoeur et al. 2003). Our lakes were all placed in medium to high alkaline, nutrient-rich catchments, with relatively poor light conditions for benthic plant growth even in shallow lakes (See Table 1). Except for a few shallow lakes, most of our lakes had little submerged vegetation, and the benthic zone was accordingly dominated by carbon-rich and oxygen demanding sediments (author, pers obs), suggesting dominance of heterotrophic processes in the benthic environment. In support of this, we generally found higher sonde based (~ whole-lake) than bottle based (~ pelagic) respiration rates, especially so in small and shallow lakes (Table 2; Fig. 6b). Also the difference between sonde and bottle based NEP declined with increasing lake depth (Table 2) and area (Fig. 6c), indicating the influence of benthic processes on whole-lake metabolism to decrease with increasing lake size. As shown in Coloso et al. (2011), diel changes in mixing depth and microstratification occurred in all of the lakes that were deep enough to stratify (12 out of 25). For these lakes, metabolic rates based on sonde measurements at shallow depth do not represent whole-lake estimates but rather the upper mixed layer (Coloso et al. 2008). The influence of benthic processes is therefore likely underestimated for our stratified lakes by a degree which depends on the volume of water below the mixed layer depth and the proportion of the lake bottom not being exposed to the upper mixed layer (Staehr et al. 2011), which in turn depends on lake morphometry and variability in mixing depth (Coloso et al. 2011). Applying hypsographic tables for the stratified lakes, we find that 40–90% (mean 57%) of the lake volume and 20–70% (mean 53%) of the lake bottom is represented within the upper mixed layers of our stratified lakes. This suggests that a variable but likely substantial benthic signal is in fact included in our sonde-based estimates of metabolism in these lakes. Removing data from stratified lakes in our analysis (open circles in Fig. 6) would furthermore only weaken and not change relationships between the influence of benthic processes on lake metabolism and lake size. Areal versus volumetric rates In agreement with expectations, the implicit scaling was much weaker for areal than volumetric rates, and only GPP was significantly related to lake area (Table 2). Weak or absent relations to areal rates may derive from the confounding effect of co-variation of lake surface area and water depth. However, light utilization for photosynthesis per unit area is also known to be relatively similar among different plant communities and among systems of different depth (Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998), and shallow lakes can accordingly be viewed as a compressed version of deeper lakes (Brylinsky and Mann 1973; Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998) with little differences in areal rates of productivity. Comparison of lake productivity amongst contrasting lakes can also be obtained by normalizing GPP to phytoplankton biomass, which serves as an index of the growth potential of algae (Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007). For the lakes in this study, chlorophyll specific GPP decreased significantly with increasing TP concentration (r = −0.42, p < 0.05), while it increased with increasing mean light availability (r = 0.47, p < 0.05). These findings suggest that the efficiency of nutrient use of the autotrophic community increases with the degree of nutrient limitation, and that light availability is more important than nutrient availability for variation of primary production. Considering that the mean available irradiance (a function of surface irradiance, light attenuation and mixing depth) was unrelated to lake area and depth (Table 2), it is not surprising that areal rates of GPP, R and NEP show weak dependencies of lake morphometry. Drivers of daily variability in metabolism According to general scaling theory, the chemical and biological components of small aquatic systems are more variable as they are more sensitive to initial conditions, have limited external exchange of material and organisms with surroundings, and low buffering capacity (Kemp et al. 2001). Studies of scaling rules in aquatic ecosystems have furthermore shown that food chain length decreases with reduced lake volume (Post et al. 2000) and these smaller lakes are less species rich, have less interspecies competition, and higher chance of rise and fall of populations. In this study, daily variability of GPP declined with lake area and was highest in small nutrient rich and productive lakes. High productivity in nutrient-rich lakes is known to be associated with high day-to-day variability in GPP, R and NEP, and this is suggested to reflect the dynamic behavior of the lake ecosystem in response to changes in incident irradiance and available irradiance in the mixed surface layers (Staehr and Sand-Jensen 2007). High day-to-day variability in GPP in small lakes may also be impacted by changes of physical processes such as advection and inflow, and a greater influence from littoral metabolism (Vadeboncoeur et al. 2001). High variability of GPP also occurred in the small DOC rich lakes, which is somewhat counter intuitive. High input of DOC may restrict photosynthesis through greater competition for available light (Staehr et al. 2010a) and greater competition for nutrients among autotrophs and heterotrophs (Krause-Jensen and Sand-Jensen 1998) tend to reduce the temporal variability of metabolism. This stabilizing effect of DOC in forested lakes may also be due to the fact that DOC is a relatively time-stable energy source to bacteria and zooplankton (Cole et al. 2002). Thus, our results suggest that the stabilizing effect of DOC on GPP to be less influential than the destabilizing effects of high levels of nutrient, short food-chain length and stronger physical disturbance found in smaller sized lakes. Our findings support the use of metabolic responses in lakes as a common metric that integrates terrestrial impacts on lake ecosystems (Williamson et al. 2008). The strong influence of lake morphometry and catchment conditions suggest that broad-scale comparisons among lakes and evaluation of their responses to human impacts (e.g., eutrophication, deforestation and climate change) need to take into account the strong implicit scaling with the physical boundary conditions. These operate directly through differences in shading, sheltering, physical mixing and indirectly through input of nutrients and organic matter. Long-term stability of cladoceran assemblages in small, shallow, Canadian Shield lakes experiencing marked calcium declines L. E. Mosscrop1 · A. M. Paterson2 · A. M. DeSellas2 · J. Kurek3 · R. Weeber4 · J. P. Smol1 Received: 14 May 2014 / Accepted: 2 July 2015 / Published online: 17 July 2015 © Crown Copyright 2015 Abstract A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats, and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. Furthermore, recent water chemistry monitoring data show that shallow lakes in Ontario are sensitive and have responded significantly to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. Here, we use paleoecological techniques to examine cladoceran assemblages in modern and pre-industrial sediments of 30 shallow lakes to determine the key environmental gradients that influence present-day assemblages, and to assess how assemblage structure has changed since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s). Redundancy analysis of present-day cladoceran assemblages and key environmental variables identified lake surface area and Secchi depth as significant predictors of assemblage composition. In our data set, Secchi depth was not correlated to water clarity but rather to macrophyte cover, suggesting that cladoceran assemblages were highly influenced by habitat structure. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where pelagic cladoceran taxa have changed significantly in relative abundance over time, cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments of shallow lakes did not differ significantly in composition. While the specific reasons for this muted response are unknown, we hypothesize that: (1) littoral taxa may be less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability may vary spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. Keywords Canadian Shield · Calcium · Cladocera · Paleolimnology · Shallow lakes Introduction Long-term declines in calcium (Ca) concentrations have been identified as a significant threat to biological communities in softwater lakes within the Precambrian Shield (Jezierski et al. 2008). In relatively deep lakes, an ominous symptom of this “aquatic osteoporosis” is a decline in the relative abundances of keystone grazers, such as the Ca-sensitive cladoceran Daphnia pulex (Jezierski et al. 2008, 2015), as lake water Ca concentrations near a laboratory-determined threshold of approximately 1.5 mg/L (Ashforth and Yan 2008). These findings were recently confirmed in paleolimnological assessments of softwater, oligotrophic lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (DeSellas et al. 2011; Jezierski et al. 2012a, b), where changes in the composition of sedimentary cladoceran assemblages since pre-industrial times were generally consistent with declining calcium concentrations in relatively deep, thermally-stratified lakes. However, it is apparent that shallow and deeper lakes may respond differently to environmental stressors, because of greater interactions at the sediment–water interface, differences in nutrient cycling and availability, and enhanced coupling of the terrestrial environment with the littoral zone in shallow systems (Scheffer 2004), in addition to differing predation regimes (Wellborn et al. 1996). In shallow lakes, the sediment–water interface typically has a higher influence on water quality, aquatic macrophytes and other biota (Tessier and Woodruff 2002; Scheffer 2004), with greater sediment–water contact resulting in increased sediment re-suspension, turbidity, internal nutrient loading, and possibly planktonic productivity. Furthermore, environmental and substrate conditions within the littoral zone are often complex and highly heterogeneous, resulting in diverse assemblages of macro- and micro-flora and fauna. Despite their prevalence across the Boreal Shield, limnological data for shallow lakes in Ontario, Canada, are sparse relative to deeper lakes. Nevertheless, recent monitoring data from softwater, shallow lakes clearly show that they are sensitive, and have responded chemically to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. For example, the shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region (referred to as the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes) have declined by 26 % in lake water calcium concentrations, on average, since monitoring began in the 1980s (Jezierski et al. 2008). What is currently unknown, however, is whether or not these marked chemical changes have altered biological communities over time, as has been reported for deeper, dimictic lakes in the region. Recent work by Shapiera et al. (2011) has shown that some littoral microcrustacean taxa (i.e., Alona rectangula, Disparalona spp., Pleuroxis truncates, and Scapholebris rammneri) have Ca burdens comparable to Ca-rich daphniids, suggesting that some of the inhabitants of the littoral zone may be less competitive at low Ca concentrations. A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats (Minns et al. 2008), and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. In order to determine the dominant factors influencing cladoceran assemblages in shallow, Canadian Shield lakes, we examine long-term changes in sedimentary cladoceran assemblages in thirty shallow lakes in the Muskoka region of south-central Ontario [a subset of the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes noted in Jezierski et al. (2008)]. These lakes are relatively undisturbed by local watershed impacts (e.g., shoreline development, forestry operations), but are affected by regional stressors, such as climate change, acidification, and declines in lake water calcium levels. Using paleolimnological techniques, we ask: (1) What are the key environmental gradients that influence sedimentary cladoceran assemblages within these shallow lakes? (2) How does water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in these shallow lakes compare to those recorded by DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) in nearby, deeper, thermally-stratified lakes? and (3) How has cladoceran assemblage structure changed in these shallow lakes since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s)? Given the significant changes in water chemistry that have been observed in these shallow lakes over the past few decades (particularly long-term declines in lake Ca concentrations), we expect cladoceran assemblage structure to respond accordingly, as has been observed in nearby, deeper lakes (e.g., Jezierski et al. 2008). Specifically, we anticipate that the relative abundance of littoral taxa requiring higher levels of Ca will be lower in modern lake sediments. Materials and methods Study area and field sampling The thirty study lakes are located within relatively remote, boreal forests of the Canadian Shield in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (Fig. 1; Table 1). The lakes were chosen from a subset of lakes sampled by the Canadian Wildlife Service (CWS) as part of Environment Canada’s Acid Rain program, a biological monitoring program designed to assess the impacts of acidifying deposition on wildlife and their habitats in eastern Canada (McNicol et al. 1996). Lakes were selected for study from the CWS lake set if they were less than 7 m in maximum depth, and within 3 km of an accessible road. The region lies at the southern limit of the Boreal Ecozone, and forest composition ranges from predominantly coniferous to mixed hardwood. Conifer, mixed, and thicket swamps are the dominant peatland types. The lakes and watersheds are underlain by Precambrian granitic bedrock (Jeffries and Snyder 1983). The shallow and acidic soils are low in nutrients, with local deposits of clay, sand and gravel apparent in some of the watersheds (Chapman and Putnam 1984). Regional stressors affecting lakes in the area are derived, in part, from seasonal cottages, recreational activities associated with cottages, and infrastructure required by populations from organized towns and hamlets. However, the majority of the shallow lakes (27 of 30) included in this study do not have residences located within their local catchments. This area has an active forestry industry and it is likely that the majority of the catchments have been logged in the past, and several have active, selective tree-cutting programs that may have contributed to recent declines in lake water Ca concentrations (Watmough et al. 2003). Fig. 1 Map showing the location of the 30 study lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Water chemistry was collected on a regular basis between 1990 and 2009 by CWS, except for Heney Lake, which has been sampled by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment’s Dorset Environmental Science Centre (DESC; www.desc.ca) since 1979. Available water chemistry data include nutrients [total phosphorus (TP), Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN), nitrate + nitrite (NO_3/NO_2), ammonia (NH_3)], dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), major cations and anions [calcium (Ca), potassium (K), sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), sulphate (SO_4), conductivity (cond)], and measures of acidity [pH, Gran alkalinity (Alk)]. TN was calculated as the mass sum of TKN and NO_3/NO_2. Maximum lake depth (Zmax) was measured on site and lake area (ha) was provided by CWS. Secchi depth (cm), surface water temperature, and an estimate of relative macrophyte cover (%; available for 25 of the study lakes) were measured at the time of core collection (July 25 to August 12, 2011). Importantly, Secchi depth estimates were not a direct measure of water clarity in six of the study lakes, where the disc was obscured by dense macrophyte growth (lakes 1204, 1215, 1230, 1331, 1336, 1511). Relative macrophyte coverage (%) was assessed by dividing each lake into sections, estimating % macrophyte coverage within sections, and then averaging these estimates to produce a single, lakewide estimate. Glew (1989) sediment cores were sampled at the deepest point of each of the 30 study lakes in the summer of 2011. The cores were extruded on shore using a Glew (1988) vertical extruder and the top and bottom 2-cm of sediment was sectioned at 0.25-cm intervals. Bottom sediments were not collected from four of the lakes because core lengths were less than 4 cm. Bottom sediments were considered only if the core was longer than 15 cm, as previous dating of sediment cores from lakes in this region has reported the background time period (i.e., pre-1850) to fall between core depths of \( \sim 15 \) and 20 cm (Mills et al. 2009; Moss-crop 2013). Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp. Statistical analyses Shallow lake set Principal components analysis (PCA: correlation matrix) was used to examine the variation in present-day water chemistry across lakes. Prior to statistical analyses, site 1503 was identified as an outlier, both chemically (>95 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of environmental data) and biologically (>90 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of cladoceran assemblage data), and thus removed from subsequent tests of the modern data. The shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region were last sampled by CWS for water chemistry in the autumns of 2007, 2008 or 2009 using a bottle grab sample from the surface waters. Although coring occurred in 2011, the 2007-09 water chemistry data were considered to be representative of present-day conditions, as water chemistry in regional lakes (Zmax: 5.8–38 m) has changed little over the past 3-5 years relative to changes that have occurred over the past three decades (Palmer et al. 2011). Environmental variables, with the exception of Alk, Secchi, pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, TN were either log (area, Zmax, cond, TP, NH3, SO4), square root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration, to stabilize variances in the data. Prior to statistical analyses, the cladoceran data were pre-screened for rare taxa. Cladoceran taxa that did not occur in at least two lakes with a relative abundance of at least 2 % were removed from further statistical analyses. Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) on square-root transformed species data, with detrending by segments, was used to determine the amount of taxa turnover. Because of the short gradient lengths of the first DCA axis of species data (i.e. <2 SD units), linear ordination techniques (PCA and Redundancy Analysis, RDA) were used to: (1) examine the variation in present-day cladoceran assemblages across lakes; and (2) explore the relationships between cladoceran species and environmental data, and to select the minimum set of environmental variables that best described the distribution of species (ter Braak and Šmilauer 2002). For RDA, manual forward selection was used to determine significant (p < 0.05) environmental predictors. Assemblage similarities were calculated using the Bray-Curtis similarity coefficient (Bray and Curtis 1957) on square-root transformed species data, and used to construct a similarity matrix among modern (present-day) and pre-industrial sediment samples. Using this matrix, a one-way analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) was calculated to test for significant differences in cladoceran assemblage composition between modern and pre-industrial sediment samples using the Paleontological Statistics (PAST) program (v2.16; Hammer et al. 2001). Following ANOSIM, dominant cladoceran taxonomic groups (Bosmina spp, Chydoridae, Daphnia, Holopedium glacialis, and Macrothricidae) in pre-industrial (bottom) and modern (top) sediments were compared individually using a Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test with corrected p-values. Comparing water chemistry and cladoceran assemblages in the 30 shallow and 41 deeper lakes DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) studied current conditions and long-term changes in cladoceran assemblages in deeper and generally larger lakes within Muskoka-Haliburton. Because the cladocerans were processed and identified in the same lab using similar techniques, it was possible to compare water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in the surface sediments of the shallow and deeper lakes. Prior to comparison, the following adjustments were made to ensure taxonomic harmonization of Cladocera in the datasets: (1) Eubosmina and Bosmina were combined, because this taxonomic differentiation was not made in the shallow lake set; (2) Daphniids were combined into D. pulex (stout pecten) and D. longispina (uniform, fine pecten) complexes; (3) Sididae were combined; and (4) Macrothricidae were combined. Water chemistry was also simplified in the comparison of shallow and deeper lakes, as there were differences in the variables analysed. We included nutrients (TP, NO3/NO2), DIC, DOC, major cations and anions (Ca, K, Na, Mg, SO4, cond), pH, and lake morphometric variables (Zmax and lake surface area). Untransformed water chemistry variables from the shallow (n = 30) and deep (n = 41) lakes were compared in SigmaStat v3.1 using Mann–Whitney Rank Sum tests. For ordination analyses, environmental variables, with the exception of pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, were either log (x + 1) (area, Zmax, cond, TP, SO4), square-root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration. RDA with manual forward selection was run on the combined dataset (including both shallow and deeper lakes) to explore the relationship between cladoceran taxa and environmental data across the broader predictor gradients. Cladoceran assemblages in the present-day sediments of shallow and deeper lakes were also compared using ANOSIM, and the cladoceran taxa responsible for the observed differences in assemblage composition between the lake sets were identified using the statistical procedure Similarity Percentages (SIMPER; Clarke 1993). Results and discussion Lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario have recorded significant changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, including increases in DOC, declines in Ca concentrations, and declines in TP concentrations (Mallory et al. 1998; Jeziorski et al. 2008; Palmer et al. 2011). For some measures (e.g., Ca), the chemical changes observed in shallow lakes were larger than those recorded in nearby, deeper lakes (Jeziorski et al. 2008). However, despite changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, and significant changes in cladoceran assemblages observed in neighbouring, deeper lakes in south-central Ontario since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), we observed minimal change in cladoceran assemblages in a comparison of modern and pre-industrial sediments of thirty small, shallow lakes. Beginning with an exploration of present-day water chemistry and its relationship to modern cladoceran assemblages, we discuss our findings below, focussing first on the shallow lake dataset, and then combining these data with previously published cladoceran analyses from nearby, deeper lakes. Water chemistry in shallow lakes The first (\( \lambda = 0.36 \)) and second (\( \lambda = 0.21 \)) PCA axes captured 57 % of the variation in the water chemistry data from shallow lakes (Fig. 2). The first axis showed strong positive correlations with pH, Alk, Ca, Mg, specific conductance, and DIC. The second PCA axis was strongly positively correlated with lake surface area (ha), Secchi depth, and SO\(_4\), and showed weaker negative correlations with TP, TN and DOC. As reported in surveys from deeper lakes (Paterson et al. 2001; DeSellas et al. 2008), the first axis likely reflects natural variation in surficial geology, from more acidic sites with shallow soils to sites with thicker deposits of till. This, in turn, regulates the sensitivity of sites to acidic deposition, with PCA axis 1 separating dilute lakes with low buffering capacities (i.e., bottom left quadrant) from lakes with relatively higher ionic concentrations (Fig. 2). As reported in other regional surveys (e.g., Paterson et al. 2001; Kurek et al. 2010b), lake area was negatively correlated with nutrient (TN, TP) and DOC concentrations. In part, this may be related to differences in drainage ratios and lake volumes, with smaller, more productive lakes in the dataset receiving higher areal inputs of nutrients and DOC. Small, shallow lakes also have lower ratios of lake volume/sediment surface area, and thus may experience higher relative inputs of nutrients from lake sediments, particularly during periods of higher productivity (i.e., during the ice-free season) (Søndergaard et al. 2003), or during periods of higher water column stability. Cladocera in the surface sediments of shallow lakes and their relationship to environmental variables In general, fossil cladocerans from both the surface (30 lakes) and pre-industrial (26 lakes) sediments of the shallow study lakes were well preserved and abundant, with the samples dominated by taxa of the families Bosminidae and Chydoridae. However, the uppermost 0–0.25 cm sediment interval had very few remains in most lakes (i.e., the top intervals were sampled conservatively in order to preserve the sediment–water interface, and contained little sediment after freeze drying), and therefore the 0.25–0.5 cm interval was used to represent modern conditions. Forty-five cladoceran taxa were identified in the surface sediments of the 30 shallow lakes, with 25 remaining for statistical analyses after removing rare taxa (Table 2). Bosmina spp. was the dominant taxon in the majority of the lakes, with a mean relative abundance of 42.7 %, and with relative abundances of more than 50 % in 16 of 30 lakes. However, four lakes (1204, 1503, 1506, 1537) had less than 10 % abundance of Bosmina spp., which tends to be a rare occurrence in larger, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008; Kurek et al. 2010b). Forward selection in RDA identified two environmental variables (Secchi depth and lake surface area) that explained significant (p = 0.005) amounts of variation in the cladoceran data (Fig. 3). When constrained to these variables, the first two RDA axes explained 20 % of the variation in the cladoceran species data, although most of the explained variation was loaded onto RDA Axis 1. In the shallow lake dataset, with the exception of a weak relationship with NO3/NO2, Secchi depth was not significantly correlated to any other water chemistry variable, despite showing strong correlations with DOC, colour, and nutrient concentrations in deeper lakes (e.g., Pérez-Fuentetaja et al. 1999). This may be because Secchi depth measurements were obscured by dense macrophyte beds in six lakes, and so was not a true measure of water clarity across the lakes. Thus, as reported in other studies of shallow lakes (e.g., Chambers and Kalff 1985; Cheruvelil and Soranno 2008), Secchi depth serves as a reasonable surrogate for percent macrophyte coverage in our dataset (Fig. 4a), reflecting differences in habitat structure among lakes. Many littoral and benthic Cladocera are influenced by macrophyte density (Tremel et al. 2000; Yarwood-Buchanan 2005; Declerck et al. 2011), and our results confirm that habitat structure is an important predictor of sedimentary cladoceran composition in shallow lakes (<7 m) in south-central Ontario. For example, Bosmina spp. were found generally at higher relative abundances in larger lakes with fewer macrophytes, whereas members of the Fig. 4 Scatterplots showing the relationship between: a percent macrophyte cover and Secchi depth; and PCA Axis 1 scores of sedimentary cladoceran remains and Secchi depth (b), for shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Chydoridae were more prevalent in the smaller, macrophyte-rich lakes (Fig. 3). A comparison of the main direction of variation in the modern cladoceran assemblage (PCA Axis 1 sample scores of the species data) with Secchi depth showed a significant linear relationship, suggesting that Secchi depth, and thus macrophyte cover (Fig. 4a), tracked an important direction of variation in the fossil cladoceran data (Fig. 4b). It is worth noting that our results differ from a recent survey of littoral microcrustacean assemblages from 22 Canadian Shield lakes in south-central Ontario. Walseng et al. (2008) examined the relative importance of acidity and habitat structure as regulators of littoral microcrustacean assemblage composition, as previous studies had reported the importance of both as predictors (e.g., acidity: Walseng et al. 2001; Hann and Turner 2000; e.g., habitat structure: Tremel et al. 2000). In their survey, Walseng et al. (2008) found little difference in assemblage composition in wave-washed sandy habitats versus more protected habitats dominated by floating-leaved macrophytes. Furthermore, lake water pH was found to be strongly correlated with the main direction of variation in the species data (Walseng et al. 2008). The apparent discrepancy in the above studies and our results likely stems from the much narrower chemical gradient examined in our study lakes (e.g., our study, pH 5.4–6.1; Walseng et al. 2008, pH 4.6–6.9), and our more general definition of habitat structure (low to high macrophyte cover). As described below (‘Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes’), we found that water chemistry increased in importance as a predictor of cladoceran assemblage composition when the chemical gradient was broadened, as was the case when we combined our shallow lake data with those from 41 deeper lakes. Similarly, in a survey of cladoceran assemblages from the surface sediments of 50 moderately deep (mean Zmax = 10.6 m) Boreal Shield lakes in northwestern Ontario, water chemistry and lake surface area explained the largest amount of unique variation in the data set (Kurek et al. 2011). Cladoceran assemblages in top–bottom paleolimnological assessments of shallow lakes The cladoceran assemblages recorded in the modern and pre-industrial sediment samples were not significantly different (Fig. 5; ANOSIM, R = 0.01, p = 0.22, n = 26), with Bosmina spp. the dominant taxon in both time periods. Univariate analyses of the dominant taxa showed that only the Macrothricidae, which in these lakes included Acantholeberis curvirostris and Ophryoxus gracilis, were significantly different (i.e., lower in relative abundance in the modern samples) in modern and pre-industrial sediments (p < 0.05). Members of this family are generally considered to be tolerant of lower ionic concentrations and more acidic conditions (Fryer 1980; Walseng et al. 2003) and, as scraper feeders, commonly live in close association with macrophytes (Elmoor-Loureiro 2007). However, these are conditions that describe many of the lakes currently, and so the decrease in Macrothricidae over time cannot easily be explained by these general ecological characteristics. The other most common cladoceran groups, including littoral taxa, did not change significantly from pre-industrial to modern times (p > 0.05), when examined across all lakes. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where significant changes in cladoceran assemblages have been observed since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), species composition in shallow lakes was remarkably stable in a comparison of present-day and pre-industrial sediments. In the deeper lakes, changes were linked to the interactive effects of several environmental stressors, resulting in long-term changes in water chemistry. Specifically, decreases in the relative abundance of pelagic, Daphnia Fig. 5 Comparison of the relative abundances of the dominant cladoceran taxa in modern and pre-industrial sediments from 26 lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada. Modern and pre-industrial cladoceran relative abundances are shown as solid and open bars, respectively spp. that require more Ca were related to declines in lake water Ca concentrations, a finding supported by laboratory evidence (Ashforth and Yan 2008), field data (Cairns 2010), and other paleoecological studies in the Muskoka-Haliburton region (Jeziorski et al. 2008, 2012a, b). Similarly, Shapiera et al. (2011) demonstrated that several littoral microcrustacean taxa differ in their Ca content, as shown for Daphnia spp. (Jeziorski and Yan 2006), suggesting littoral cladoceran composition may be sensitive to changes in Ca levels. However, the lack of change in littoral taxa, despite low lake water Ca concentrations and evidence of declining Ca over time, may indicate that: (1) littoral taxa are less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed, or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability varies spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. The observed differences in the biological response in shallow and deep lakes may also be influenced by other factors, such as a differential response of lakes of varying depths to climatic change. For example, dimictic lakes in south-central Ontario have increased in thermal stability since the 1980s (Palmer et al. 2014), and mixing depths have become shallower because of climate-driven increases in dissolved organic carbon concentrations (Keller 2007). Daphniids, in particular, have been shown to be sensitive to increases in lake water temperatures, and an increased growing season with warming may provide some taxa with an advantage over macroinvertebrate predators, such as Chaoborus (Neill 1981). However, in a recent assessment of long-term trends in zooplankton in Dorset, Ontario lakes (Yan et al. 2008), changes in mean cladoceran body size (the strongest trend) were unrelated to changes in climate indices, and Sweetman et al. (2008) reported no consistent change in planktonic cladoceran communities (bosminids and daphniids) in a top–bottom paleolimnological study of 50 lakes from central Canada, a region that has warmed considerably over the last century. Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes Despite similarities in trends over time (e.g., for Ca, Jeziorski et al. 2008), a comparison of modern water chemistry from shallow and nearby, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008) revealed many significant differences (Fig. 6, Table 3). In general, shallow lakes are smaller, of lower ionic content, and higher in DOC concentrations. The shallow and deeper lakes did not differ significantly in TP concentrations, but NO3/NO2 concentrations were significantly lower in the shallow lakes at the time of sampling (October). Presumably, this was due to its rapid uptake by phytoplankton and periphytic algal communities at the end of the growing season, and because of higher denitrification rates in the more productive shallow lake systems (Søndergaard et al. 2005). Of interest to our study were differences in Ca concentrations, which were significantly lower in the shallow lakes (Fig. 6; Table 3). Although the specific reasons for this difference need to be explored further, lake water Ca concentrations reflect a balance of inputs and losses, with the primary input coming from exchangeable soil sites within the watershed (Houle et al. 2006). It is likely that the smaller, shallow lakes also have smaller catchment areas that are less likely to contain deeper soils, resulting in lower areal export of Ca to surface waters. Furthermore, selective tree-cutting programs in these catchments may have further lowered Ca concentrations through the removal of this Ca pool from the watershed, and its accelerated uptake during forest regrowth (Watmough et al. 2003). Finally, the uptake of calcium by macrophytes in the shallow lakes may also contribute to lower ambient Ca levels, particularly at the end of the growing season, prior to senescence. The combined data set of shallow and deep lakes extended the gradients of all physical and water chemistry variables. As a result, RDA identified lake surface area, maximum depth, Ca, Mg, and SO4 as variables explaining the main direction of variation in the cladoceran assemblage data (Fig. 7). RDA Axis 1 clearly separated the small, shallow lakes from the larger, deeper lakes examined by DeSellas et al. (2008). A closer examination of the data showed that certain pelagic taxa, such as Daphnia (both the D. pulex and D. longispina complexes), were rarely found in the shallow lakes (on average only 2 % relative abundance). Larger Daphnia species, for example, may experience reduced predation pressure in deeper lakes with vertical diel migration (Jeppesen et al. 1997). In support of this hypothesis, the separation of assemblages based on lake depth occurred at approximately 7 m (Fig. 8), a depth which broadly distinguishes dimictic from polymictic lakes in the region, acknowledging variation associated with differences in local topography, lake fetch and DOC concentrations (colour). This finding is consistent with an earlier study from the region (Jeziorski et al. 2012b) that identified 6 metres as an important depth threshold for cladoceran species composition. These results were confirmed by ANOSIM, where cladoceran assemblages recorded in the surface sediments of deeper and shallow lakes differed significantly (ANOSIM, R = 0.59, p = 0.001), with SIMPER analysis showing that nine taxa contributed to \( \sim 80\ \% \) of the dissimilarity between assemblages in deep and shallow lakes (Table 4). Three pelagic taxa (Bosmina spp., D. pulex complex and Daphnia longispina complex) contributed to more than half of the dissimilarity (Table 4), occurring in higher relative abundances in the deeper lakes, again reflecting the clear separation of assemblages based on lake depth and corresponding habitat dominance of either the pelagic or littoral zone (Fig. 8). Conclusions In an examination of cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments from thirty shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, we found modern cladoceran assemblages to be highly influenced by habitat structure. Secchi depth (related to macrophyte cover) and lake area were shown to be important predictors of assemblage composition in lakes <7 m in depth. A top–bottom paleolimnological analyses revealed that cladoceran assemblage structure was relatively stable through time in the shallow lakes, despite significant changes in our water chemistry data over the last few decades. These results suggest that littoral Cladocera are less influenced by changes in water chemistry than pelagic taxa, including significant declines in Ca concentrations, a surprising result given the variation that exists among littoral taxa in Ca content (Shapiera et al. 2011), and evidence of significant biological change having occurred in nearby, deeper lakes. Further analyses on continuous sedimentary records are recommended to confirm these patterns through time, and to obtain additional information on changes in water quality and biological condition in shallow lakes in the region. These analyses should include an examination of other palaeoecological indicators (e.g., diatoms; sedimentary chlorophyll \( a \)) to reconstruct long-term changes in water quality and ecological condition. Long-term stability of cladoceran assemblages in small, shallow, Canadian Shield lakes experiencing marked calcium declines L. E. Mosscrop1 · A. M. Paterson2 · A. M. DeSellas2 · J. Kurek3 · R. Weeber4 · J. P. Smol1 Received: 14 May 2014 / Accepted: 2 July 2015 / Published online: 17 July 2015 © Crown Copyright 2015 Abstract A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats, and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. Furthermore, recent water chemistry monitoring data show that shallow lakes in Ontario are sensitive and have responded significantly to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. Here, we use paleoecological techniques to examine cladoceran assemblages in modern and pre-industrial sediments of 30 shallow lakes to determine the key environmental gradients that influence present-day assemblages, and to assess how assemblage structure has changed since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s). Redundancy analysis of present-day cladoceran assemblages and key environmental variables identified lake surface area and Secchi depth as significant predictors of assemblage composition. In our data set, Secchi depth was not correlated to water clarity but rather to macrophyte cover, suggesting that cladoceran assemblages were highly influenced by habitat structure. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where pelagic cladoceran taxa have changed significantly in relative abundance over time, cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments of shallow lakes did not differ significantly in composition. While the specific reasons for this muted response are unknown, we hypothesize that: (1) littoral taxa may be less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability may vary spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. Keywords Canadian Shield · Calcium · Cladocera · Paleolimnology · Shallow lakes Introduction Long-term declines in calcium (Ca) concentrations have been identified as a significant threat to biological communities in softwater lakes within the Precambrian Shield (Jezierski et al. 2008). In relatively deep lakes, an ominous symptom of this “aquatic osteoporosis” is a decline in the relative abundances of keystone grazers, such as the Ca-sensitive cladoceran Daphnia pulex (Jezierski et al. 2008, 2015), as lake water Ca concentrations near a laboratory-determined threshold of approximately 1.5 mg/L (Ashforth and Yan 2008). These findings were recently confirmed in paleolimnological assessments of softwater, oligotrophic lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (DeSellas et al. 2011; Jezierski et al. 2012a, b), where changes in the composition of sedimentary cladoceran assemblages since pre-industrial times were generally consistent with declining calcium concentrations in relatively deep, thermally-stratified lakes. However, it is apparent that shallow and deeper lakes may respond differently to environmental stressors, because of greater interactions at the sediment–water interface, differences in nutrient cycling and availability, and enhanced coupling of the terrestrial environment with the littoral zone in shallow systems (Scheffer 2004), in addition to differing predation regimes (Wellborn et al. 1996). In shallow lakes, the sediment–water interface typically has a higher influence on water quality, aquatic macrophytes and other biota (Tessier and Woodruff 2002; Scheffer 2004), with greater sediment–water contact resulting in increased sediment re-suspension, turbidity, internal nutrient loading, and possibly planktonic productivity. Furthermore, environmental and substrate conditions within the littoral zone are often complex and highly heterogeneous, resulting in diverse assemblages of macro- and micro-flora and fauna. Despite their prevalence across the Boreal Shield, limnological data for shallow lakes in Ontario, Canada, are sparse relative to deeper lakes. Nevertheless, recent monitoring data from softwater, shallow lakes clearly show that they are sensitive, and have responded chemically to environmental stressors such as acid deposition and lake water calcium decline. For example, the shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region (referred to as the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes) have declined by 26 % in lake water calcium concentrations, on average, since monitoring began in the 1980s (Jezierski et al. 2008). What is currently unknown, however, is whether or not these marked chemical changes have altered biological communities over time, as has been reported for deeper, dimictic lakes in the region. Recent work by Shapiera et al. (2011) has shown that some littoral microcrustacean taxa (i.e., Alona rectangula, Disparalona spp., Pleuroxis truncates, and Scapholebris rammneri) have Ca burdens comparable to Ca-rich daphniids, suggesting that some of the inhabitants of the littoral zone may be less competitive at low Ca concentrations. A greater appreciation of biotic responses to environmental changes is warranted in small, shallow lakes because of the high number of these habitats (Minns et al. 2008), and their unique contributions to regional biodiversity. In order to determine the dominant factors influencing cladoceran assemblages in shallow, Canadian Shield lakes, we examine long-term changes in sedimentary cladoceran assemblages in thirty shallow lakes in the Muskoka region of south-central Ontario [a subset of the “Muskoka (CWS)” lakes noted in Jezierski et al. (2008)]. These lakes are relatively undisturbed by local watershed impacts (e.g., shoreline development, forestry operations), but are affected by regional stressors, such as climate change, acidification, and declines in lake water calcium levels. Using paleolimnological techniques, we ask: (1) What are the key environmental gradients that influence sedimentary cladoceran assemblages within these shallow lakes? (2) How does water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in these shallow lakes compare to those recorded by DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) in nearby, deeper, thermally-stratified lakes? and (3) How has cladoceran assemblage structure changed in these shallow lakes since pre-industrial times (pre-1850s)? Given the significant changes in water chemistry that have been observed in these shallow lakes over the past few decades (particularly long-term declines in lake Ca concentrations), we expect cladoceran assemblage structure to respond accordingly, as has been observed in nearby, deeper lakes (e.g., Jezierski et al. 2008). Specifically, we anticipate that the relative abundance of littoral taxa requiring higher levels of Ca will be lower in modern lake sediments. Materials and methods Study area and field sampling The thirty study lakes are located within relatively remote, boreal forests of the Canadian Shield in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario (Fig. 1; Table 1). The lakes were chosen from a subset of lakes sampled by the Canadian Wildlife Service (CWS) as part of Environment Canada’s Acid Rain program, a biological monitoring program designed to assess the impacts of acidifying deposition on wildlife and their habitats in eastern Canada (McNicol et al. 1996). Lakes were selected for study from the CWS lake set if they were less than 7 m in maximum depth, and within 3 km of an accessible road. The region lies at the southern limit of the Boreal Ecozone, and forest composition ranges from predominantly coniferous to mixed hardwood. Conifer, mixed, and thicket swamps are the dominant peatland types. The lakes and watersheds are underlain by Precambrian granitic bedrock (Jeffries and Snyder 1983). The shallow and acidic soils are low in nutrients, with local deposits of clay, sand and gravel apparent in some of the watersheds (Chapman and Putnam 1984). Regional stressors affecting lakes in the area are derived, in part, from seasonal cottages, recreational activities associated with cottages, and infrastructure required by populations from organized towns and hamlets. However, the majority of the shallow lakes (27 of 30) included in this study do not have residences located within their local catchments. This area has an active forestry industry and it is likely that the majority of the catchments have been logged in the past, and several have active, selective tree-cutting programs that may have contributed to recent declines in lake water Ca concentrations (Watmough et al. 2003). Fig. 1 Map showing the location of the 30 study lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Water chemistry was collected on a regular basis between 1990 and 2009 by CWS, except for Heney Lake, which has been sampled by the Ontario Ministry of the Environment’s Dorset Environmental Science Centre (DESC; www.desc.ca) since 1979. Available water chemistry data include nutrients [total phosphorus (TP), Total Kjeldahl Nitrogen (TKN), nitrate + nitrite (NO_3/NO_2), ammonia (NH_3)], dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), dissolved organic carbon (DOC), major cations and anions [calcium (Ca), potassium (K), sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), sulphate (SO_4), conductivity (cond)], and measures of acidity [pH, Gran alkalinity (Alk)]. TN was calculated as the mass sum of TKN and NO_3/NO_2. Maximum lake depth (Zmax) was measured on site and lake area (ha) was provided by CWS. Secchi depth (cm), surface water temperature, and an estimate of relative macrophyte cover (%; available for 25 of the study lakes) were measured at the time of core collection (July 25 to August 12, 2011). Importantly, Secchi depth estimates were not a direct measure of water clarity in six of the study lakes, where the disc was obscured by dense macrophyte growth (lakes 1204, 1215, 1230, 1331, 1336, 1511). Relative macrophyte coverage (%) was assessed by dividing each lake into sections, estimating % macrophyte coverage within sections, and then averaging these estimates to produce a single, lakewide estimate. Glew (1989) sediment cores were sampled at the deepest point of each of the 30 study lakes in the summer of 2011. The cores were extruded on shore using a Glew (1988) vertical extruder and the top and bottom 2-cm of sediment was sectioned at 0.25-cm intervals. Bottom sediments were not collected from four of the lakes because core lengths were less than 4 cm. Bottom sediments were considered only if the core was longer than 15 cm, as previous dating of sediment cores from lakes in this region has reported the background time period (i.e., pre-1850) to fall between core depths of \( \sim 15 \) and 20 cm (Mills et al. 2009; Moss-crop 2013). Laboratory analyses Replicate microscope slides from the top and bottom samples from each of the 30 lakes were prepared for cladoceran analyses following techniques outlined in Korhola and Rautio (2001). Sediment was deflocculated in a 10 % KOH solution and heated at 80 °C for approximately 30 min. The sediment was then passed through a 37-μm sieve and rinsed with de-ionized water. The residue that was retained on the sieve was transferred to a small vial using de-ionized water. Two to three drops of ethanol were added to prevent fungal growth, and two to three drops of safranin-glycerin solution were added to stain the cladoceran remains. Finally, samples were mixed and 50-μl aliquots were pipetted on to slides, and permanent slides were made using glycerin jelly. Taxonomic identifications of fossil cladocerans followed Szeroczynska and Sarmaja-Korjonen (2007) and Korosi and Smol (2012a, b). Cladoceran remains were identified under 20× or 40× magnification (10× ocular lens) using a Leica DMRB light microscope with bright field optics. Slides were scanned in their entirety to ensure that all identifiable remains were counted. All cladoceran remains (e.g., carapaces, headshields and post-abdominal claws) were tabulated separately for each taxon. The most abundant remain was then used to calculate the number of individuals (Frey 1986). Usually 2–5 slides were sufficient to enumerate 100 individual cladocerans; however, five of the 30 lakes had low cladoceran counts (i.e., under 100 individuals), although above the recommended minimum of 70 individuals (Kurek et al. 2010a). Daphnia were separated into two groups based on postabdominal claw morphology [i.e., D. pulex complex (stout middle pectin) or D. longispina complex (uniform middle pectin); Korosi et al. (2011)]. Bosminids were not separated into individual species (i.e., Eubosmina and Bosmina longirostris) but were grouped as Bosmina spp. Statistical analyses Shallow lake set Principal components analysis (PCA: correlation matrix) was used to examine the variation in present-day water chemistry across lakes. Prior to statistical analyses, site 1503 was identified as an outlier, both chemically (>95 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of environmental data) and biologically (>90 % CI of PCA Axis 1 scores of cladoceran assemblage data), and thus removed from subsequent tests of the modern data. The shallow lakes of the Muskoka-Haliburton region were last sampled by CWS for water chemistry in the autumns of 2007, 2008 or 2009 using a bottle grab sample from the surface waters. Although coring occurred in 2011, the 2007-09 water chemistry data were considered to be representative of present-day conditions, as water chemistry in regional lakes (Zmax: 5.8–38 m) has changed little over the past 3-5 years relative to changes that have occurred over the past three decades (Palmer et al. 2011). Environmental variables, with the exception of Alk, Secchi, pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, TN were either log (area, Zmax, cond, TP, NH3, SO4), square root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration, to stabilize variances in the data. Prior to statistical analyses, the cladoceran data were pre-screened for rare taxa. Cladoceran taxa that did not occur in at least two lakes with a relative abundance of at least 2 % were removed from further statistical analyses. Detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) on square-root transformed species data, with detrending by segments, was used to determine the amount of taxa turnover. Because of the short gradient lengths of the first DCA axis of species data (i.e. <2 SD units), linear ordination techniques (PCA and Redundancy Analysis, RDA) were used to: (1) examine the variation in present-day cladoceran assemblages across lakes; and (2) explore the relationships between cladoceran species and environmental data, and to select the minimum set of environmental variables that best described the distribution of species (ter Braak and Šmilauer 2002). For RDA, manual forward selection was used to determine significant (p < 0.05) environmental predictors. Assemblage similarities were calculated using the Bray-Curtis similarity coefficient (Bray and Curtis 1957) on square-root transformed species data, and used to construct a similarity matrix among modern (present-day) and pre-industrial sediment samples. Using this matrix, a one-way analysis of similarities (ANOSIM) was calculated to test for significant differences in cladoceran assemblage composition between modern and pre-industrial sediment samples using the Paleontological Statistics (PAST) program (v2.16; Hammer et al. 2001). Following ANOSIM, dominant cladoceran taxonomic groups (Bosmina spp, Chydoridae, Daphnia, Holopedium glacialis, and Macrothricidae) in pre-industrial (bottom) and modern (top) sediments were compared individually using a Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test with corrected p-values. Comparing water chemistry and cladoceran assemblages in the 30 shallow and 41 deeper lakes DeSellas et al. (2008, 2011) studied current conditions and long-term changes in cladoceran assemblages in deeper and generally larger lakes within Muskoka-Haliburton. Because the cladocerans were processed and identified in the same lab using similar techniques, it was possible to compare water chemistry and cladoceran assemblage structure in the surface sediments of the shallow and deeper lakes. Prior to comparison, the following adjustments were made to ensure taxonomic harmonization of Cladocera in the datasets: (1) Eubosmina and Bosmina were combined, because this taxonomic differentiation was not made in the shallow lake set; (2) Daphniids were combined into D. pulex (stout pecten) and D. longispina (uniform, fine pecten) complexes; (3) Sididae were combined; and (4) Macrothricidae were combined. Water chemistry was also simplified in the comparison of shallow and deeper lakes, as there were differences in the variables analysed. We included nutrients (TP, NO3/NO2), DIC, DOC, major cations and anions (Ca, K, Na, Mg, SO4, cond), pH, and lake morphometric variables (Zmax and lake surface area). Untransformed water chemistry variables from the shallow (n = 30) and deep (n = 41) lakes were compared in SigmaStat v3.1 using Mann–Whitney Rank Sum tests. For ordination analyses, environmental variables, with the exception of pH, Mg, K, NO3/NO2, were either log (x + 1) (area, Zmax, cond, TP, SO4), square-root (DIC) or ln (x + 1) (Ca, DOC) transformed, where x was the environmental variable under consideration. RDA with manual forward selection was run on the combined dataset (including both shallow and deeper lakes) to explore the relationship between cladoceran taxa and environmental data across the broader predictor gradients. Cladoceran assemblages in the present-day sediments of shallow and deeper lakes were also compared using ANOSIM, and the cladoceran taxa responsible for the observed differences in assemblage composition between the lake sets were identified using the statistical procedure Similarity Percentages (SIMPER; Clarke 1993). Results and discussion Lakes in the Muskoka-Haliburton region of south-central Ontario have recorded significant changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, including increases in DOC, declines in Ca concentrations, and declines in TP concentrations (Mallory et al. 1998; Jeziorski et al. 2008; Palmer et al. 2011). For some measures (e.g., Ca), the chemical changes observed in shallow lakes were larger than those recorded in nearby, deeper lakes (Jeziorski et al. 2008). However, despite changes in water chemistry over the past few decades, and significant changes in cladoceran assemblages observed in neighbouring, deeper lakes in south-central Ontario since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), we observed minimal change in cladoceran assemblages in a comparison of modern and pre-industrial sediments of thirty small, shallow lakes. Beginning with an exploration of present-day water chemistry and its relationship to modern cladoceran assemblages, we discuss our findings below, focussing first on the shallow lake dataset, and then combining these data with previously published cladoceran analyses from nearby, deeper lakes. Water chemistry in shallow lakes The first (\( \lambda = 0.36 \)) and second (\( \lambda = 0.21 \)) PCA axes captured 57 % of the variation in the water chemistry data from shallow lakes (Fig. 2). The first axis showed strong positive correlations with pH, Alk, Ca, Mg, specific conductance, and DIC. The second PCA axis was strongly positively correlated with lake surface area (ha), Secchi depth, and SO\(_4\), and showed weaker negative correlations with TP, TN and DOC. As reported in surveys from deeper lakes (Paterson et al. 2001; DeSellas et al. 2008), the first axis likely reflects natural variation in surficial geology, from more acidic sites with shallow soils to sites with thicker deposits of till. This, in turn, regulates the sensitivity of sites to acidic deposition, with PCA axis 1 separating dilute lakes with low buffering capacities (i.e., bottom left quadrant) from lakes with relatively higher ionic concentrations (Fig. 2). As reported in other regional surveys (e.g., Paterson et al. 2001; Kurek et al. 2010b), lake area was negatively correlated with nutrient (TN, TP) and DOC concentrations. In part, this may be related to differences in drainage ratios and lake volumes, with smaller, more productive lakes in the dataset receiving higher areal inputs of nutrients and DOC. Small, shallow lakes also have lower ratios of lake volume/sediment surface area, and thus may experience higher relative inputs of nutrients from lake sediments, particularly during periods of higher productivity (i.e., during the ice-free season) (Søndergaard et al. 2003), or during periods of higher water column stability. Cladocera in the surface sediments of shallow lakes and their relationship to environmental variables In general, fossil cladocerans from both the surface (30 lakes) and pre-industrial (26 lakes) sediments of the shallow study lakes were well preserved and abundant, with the samples dominated by taxa of the families Bosminidae and Chydoridae. However, the uppermost 0–0.25 cm sediment interval had very few remains in most lakes (i.e., the top intervals were sampled conservatively in order to preserve the sediment–water interface, and contained little sediment after freeze drying), and therefore the 0.25–0.5 cm interval was used to represent modern conditions. Forty-five cladoceran taxa were identified in the surface sediments of the 30 shallow lakes, with 25 remaining for statistical analyses after removing rare taxa (Table 2). Bosmina spp. was the dominant taxon in the majority of the lakes, with a mean relative abundance of 42.7 %, and with relative abundances of more than 50 % in 16 of 30 lakes. However, four lakes (1204, 1503, 1506, 1537) had less than 10 % abundance of Bosmina spp., which tends to be a rare occurrence in larger, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008; Kurek et al. 2010b). Forward selection in RDA identified two environmental variables (Secchi depth and lake surface area) that explained significant (p = 0.005) amounts of variation in the cladoceran data (Fig. 3). When constrained to these variables, the first two RDA axes explained 20 % of the variation in the cladoceran species data, although most of the explained variation was loaded onto RDA Axis 1. In the shallow lake dataset, with the exception of a weak relationship with NO3/NO2, Secchi depth was not significantly correlated to any other water chemistry variable, despite showing strong correlations with DOC, colour, and nutrient concentrations in deeper lakes (e.g., Pérez-Fuentetaja et al. 1999). This may be because Secchi depth measurements were obscured by dense macrophyte beds in six lakes, and so was not a true measure of water clarity across the lakes. Thus, as reported in other studies of shallow lakes (e.g., Chambers and Kalff 1985; Cheruvelil and Soranno 2008), Secchi depth serves as a reasonable surrogate for percent macrophyte coverage in our dataset (Fig. 4a), reflecting differences in habitat structure among lakes. Many littoral and benthic Cladocera are influenced by macrophyte density (Tremel et al. 2000; Yarwood-Buchanan 2005; Declerck et al. 2011), and our results confirm that habitat structure is an important predictor of sedimentary cladoceran composition in shallow lakes (<7 m) in south-central Ontario. For example, Bosmina spp. were found generally at higher relative abundances in larger lakes with fewer macrophytes, whereas members of the Fig. 4 Scatterplots showing the relationship between: a percent macrophyte cover and Secchi depth; and PCA Axis 1 scores of sedimentary cladoceran remains and Secchi depth (b), for shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, Canada Chydoridae were more prevalent in the smaller, macrophyte-rich lakes (Fig. 3). A comparison of the main direction of variation in the modern cladoceran assemblage (PCA Axis 1 sample scores of the species data) with Secchi depth showed a significant linear relationship, suggesting that Secchi depth, and thus macrophyte cover (Fig. 4a), tracked an important direction of variation in the fossil cladoceran data (Fig. 4b). It is worth noting that our results differ from a recent survey of littoral microcrustacean assemblages from 22 Canadian Shield lakes in south-central Ontario. Walseng et al. (2008) examined the relative importance of acidity and habitat structure as regulators of littoral microcrustacean assemblage composition, as previous studies had reported the importance of both as predictors (e.g., acidity: Walseng et al. 2001; Hann and Turner 2000; e.g., habitat structure: Tremel et al. 2000). In their survey, Walseng et al. (2008) found little difference in assemblage composition in wave-washed sandy habitats versus more protected habitats dominated by floating-leaved macrophytes. Furthermore, lake water pH was found to be strongly correlated with the main direction of variation in the species data (Walseng et al. 2008). The apparent discrepancy in the above studies and our results likely stems from the much narrower chemical gradient examined in our study lakes (e.g., our study, pH 5.4–6.1; Walseng et al. 2008, pH 4.6–6.9), and our more general definition of habitat structure (low to high macrophyte cover). As described below (‘Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes’), we found that water chemistry increased in importance as a predictor of cladoceran assemblage composition when the chemical gradient was broadened, as was the case when we combined our shallow lake data with those from 41 deeper lakes. Similarly, in a survey of cladoceran assemblages from the surface sediments of 50 moderately deep (mean Zmax = 10.6 m) Boreal Shield lakes in northwestern Ontario, water chemistry and lake surface area explained the largest amount of unique variation in the data set (Kurek et al. 2011). Cladoceran assemblages in top–bottom paleolimnological assessments of shallow lakes The cladoceran assemblages recorded in the modern and pre-industrial sediment samples were not significantly different (Fig. 5; ANOSIM, R = 0.01, p = 0.22, n = 26), with Bosmina spp. the dominant taxon in both time periods. Univariate analyses of the dominant taxa showed that only the Macrothricidae, which in these lakes included Acantholeberis curvirostris and Ophryoxus gracilis, were significantly different (i.e., lower in relative abundance in the modern samples) in modern and pre-industrial sediments (p < 0.05). Members of this family are generally considered to be tolerant of lower ionic concentrations and more acidic conditions (Fryer 1980; Walseng et al. 2003) and, as scraper feeders, commonly live in close association with macrophytes (Elmoor-Loureiro 2007). However, these are conditions that describe many of the lakes currently, and so the decrease in Macrothricidae over time cannot easily be explained by these general ecological characteristics. The other most common cladoceran groups, including littoral taxa, did not change significantly from pre-industrial to modern times (p > 0.05), when examined across all lakes. In contrast to nearby, deeper lakes, where significant changes in cladoceran assemblages have been observed since pre-industrial times (DeSellas et al. 2011), species composition in shallow lakes was remarkably stable in a comparison of present-day and pre-industrial sediments. In the deeper lakes, changes were linked to the interactive effects of several environmental stressors, resulting in long-term changes in water chemistry. Similarly, Shapiera et al. (2011) demonstrated that several littoral microcrustacean taxa differ in their Ca content, as shown for Daphnia spp. (Jeziorski and Yan 2006), suggesting littoral cladoceran composition may be sensitive to changes in Ca levels. However, the lack of change in littoral taxa, despite low lake water Ca concentrations and evidence of declining Ca over time, may indicate that: (1) littoral taxa are less sensitive to low Ca concentrations, or ecological thresholds have not yet been crossed, or are lower for littoral taxa; (2) calcium availability varies spatially within shallow lakes, and this is not captured in a single measure of water chemistry from the centre of the lake; and/or (3) habitat structure is more important than water chemistry as a predictor of assemblage composition in these study lakes, and this has not changed significantly over time. The observed differences in the biological response in shallow and deep lakes may also be influenced by other factors, such as a differential response of lakes of varying depths to climatic change. For example, dimictic lakes in south-central Ontario have increased in thermal stability since the 1980s (Palmer et al. 2014), and mixing depths have become shallower because of climate-driven increases in dissolved organic carbon concentrations (Keller 2007). Daphniids, in particular, have been shown to be sensitive to increases in lake water temperatures, and an increased growing season with warming may provide some taxa with an advantage over macroinvertebrate predators, such as Chaoborus (Neill 1981). However, in a recent assessment of long-term trends in zooplankton in Dorset, Ontario lakes (Yan et al. 2008), changes in mean cladoceran body size (the strongest trend) were unrelated to changes in climate indices, and Sweetman et al. (2008) reported no consistent change in planktonic cladoceran communities (bosminids and daphniids) in a top–bottom paleolimnological study of 50 lakes from central Canada, a region that has warmed considerably over the last century.
