Comparing water chemistry and Cladocera in shallow and deeper lakes Despite similarities in trends over time (e.g., for Ca, Jeziorski et al. 2008), a comparison of modern water chemistry from shallow and nearby, deeper lakes (DeSellas et al. 2008) revealed many significant differences (Fig. 6, Table 3). In general, shallow lakes are smaller, of lower ionic content, and higher in DOC concentrations. The shallow and deeper lakes did not differ significantly in TP concentrations, but NO3/NO2 concentrations were significantly lower in the shallow lakes at the time of sampling (October). Presumably, this was due to its rapid uptake by phytoplankton and periphytic algal communities at the end of the growing season, and because of higher denitrification rates in the more productive shallow lake systems (Søndergaard et al. 2005). Of interest to our study were differences in Ca concentrations, which were significantly lower in the shallow lakes (Fig. 6; Table 3). Although the specific reasons for this difference need to be explored further, lake water Ca concentrations reflect a balance of inputs and losses, with the primary input coming from exchangeable soil sites within the watershed (Houle et al. 2006). It is likely that the smaller, shallow lakes also have smaller catchment areas that are less likely to contain deeper soils, resulting in lower areal export of Ca to surface waters. Furthermore, selective tree-cutting programs in these catchments may have further lowered Ca concentrations through the removal of this Ca pool from the watershed, and its accelerated uptake during forest regrowth (Watmough et al. 2003). Finally, the uptake of calcium by macrophytes in the shallow lakes may also contribute to lower ambient Ca levels, particularly at the end of the growing season, prior to senescence. The combined data set of shallow and deep lakes extended the gradients of all physical and water chemistry variables. As a result, RDA identified lake surface area, maximum depth, Ca, Mg, and SO4 as variables explaining the main direction of variation in the cladoceran assemblage data (Fig. 7). RDA Axis 1 clearly separated the small, shallow lakes from the larger, deeper lakes examined by DeSellas et al. (2008). A closer examination of the data showed that certain pelagic taxa, such as Daphnia (both the D. pulex and D. longispina complexes), were rarely found in the shallow lakes (on average only 2 % relative abundance). Larger Daphnia species, for example, may experience reduced predation pressure in deeper lakes with vertical diel migration (Jeppesen et al. 1997). In support of this hypothesis, the separation of assemblages based on lake depth occurred at approximately 7 m (Fig. 8), a depth which broadly distinguishes dimictic from polymictic lakes in the region, acknowledging variation associated with differences in local topography, lake fetch and DOC concentrations (colour). This finding is consistent with an earlier study from the region (Jeziorski et al. 2012b) that identified 6 metres as an important depth threshold for cladoceran species composition. These results were confirmed by ANOSIM, where cladoceran assemblages recorded in the surface sediments of deeper and shallow lakes differed significantly (ANOSIM, R = 0.59, p = 0.001), with SIMPER analysis showing that nine taxa contributed to \( \sim 80\ \% \) of the dissimilarity between assemblages in deep and shallow lakes (Table 4). Three pelagic taxa (Bosmina spp., D. pulex complex and Daphnia longispina complex) contributed to more than half of the dissimilarity (Table 4), occurring in higher relative abundances in the deeper lakes, again reflecting the clear separation of assemblages based on lake depth and corresponding habitat dominance of either the pelagic or littoral zone (Fig. 8). Conclusions In an examination of cladoceran assemblages in present-day and pre-industrial sediments from thirty shallow lakes in south-central Ontario, we found modern cladoceran assemblages to be highly influenced by habitat structure. Secchi depth (related to macrophyte cover) and lake area were shown to be important predictors of assemblage composition in lakes <7 m in depth. A top–bottom paleolimnological analyses revealed that cladoceran assemblage structure was relatively stable through time in the shallow lakes, despite significant changes in our water chemistry data over the last few decades. These results suggest that littoral Cladocera are less influenced by changes in water chemistry than pelagic taxa, including significant declines in Ca concentrations, a surprising result given the variation that exists among littoral taxa in Ca content (Shapiera et al. 2011), and evidence of significant biological change having occurred in nearby, deeper lakes. Further analyses on continuous sedimentary records are recommended to confirm these patterns through time, and to obtain additional information on changes in water quality and biological condition in shallow lakes in the region. These analyses should include an examination of other palaeoecological indicators (e.g., diatoms; sedimentary chlorophyll \( a \)) to reconstruct long-term changes in water quality and ecological condition. Measurements of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton using ethanol as extraction solvent By ANNE-METTE JESPERSEN and KIRSTEN CHRISTOFFERSEN With 2 figures and 4 tables in the text Abstract The use of ethanol as extraction solvent for the determination of chlorophyll-a was evaluated on a variety of cultures and natural populations of phytoplankton. Ethanol was equally efficient as methanol in the extraction of chlorophyll-a from cultures or natural populations of phytoplankton. An extraction period of 6 hours in cold ethanol was in most cases sufficient to complete the extraction, but longer extraction time or heating the solvent may be necessary when green algae dominate the plankton. The extraction efficiency decreases 10—25 %, when water reduced the ethanol concentration from 96 % to 83.5 %. Interference from chlorophyll-b in the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol comprised 3—9 % and should be ignored in routine determinations of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton. Introduction Measurement of the chlorophyll-a content in phytoplankton is often used as an index for biomass, which is an important parameter in many ecological studies in aquatic environments. Since Strickland & Parsons published a procedure in 1968 involving extraction in 90 % acetone a large number of methodological changes have been published. Despite the fact that acetone is still commonly used in many marine studies, it is now recognised, that the extraction efficiency is low in the presence of many green and bluegreen algae (Marker 1972, Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Riemann & Ernst 1982), which are commonly found in eutrophic lakes and coastal marine environments. As an alternative, alcoholic extraction solvents have been proposed. Holm-Hansen & Riemann (1978) concluded that methanol was a fast and efficient extraction solvent, but it has been criticized because of its unhealthy characteristics (Nusch & Palme 1980). Ethanol was introduced several years ago (Nusch & Palme 1975), but the extent to which calibrations and evaluations have been carried out is still limited. However, some studies (Moed & Hallegraef 1978, Nusch 1980, Arvola 1981) have demonstrated that the extraction efficiency of ethanol is comparable to that obtained by methanol. The Danish Standardization Council recently has chosen ethanol as the Danish Standard (DS 1985) and this solvent may emerge as the general extraction solvent for both freshwater and marine environments. The aim of this work was to evaluate (1) the extraction efficiency of hot and cold ethanol using a variety of phytoplankton cultures and natural populations, (2) the effect of water content in the solvent, and (3) the interference of chlorophyll-b on the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a. Materials and methods Water samples were collected from 12 different lakes situated in the central part of Jutland and North Zealand (Denmark) from september to december 1983. Phytoplankton primary productivity and the algal composition of the lakes are listed in Table 1. Surface water samples were collected in 5-litre plastic bottles, and subsamples were filtered through Whatman GF/C (47 mm) filters using a vacuum pressure of approximately 20 cm Hg. The filters were sucked dry and stored at −20 °C prior to use. The algae composition was determined from water samples fixed with Lugols iodine. Phytoplankton cultures included Scenedesmus quadricauda (Brebisson), Chlorella vulgaris (Beijerinck), Selenastrum capricornutum (Printz) and Pediastrum duplex (Meyen), grown in a modified Österlind B medium (Steemann Nielsen & Wiium-Andersen 1970), in a 12/12 hours light and dark cycle at 25 °C. Light source was a Phillips LTD 18w/84 and light intensity was 260 \( \mu \)E m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\). The growth conditions of the culture were checked from cell counts using a haemocytometer. Aliquots of cultures in log or stationary phases were filtered through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) at 20 cm Hg and used immediately. Filters containing phytoplankton cultures and natural phytoplankton were extracted in 5 ml of either 96 % ethanol or absolute methanol. In one experiment, ethanol concentrations from 96 % to 83.5 % were used. Table 1. Dominating species and annual phytoplankton primary productivity from the 12 Danish lakes studied.
Lake Dominating algae Productivity g C m−2 year−1 Reference

Arresø Microcystis 700 Hovedstadsrådet 1982

Frederiksborg Slotssø Diatoms 600 Andersen & Jacobsen 1979
In another experiment, 96 % ethanol were heated to 70 °C (in water bath) for 2—6 minutes, otherwise "cold" (20 °C) ethanol were used. Extraction time varied from 6 to 24 hours. All samples were measured spectrophotometrically after refiltering the pigment extract through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) as described in Riemann & Ernst (1982). A Beckmann 26 spectrophotometer was used (1 cm cuvettes). Maximum absorbance in the red region of the spectrum was at 665 nm for chlorophyll-a in absolute methanol and 96 % ethanol. Corrections for turbidity were made by subtracting the absorbance at 750 nm which never exceeded 5 % of the 665 nm measurements. Maximum absorbance for chlorophyll-b was at 650 nm and 652 nm in ethanol and methanol, respectively. The following specific absorption coefficients were applied: chlorophyll-a in ethanol 83.4 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965), in methanol 77.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) cm (Riemann 1978), and chlorophyll-b in ethanol 45.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965). Reproducibility of the chlorophyll measurements was tested using two phytoplankton cultures and one natural phytoplankton population. The coefficient of variation ranged from 1.7 % to 7.8 % (n = 10). Analysis of data were performed using Student t-test and two-factor analysis of variance (P < 0.05). Results and discussion The extraction efficiency of ethanol Two experiments were set up to compare the extraction efficiencies of ethanol and methanol. In the first experiment, four species of green algae and one natural population of phytoplankton were extracted for 6 hours in 96 % ethanol and absolute methanol. In addition, the pigments were extracted in hot and cold ethanol for various times. Except for Scenedesmus and Chlorella in stationary phases, no significant differences were found in the amount of chlorophyll-a extracted from any of the cultures, regardless solvent, heating procedure or length of extraction period (Fig. 1A—D). Furthermore, no significant differences were observed between the methanol, cold and hot ethanol extractions in the natural population of phytoplankton (Fig. 1 E). The chlorophyll-a extracted from Scenedesmus after 6 hours using hot ethanol was 54 % higher than after 6 hours methanol extraction (Fig. 1F). No significant differences were observed after 6 hours using methanol and cold ethanol, but the chlorophyll-a concentration in cold ethanol increased during the extraction period, and after 24 hours the chlorophyll concentration was 46 % higher, compared with the results obtained from methanol extraction. There were no significant differences between the extracted chlorophyll-a concentrations after 18 hours in cold and hot ethanol. Assuming that 6 hours is a sufficient extraction period using methanol (Riemann & Ernst 1982), the results obtained from Chlorella (in log phase), Selenastrum, Pediastrum and the natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø suggested a complete extraction after 6 hours in cold Fig. 1 A—F. Chlorophyll-a (mg l^{-1}) extracted from various algae cultures using absolute methanol for 6 hours or 96% cold and hot ethanol for 6, 12, 18 and 24 hours. Chlorella vulgaris was extracted during both stationary and exponential growth phase, Selenastrum capricornutum, Pediastrum duplex, and Scenedesmus quadricauda during exponential growth phase. The sample after 12 hours extraction using Pediastrum was lost. Black columns represent methanol, white columns cold ethanol, and hatched columns hot ethanol extrations (n = 3). Bars represent standard deviations. ethanol. In contrast, methanol extraction of Scenedesmus was not efficient enough to remove chlorophyll-a from the cells, since hot ethanol gave more chlorophyll-a than the cold solvents. In a similar experiment Nusch (1980) reported that methanol and ethanol were equally efficient and always more efficient than acetone. This is in contradiction to the results reported by Arvola (1981), who found that methanol was superior to ethanol. Riemann & Ernst (1982) demonstrated that methanol extracted more chlorophyll-a from Scenedesmus acutus compared with ethanol extractions. Thus, extraction efficiencies for the various solvents may be species specific. According to our results a 6 hour extraction in cold ethanol, without further treatment, is sufficient to complete the extraction in most cases. When certain green algae are dominating, longer extraction time or heating the solvents may be necessary. In a second experiment, the extraction efficiency of cold ethanol was compared with methanol extraction on natural populations of phytoplankton, to investigate the influence of phytoplankton composition on the extraction efficiency. Based on the first experiment, an 18 hour extraction time was chosen. No significant differences were found between the results obtained from ethanol or methanol extractions (Table 2), except in the samples from Ellesø and Thorsø. In Ellesø, 7% more chlorophyll was extracted with ethanol than with methanol, and in Thorsø the methanol extraction gave 3% more chlorophyll than the ethanol extraction. Table 2. To investigate the influence of temperature on the extraction efficiency, samples from 6 different lakes were heated for 2 to 6 minutes and the results were compared with results obtained from cold ethanol extraction (Table 3). The hot ethanol extractions were generally more efficient than the cold ethanol, but no significant differences were found except from Skanderborg Lillesø, where 10—15 % more chlorophyll was obtained by heating for 2 to 6 minutes, and from Ellesø after 4 minutes. The results from the natural populations of phytoplankton support the conclusion that cold ethanol is an equally efficient extraction solvent as methanol. In the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø, which was totally dominated by *Scenedesmus*, more chlorophyll was obtained by heating the solvent. It is known from the literature that different treatments such as homogenization, ultrasonic treatments and heating (Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Nusch 1980, Riemann & Ernst 1982) optimize the extraction conditions, especially when algae belonging to Chlorophyceae and Cyanophyceae dominate. However, the pigment concentration in the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø was extremely high and this may have reduced the extraction efficiency and furthermore caused an increased amount of water in the solvent, which also result in reduced extraction efficiency (see below). The effect of water content in the extraction solvent The effect of water in the ethanol was tested on *Chlorella, Scenedesmus* and on a natural population of phytoplankton. When distilled water was passed through GF/C filters during the standard procedure, the retained water was 0.139 ml (SD = 0.006; n = 3) on 25 mm GF/C filters, and 0.396 ml (SD = 0.003; n = 3) on 47 mm GF/C filters. This increased water content resulted in a 3—7 % reduction in the ethanol concentration. Based on these data, ethanol concentrations between 83.5 % and 96 % were tested. Fig. 2 A—C. Chlorophyll-a (mg l\(^{-1}\)) extracted from *Chlorella vulgaris*, *Scenedesmus quadricauda* and a natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø, using varying percentages of ethanol (diluted with distilled water). Bars represent standard deviations (n = 3). When the ethanol concentration was reduced from 96% to 83.5%, 10% less chlorophyll was extracted from *Chlorella*, 14% less from the natural population of phytoplankton, and 25% less from *Scenedesmus* (Fig. 2). The relative large reduction in chlorophyll extracted from *Scenedesmus* is probably related to its morphology, which increases the possibility of water adhesion to the cells. Furthermore, the results in Fig. 2 are underestimated, since the true water content on filters containing algae, bacteria, and detritus is higher than those predicted from experiments using distilled water. Previous findings have demonstrated that the extraction efficiencies in methanol (Rie- MANN 1980) and ethanol (NUSCH 1980), were reduced when the water content was increased. Thus, the water content in ethanol extraction should be kept as low as possible. Spectrophotometric interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol Pigment extracts from natural populations of phytoplankton often contain chlorophyll-b and -c, which have absorption maxima close to that of chlorophyll-a in the red region of the spectrum. The interference from chlorophyll-b leads to an overestimation of chlorophyll-a, while the interference of chlorophyll-c in most cases may be ignored, since the absorption maximum of chlorophyll-c is 30—35 nm from the absorption peak of chlorophyll-a (MARKER et al. 1980). To investigate the interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol, the absorption at 665 nm was read at different mixed solutions of the two pigments (Table 4). When chlorophyll-b constituted from 5 % to 100 % of the chlorophyll-a (by weight), the absorbance at 665 nm increased from 1.5 % to 35.1 %. In similar experiments using methanol RIEMANN (1978) found an 1.4 % to 44.6 % overestimation, when chlorophyll-b constituted 5 % to 90 % of the chlorophyll-a content. This interference is higher than for ethanol, because the maximum absorbance of chlorophyll-b is closer to the peak of chlorophyll-a in methanol. LOFTUS & CARPENTER (1971) reported, that chlorophyll-b rarely constituted more than 10—20 % of the chlorophyll-a content in natural populations of phytoplankton, dominated by green algae or other algae containing chlorophyll-b. Only in one sample they found 40 % chlorophyll-b. RIEMANN & ERNST (1982) investigated six green algae and found, after optimal extraction, that chlorophyll-b constituted 13—33 % of the chlorophyll-a in methanol extracts. Table 4. Assuming that chlorophyll-b will constitute at most 30% of chlorophyll-a in natural populations of phytoplankton, the maximum interference of chlorophyll-b leads to an 9.3% overestimation of chlorophyll-a in ethanol. To correct for this interference involves either 1) a detailed spectrophotometric determination at different wavelengths (Strickland & Parsons 1972), or 2) a chromatographic separation of the chlorophylls. The first method is not recommended (Marker et al. 1980) because chlorophyll-a thereby is overestimated and a chromatographic separation is still not applicable in routine measurements. As a consequence, it is suggested that interference from chlorophyll-b in ethanol extracts may be ignored when chlorophyll-a is determined from phytoplankton. Measurements of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton using ethanol as extraction solvent By ANNE-METTE JESPERSEN and KIRSTEN CHRISTOFFERSEN With 2 figures and 4 tables in the text Abstract The use of ethanol as extraction solvent for the determination of chlorophyll-a was evaluated on a variety of cultures and natural populations of phytoplankton. Ethanol was equally efficient as methanol in the extraction of chlorophyll-a from cultures or natural populations of phytoplankton. An extraction period of 6 hours in cold ethanol was in most cases sufficient to complete the extraction, but longer extraction time or heating the solvent may be necessary when green algae dominate the plankton. The extraction efficiency decreases 10—25 %, when water reduced the ethanol concentration from 96 % to 83.5 %. Interference from chlorophyll-b in the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol comprised 3—9 % and should be ignored in routine determinations of chlorophyll-a from phytoplankton. Introduction Measurement of the chlorophyll-a content in phytoplankton is often used as an index for biomass, which is an important parameter in many ecological studies in aquatic environments. Since Strickland & Parsons published a procedure in 1968 involving extraction in 90 % acetone a large number of methodological changes have been published. Despite the fact that acetone is still commonly used in many marine studies, it is now recognised, that the extraction efficiency is low in the presence of many green and bluegreen algae (Marker 1972, Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Riemann & Ernst 1982), which are commonly found in eutrophic lakes and coastal marine environments. As an alternative, alcoholic extraction solvents have been proposed. Holm-Hansen & Riemann (1978) concluded that methanol was a fast and efficient extraction solvent, but it has been criticized because of its unhealthy characteristics (Nusch & Palme 1980). Ethanol was introduced several years ago (Nusch & Palme 1975), but the extent to which calibrations and evaluations have been carried out is still limited. However, some studies (Moed & Hallegraef 1978, Nusch 1980, Arvola 1981) have demonstrated that the extraction efficiency of ethanol is comparable to that obtained by methanol. The Danish Standardization Council recently has chosen ethanol as the Danish Standard (DS 1985) and this solvent may emerge as the general extraction solvent for both freshwater and marine environments. The aim of this work was to evaluate (1) the extraction efficiency of hot and cold ethanol using a variety of phytoplankton cultures and natural populations, (2) the effect of water content in the solvent, and (3) the interference of chlorophyll-b on the spectrophotometric determination of chlorophyll-a. Materials and methods Water samples were collected from 12 different lakes situated in the central part of Jutland and North Zealand (Denmark) from september to december 1983. Phytoplankton primary productivity and the algal composition of the lakes are listed in Table 1. Surface water samples were collected in 5-litre plastic bottles, and subsamples were filtered through Whatman GF/C (47 mm) filters using a vacuum pressure of approximately 20 cm Hg. The filters were sucked dry and stored at −20 °C prior to use. The algae composition was determined from water samples fixed with Lugols iodine. Phytoplankton cultures included Scenedesmus quadricauda (Brebisson), Chlorella vulgaris (Beijerinck), Selenastrum capricornutum (Printz) and Pediastrum duplex (Meyen), grown in a modified Österlind B medium (Steemann Nielsen & Wiium-Andersen 1970), in a 12/12 hours light and dark cycle at 25 °C. Light source was a Phillips LTD 18w/84 and light intensity was 260 \( \mu \)E m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\). The growth conditions of the culture were checked from cell counts using a haemocytometer. Aliquots of cultures in log or stationary phases were filtered through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) at 20 cm Hg and used immediately. Filters containing phytoplankton cultures and natural phytoplankton were extracted in 5 ml of either 96 % ethanol or absolute methanol. In one experiment, ethanol concentrations from 96 % to 83.5 % were used. Table 1. Dominating species and annual phytoplankton primary productivity from the 12 Danish lakes studied.

In another experiment, 96 % ethanol were heated to 70 °C (in water bath) for 2—6 minutes, otherwise "cold" (20 °C) ethanol were used. Extraction time varied from 6 to 24 hours. All samples were measured spectrophotometrically after refiltering the pigment extract through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) as described in Riemann & Ernst (1982). A Beckmann 26 spectrophotometer was used (1 cm cuvettes). Maximum absorbance in the red region of the spectrum was at 665 nm for chlorophyll-a in absolute methanol and 96 % ethanol. Corrections for turbidity were made by subtracting the absorbance at 750 nm which never exceeded 5 % of the 665 nm measurements. Maximum absorbance for chlorophyll-b was at 650 nm and 652 nm in ethanol and methanol, respectively. The following specific absorption coefficients were applied: chlorophyll-a in ethanol 83.4 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965), in methanol 77.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) cm (Riemann 1978), and chlorophyll-b in ethanol 45.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965). Reproducibility of the chlorophyll measurements was tested using two phytoplankton cultures and one natural phytoplankton population. The coefficient of variation ranged from 1.7 % to 7.8 % (n = 10). Analysis of data were performed using Student t-test and two-factor analysis of variance (P < 0.05). Results and discussion The extraction efficiency of ethanol Two experiments were set up to compare the extraction efficiencies of ethanol and methanol. In the first experiment, four species of green algae and one natural population of phytoplankton were extracted for 6 hours in 96 % ethanol and absolute methanol. In addition, the pigments were extracted in hot and cold ethanol for various times. Except for Scenedesmus and Chlorella in stationary phases, no significant differences were found in the amount of chlorophyll-a extracted from any of the cultures, regardless solvent, heating procedure or length of extraction period (Fig. 1A—D). Furthermore, no significant differences were observed between the methanol, cold and hot ethanol extractions in the natural population of phytoplankton (Fig. 1 E). The chlorophyll-a extracted from Scenedesmus after 6 hours using hot ethanol was 54 % higher than after 6 hours methanol extraction (Fig. 1F). No significant differences were observed after 6 hours using methanol and cold ethanol, but the chlorophyll-a concentration in cold ethanol increased during the extraction period, and after 24 hours the chlorophyll concentration was 46 % higher, compared with the results obtained from methanol extraction. There were no significant differences between the extracted chlorophyll-a concentrations after 18 hours in cold and hot ethanol. Assuming that 6 hours is a sufficient extraction period using methanol (Riemann & Ernst 1982), the results obtained from Chlorella (in log phase), Selenastrum, Pediastrum and the natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø suggested a complete extraction after 6 hours in cold Fig. 1 A—F. Chlorophyll-a (mg l^{-1}) extracted from various algae cultures using absolute methanol for 6 hours or 96% cold and hot ethanol for 6, 12, 18 and 24 hours. Chlorella vulgaris was extracted during both stationary and exponential growth phase, Selenastrum capricornutum, Pediastrum duplex, and Scenedesmus quadricauda during exponential growth phase. The sample after 12 hours extraction using Pediastrum was lost. Black columns represent methanol, white columns cold ethanol, and hatched columns hot ethanol extrations (n = 3). Bars represent standard deviations. ethanol. In contrast, methanol extraction of Scenedesmus was not efficient enough to remove chlorophyll-a from the cells, since hot ethanol gave more chlorophyll-a than the cold solvents. In a similar experiment Nusch (1980) reported that methanol and ethanol were equally efficient and always more efficient than acetone. This is in contradiction to the results reported by Arvola (1981), who found that methanol was superior to ethanol. Riemann & Ernst (1982) demonstrated that methanol extracted more chlorophyll-a from Scenedesmus acutus compared with ethanol extractions. Thus, extraction efficiencies for the various solvents may be species specific. According to our results a 6 hour extraction in cold ethanol, without further treatment, is sufficient to complete the extraction in most cases. When certain green algae are dominating, longer extraction time or heating the solvents may be necessary. In a second experiment, the extraction efficiency of cold ethanol was compared with methanol extraction on natural populations of phytoplankton, to investigate the influence of phytoplankton composition on the extraction efficiency. Based on the first experiment, an 18 hour extraction time was chosen. No significant differences were found between the results obtained from ethanol or methanol extractions (Table 2), except in the samples from Ellesø and Thorsø. In Ellesø, 7% more chlorophyll was extracted with ethanol than with methanol, and in Thorsø the methanol extraction gave 3% more chlorophyll than the ethanol extraction. Table 2. To investigate the influence of temperature on the extraction efficiency, samples from 6 different lakes were heated for 2 to 6 minutes and the results were compared with results obtained from cold ethanol extraction (Table 3). The hot ethanol extractions were generally more efficient than the cold ethanol, but no significant differences were found except from Skanderborg Lillesø, where 10—15 % more chlorophyll was obtained by heating for 2 to 6 minutes, and from Ellesø after 4 minutes. The results from the natural populations of phytoplankton support the conclusion that cold ethanol is an equally efficient extraction solvent as methanol. In the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø, which was totally dominated by *Scenedesmus*, more chlorophyll was obtained by heating the solvent. It is known from the literature that different treatments such as homogenization, ultrasonic treatments and heating (Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Nusch 1980, Riemann & Ernst 1982) optimize the extraction conditions, especially when algae belonging to Chlorophyceae and Cyanophyceae dominate. However, the pigment concentration in the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø was extremely high and this may have reduced the extraction efficiency and furthermore caused an increased amount of water in the solvent, which also result in reduced extraction efficiency (see below). The effect of water content in the extraction solvent The effect of water in the ethanol was tested on *Chlorella, Scenedesmus* and on a natural population of phytoplankton. When distilled water was passed through GF/C filters during the standard procedure, the retained water was 0.139 ml (SD = 0.006; n = 3) on 25 mm GF/C filters, and 0.396 ml (SD = 0.003; n = 3) on 47 mm GF/C filters. This increased water content resulted in a 3—7 % reduction in the ethanol concentration. Based on these data, ethanol concentrations between 83.5 % and 96 % were tested. Fig. 2 A—C. Chlorophyll-a (mg l\(^{-1}\)) extracted from *Chlorella vulgaris*, *Scenedesmus quadricauda* and a natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø, using varying percentages of ethanol (diluted with distilled water). Bars represent standard deviations (n = 3). When the ethanol concentration was reduced from 96% to 83.5%, 10% less chlorophyll was extracted from *Chlorella*, 14% less from the natural population of phytoplankton, and 25% less from *Scenedesmus* (Fig. 2). The relative large reduction in chlorophyll extracted from *Scenedesmus* is probably related to its morphology, which increases the possibility of water adhesion to the cells. Furthermore, the results in Fig. 2 are underestimated, since the true water content on filters containing algae, bacteria, and detritus is higher than those predicted from experiments using distilled water. Previous findings have demonstrated that the extraction efficiencies in methanol (Rie- MANN 1980) and ethanol (NUSCH 1980), were reduced when the water content was increased. Thus, the water content in ethanol extraction should be kept as low as possible. Spectrophotometric interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol Pigment extracts from natural populations of phytoplankton often contain chlorophyll-b and -c, which have absorption maxima close to that of chlorophyll-a in the red region of the spectrum. The interference from chlorophyll-b leads to an overestimation of chlorophyll-a, while the interference of chlorophyll-c in most cases may be ignored, since the absorption maximum of chlorophyll-c is 30—35 nm from the absorption peak of chlorophyll-a (MARKER et al. 1980). To investigate the interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol, the absorption at 665 nm was read at different mixed solutions of the two pigments (Table 4). When chlorophyll-b constituted from 5 % to 100 % of the chlorophyll-a (by weight), the absorbance at 665 nm increased from 1.5 % to 35.1 %. In similar experiments using methanol RIEMANN (1978) found an 1.4 % to 44.6 % overestimation, when chlorophyll-b constituted 5 % to 90 % of the chlorophyll-a content. This interference is higher than for ethanol, because the maximum absorbance of chlorophyll-b is closer to the peak of chlorophyll-a in methanol. LOFTUS & CARPENTER (1971) reported, that chlorophyll-b rarely constituted more than 10—20 % of the chlorophyll-a content in natural populations of phytoplankton, dominated by green algae or other algae containing chlorophyll-b. Only in one sample they found 40 % chlorophyll-b. RIEMANN & ERNST (1982) investigated six green algae and found, after optimal extraction, that chlorophyll-b constituted 13—33 % of the chlorophyll-a in methanol extracts. Table 4. Assuming that chlorophyll-b will constitute at most 30% of chlorophyll-a in natural populations of phytoplankton, the maximum interference of chlorophyll-b leads to an 9.3% overestimation of chlorophyll-a in ethanol. To correct for this interference involves either 1) a detailed spectrophotometric determination at different wavelengths (Strickland & Parsons 1972), or 2) a chromatographic separation of the chlorophylls. The first method is not recommended (Marker et al. 1980) because chlorophyll-a thereby is overestimated and a chromatographic separation is still not applicable in routine measurements. As a consequence, it is suggested that interference from chlorophyll-b in ethanol extracts may be ignored when chlorophyll-a is determined from phytoplankton. Measuring the trophic status of ponds: Relationships between summer rate of periphytic net primary productivity and water physico-chemistry Lionel Sager* Laboratory of Ecology and Aquatic Biology (LEBA), University of Geneva, Chemin des Clochettes 18, CH-1206 Geneva, Switzerland ARTICLE INFO Article history: Received 2 July 2008 Received in revised form 22 December 2008 Accepted 23 December 2008 Published online 3 January 2009 Keywords: AFDW Alternative stable states Assessment Eutrophication Nitrogen Phosphorus Submerged macrophytes ABSTRACT The monitoring of the water quality is a major environmental concern and specific method of assessment needs to be addressed for ponds. Among threats on freshwater, eutrophication remains an important and widespread problem. To assess if the trophic state of ponds can be significantly predicted by physico-chemical surrogates, parallel measurements of water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) were performed on a set of nine lowland Swiss ponds representing the whole spectrum of trophic states. The developed methods to measure periphytic NPP on artificial substrates give similar values between the pseudo-replicates and are functional for ponds. The winter concentration of total nitrogen (TN) in the water is a significant predictor of the average summer rates of NPP while in submerged macrophyte beds total phosphorus (TP) is a better predictor. Rates of NPP measured in open water were most often higher and water transparency lower than in macrophyte beds, highlighting the positive influence of macrophytes on water quality and a possible co-occurrence in a pond of contrasting conditions when submerged species are present. This emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds to improve the water quality. 1. Introduction Monitoring and quality improvement of surface freshwater are major environmental concerns worldwide (Johnson et al., 2001). In European countries, the Water Framework Directive (WFD, Council of the European Communities, 2000) provides clear objectives to obtain at least a good qualitative and quantitative status of all waters in Europe by 2015. To attain these goals, all the aquatic compartments have to be considered and assessed with specific methods to classify them into high, good, moderate, bad and poor ecological quality. As ponds are recognized as distinct aquatic compartments from rivers and lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2005a) and react in a different manner to impacts, specific methods are required for their assessment; some are currently being developed (Menetrey et al., 2005) or are already operational (Biggs et al., 2000; Boix et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2005), review in Indermuehle et al. (2005). Moreover, recent works have established ponds as being very significant components of the freshwater resource, in terms of their contribution to both local and regional biodiversity (Murphy, 2002; Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003), confirming their importance to the concept of integrated catchments management. Practically, however, ponds are neglected in the implementation of the WFD as many countries have set a lower size limit of 50 ha to apply the directive on water bodies (Nicolet et al., 2007). Among the current threat on freshwater, eutrophication through diffuse pollution from agriculture (Havens et al., 2001) remain as an important, widespread and even growing problem for freshwater and coastal oceans (Carpenter et al., 1999; Bronmark and Hansson, 2002; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003; Craft et al., 2007). Accelerated rates of eutrophication linked to human activities have generated much interest during the last decades and many studies have been carried out, particularly in large lakes and rivers. Notably, an international research program of OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) associated ranges of quantifiable environmental parameters to each of 5 classes of trophic state (ultra-oligotrophic, oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic, hypertrophic) that were previously attributed with an expert system to 100 northern temperate lakes. To implement the WFD in Danish lakes, Sondergaard et al. (2005b) proposed a pre-classification of lakes based on their trophic status given by the concentration of total phosphorus (TP), in order to identify biological indicators of eutrophication. Focusing on the assessment of eutrophication, one must take into account that high nutrient concentration in small lakes or ponds do not necessarily bring a high phytoplankton biomass and a turbid water as observed in larger lakes (Sondergaard et al., 2005a), because other controlling factors are implicated including a possible scale effect (Schindler, 1998). In this way, the ranges of concentrations of nutrients in the water assigned by OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) to each trophic class for lakes are not necessarily valid for ponds. Eutrophication is historically described as a regular increase of the phytoplankton primary productivity following larger inputs of inorganic nutrients (Naumann, 1927). This emphasis that any classification of water bodies in trophic state is an artificial reading of a continuous biological process. This continuity in eutrophication process complicates the establishment of well-defined limits between classes and furthermore the assignment of biological indicators values to a trophic state (Sondergaard et al., 2005b). As already pointed out by Rodhe (1969), the trophic state is expressed by a rate and must be determined by measuring primary production. Thus measuring rates of primary production in ponds varying in water concentration of major nutrients would permit to determine which parameters are best correlated and best predictors of the measured production and so eutrophication, even if these parameters are not the only factors determining the primary productivity as early underlined by Naumann (1932). Additionally, eutrophication is coupled at least in lakes by a shift from the dominance of benthic to pelagic production (Sand-Jensen and Borum, 1991; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003). As the rate of primary productivity can be spatially and temporally heterogeneous for a given water body (Liboriussen and Jeppesen, 2006), a simple physico-chemical surrogate valid for ponds would be very valuable for ecological assessment. To record primary productivity in ponds varying in trophic status, the chosen method must be standardized and usable on the full range of trophic conditions. Ponds have generally a high littoral surface area relative to their pelagic volume and therefore an important potential for macrophyte and periphyton growth (Wetzel, 1990). For that reason, the benthic contribution to primary production can be more important in shallow systems like ponds than in deep lakes. Taking this benthic fraction into account is of prime importance, particularly for oligotrophic systems where it can represent the majority of the primary production (Vadeboncoeur et al., 2002). In addition, measuring periphytic productivity rather than macrophyte biomass could be more pertinent as the development of submerged vegetation is known to be discontinuous along trophic gradients (Scheffer, 1990). Moreover, Smoot et al. (1998) have shown that on artificial substrate the response of periphyton growth to nutrients is similar to the response of phytoplankton, making periphyton a valuable descriptor of phytoplankton response. This property allows the use of this indicator on the full spectrum of trophic conditions as it can grow in ponds with oligotrophic to hypertrophic conditions, where planktonic algae become the main producers and replace the benthic fraction. To focus on water quality, submerged macrophytes have the capacity to link the sediment with the overlying water and so to mobilize nutrients from the sediments (Graneli and Solander, 1988), in contrast to periphyton that cannot directly uptake nutrients stocked in the sediment (except for the epipelon (Hansson, 1992)). To standardize the measure of periphytic productivity, independent of the grazing pressure by zooplankton and macroinvertebrates, it has to be performed in controlled conditions with no access to grazers. Furthermore, the measurement must take into account the presence of macrophyte beds. Actually these can influence the abundance of periphyton by several mechanisms, notably competition for nutrient resources, release of allelopathic substances (Wium-Andersen, 1987; Ervin and Wetzel, 2003; Gross et al., 2003) or sheltering of the zooplanktonic and macroinvertebrate communities from predation (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997). Moreover, parallel measurements of periphytic productivity performed outside and inside beds of submerged plants permit to calculate a mean value of productivity between results obtained in open water and in macrophyte beds and also to detect potential co-occurrence within a pond of contrasting conditions linked by a continuous gradient between clear water zone colonized by submerged macrophytes and turbid zone without submerged vegetation. Co-occurring contrasting conditions have already been described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes of greater surfaces than the ponds considered here. Since there is an important nutrient recycling and rapid turnover in ponds and other shallow systems, water concentrations of nutrients show considerable fluctuation during the growing season, and a large part are mobilized in the biota and are not measurable in the water. During winter however, for ponds located at medium and high latitude, biological activity and primary productivity are very low and nutrients are in the water column for the most part, in dissolved or particle forms (Linton and Goulder, 2000). Hansson (1992) notably observed the peak of total phosphorus (TP) in open water occurring during winter for high latitudes lakes. Thus, winter values are expected to give a better picture of the potential of primary productivity by quantifying the amounts available in spring for the growth of producers. Furthermore, winter values avoid the confounding effects of uptake of phosphorus and denitrification that occur with summer readings (James et al., 2005). By performing parallel measurements of winter water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic productivity on a small dataset of ponds, this study aims to: 1) identify correlations between periphytic productivity and physico-chemical indicators of the trophic state, 2) detect a possible co-occurrence of contrasting conditions of turbidity and periphytic productivity in a given pond, 3) assess if a single chemical surrogate of primary productivity can potentially be used to classify ponds in the same biogeographic area according to their trophic state. Such a surrogate could serve as a basis to calibrate ecological value by species and select biological metrics of eutrophication. Additionally, this study will provide an opportunity to test the reliability of the method adapted for measuring the periphytic net primary productivity in ponds. 2. Material and methods 2.1. Study sites This study took place in the western part of the Swiss Plateau, a distinct biogeographic area (sensus Gonseth et al., 2001). The landscape of this area, where human population and agriculture are concentrated, has been intensely modified during the 20th century by increase in urbanisation and the intensification of agricultural practices (Lundstrom-Gillieron and Schlaepfer, 2003), resulting in the fragmentation of natural areas. The nine permanent ponds surveyed for this analysis represent a gradient of primary productivity from oligomesotrophic to hypertrophic. These ponds, located between 420 and 773 m a.s.l, are small and shallow, ranging from 327 to 10,616 m^2 in surface area, (mean: 3087 m^2, median: 2733 m^2) and from 0.38 to 1.03 m in mean depths (mean and median: 0.7 m). All these sites are colonized by fish. Four of the nine water bodies are colonized by submerged species of macrophytes (S), three by floating-leaves species (F) but without submerged hydrophytes and two supports only emerged vegetation (E). The location and the main morphometric characteristics of the ponds are given in Fig. 1 and Table 1. The sampling of the vegetation was made with the standardized method of Oertli et al. (2005) and consists of prospection by square quadrats (0.25 m^2) disposed equidistantly along transects perpendicular to the longest axis of the pond and located at regular intervals according to the pond size. The minimum number of quadrat prospected per pond (n) is related to the water surface area (m^2) by the equation \( n = 1.96 - 2.8 \times \log_{10}(\text{area}) + 2.6 \times (\log_{10}(\text{area}))^2 \). Such a strategy was shown to sample at least 70% of the real richness. A specie list was noted for each quadrat along with abundance in semi-quantitative classes. The number of quadrats prospected and the main species of macrophytes by site are given in Table 2 along with an estimation of their abundance at the pond scale. ![Map showing the study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds.](page_1092_186_1017_670.png) Fig. 1 – Study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds. 2.2. Periphytic primary productivity Rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) on artificial substrates and in absence of herbivores (method adapted from Clesceri et al., 1998; Chase, 2003) were directly recorded in situ in each pond as a measure of periphytic primary productivity at two points chosen with criterion detailed thereafter. All measures were performed at location with similar water depths (0.8 m) and in areas with minimal shading from terrestrial vegetation or from surrounding plants for measures in macrophyte beds. In all cases the shading at the location of the measurement point never attain five percent of the surface. Measurements were performed continuously from June 6, 2005 to August 2, 2005, across the period of longest daytime in northern hemisphere and until the aquatic vegetation biomass summer peak (Jackson et al., 1994). This period correspond to the time of optimal growth conditions for periphyton on artificial substrate as identified by Jobgen et al. (2004). Submerged macrophyte presence in four ponds and floating-leaves species presence in three ponds were taken into account by measuring productivity inside vegetation stands and in open water. Growth rates were determined by measuring the accumulation of periphyton on the inner side of transparent plastic boxes (polystyrene PS) offering each a colonisable surface of 0.023 m^2 (Fig. 2). Boxes were covered by a net on their open face (mesh size 0.25 mm) to prevent, or at least limit the income of grazers, and were positioned two to three centimeters below the water surface in groups of three pseudo-replicates fixed around a pole planted in the pond base. According to Chase and Ryberg (2004), such a mesh retains about 10% of the available light “but did not significantly reduce algal growth in a controlled experiment performed in the absence of grazers”. Preventing the access of grazers is of prime importance for this study and as Jones et al. (2002) pointed out, the grazing pressure is a stronger limiting factor of the net production of periphyton than the water nutrient concentration. To reduce to the minimum meteorologically related variation among ponds, sampling and replacement of the boxes of all nine ponds were carried out over the shortest possible time period (two days). 2.3. Physico-chemistry Water physico-chemistry was measured once in winter and physical parameters were measured five times in summer (at each box replacement). The winter fieldwork was undertaken during three consecutive days (from 9 to 11 February, 2005) after a long frost period. Water sampling and field measurements were made at the deeper central point of each pond by drilling a hole in the ice cover. Water samples were taken at 20 cm below the icy surface with a sampling bottle, and then stocked in acid pre-rinse PE plastic bottles immediately before being stored in the dark in a refrigerated box. Water samples for the analysis of dissolved components (PO₄-P (soluble reactive phosphorus = SRP), NO₃-N, NH₃-N) were filtered in situ trough 0.45 μm filters (Schleicher & Schuell ME 25). Unfiltered samples were kept for total phosphorus (TP) and total nitrogen (TN) analyses. All samples were stored in the dark at 4 °C and analysed within 48 h after field collection. The SESA water quality laboratory (VD) analyzed all the water samples with standard methods. TP was determined after potassium persulphate digestion at 121 °C and under pressure for half an hour; SRP was further measured by the ascorbate acid/molybdenum blue method (Clesceri et al., 1998). TN was determined by chemiluminescence after oxidization in NO at high temperature and reaction with ozone. NH₃-N was determined by colorimetry with the salicylate method. NO₃-N was determined by ion chromatography. A deep profile was made in the field for physical parameters (temperature, pH, conductivity) using a multi-parameters probe (YSI 556®, YSI Incorporated, Yellowspring, USA). Water turbidity (NTU) and transparency (cm) were also measured in the field with a turbidity meter (WTW Turb 355 IR®, WTW GmbH, Weilheim, D) and a Snellen tube of 60 cm length. 2.4. Data analyses To assess the reliability of the primary productivity measurement method, mean rate of productivity and variance were calculated for each measurement point and sampling occasion. In parallel, productivity rates by pseudo-replicates were box-plotted by point and sampling occasion to visually detect eventual outliers. To test if any measured physical and chemical variables could explain the differences of periphytic productivity among ponds, multiple stepwise linear regressions were performed (threshold of entry \( p \leq 0.05 \), removal \( \geq 0.1 \)). As we wanted to explore the relationships between summer periphytic growth rate and winter concentrations of TP or TN, linear stepwise regressions were performed with these two parameters in a first set of predictors and physical parameters in a second set to see if their inclusion could improve the \( R^2 \) and significance of the models. Regressions were performed between seasonal productivity rates of each pond and the corresponding mean of physical parameters of the water as well as winter concentrations of nutrients. Mean productivity rate by pond is the sum of the means of the two sampling points of each sampling occasion. To refine the regressions according to the sampling points, the same above procedure was applied separately for three subsets of the data (open water (O), submerged species (S) and floating-leaves species (F)). As one of the ponds shows very high rates of productivity, we reapplied the whole procedure after removing this extreme value from the dataset to verify if the identified regressions remained significant. The critical \( \alpha \) values were corrected by applying the Bonferroni corrections for non-independent comparisons (Maxwell and Delaney, 1990). As a second objective we wanted to compare the rates of periphytic productivity between sampling points located in the same pond, respectively inside versus outside macrophyte stands. With all sampling occasions, there were enough data to test the significance of the differences among locations with an unparametric test (Mann–Whitney) between productivity by boxes at the sampling points. As there were not enough pseudo-replicates to validate the statistical test by sampling occasion, simple box plot by sampling points and by sampling occasion were plotted for each pond. This revealed if differences were detectable, and helped rank productivity rates at each vegetated sampling point in space and time as lower, equal or higher to unvegetated points. 3. Results The set of ponds display a wide range of periphytic growth rate, nutrient concentrations and water physical parameters. Measures of periphytic growth rate by single point and sampling occasion ranged from 0.022 to 48.406 gC/m²/14 days (0.0016–3.458 gC/m²/day) and the mean seasonal value for ponds ranged from 1.284 to 52.950 gC/m²/56 days (0.023– 0.946 gC/m²/day). The daily mean seasonal value by point and by pond and the mean value by point and by sampling occasions are given in Table 3 along with variance between pseudo-replicates, except for the first sampling occasions where the three boxes by point were weighted together. Rates for the last sampling occasion in open water of pond P3 could not be retained for the analyses because the boxes emerged during sampling. Six exposed boxes were also damaged and the measurements were removed from the dataset. Winter nutrient concentrations of TP ranged from 0.002 to 0.346 mg L⁻¹ and TN varied from 0.7 to 5.83 mg L⁻¹. Ranges and mean values for summer and winter measurements of physico-chemical parameters are given in Table 4 3.1. Regressions of productivity rates with physico-chemical parameters The mean seasonal rates of periphytic primary productivity by pond defined as the sum of the mean value by pond for each sampling occasion are positively correlated to the water concentration of total nitrogen (TN) measured during the previous winter (linear regression for the whole season, Table 5, model 1, \( r^2 = 0.974, p = 8.55e-07 \)). With the stepwise procedure, the regression remained the same with winter TN as unique predictor. Without the extreme value of the hypertrophic site (P6), the regression between the seasonal productivity by pond and the winter concentration of TN remained valid, even if less significant and less strong (model 2, Table 5, \( r^2 = 0.754, p = 5.16e-03 \)). In that case, the stepwise regression retained the mean water transparency as second predictor negatively correlated with productivity, improving the performance of the model (model 3, Table 5). The scatter plot of the seasonal values of productivity versus TN or TP presented in Fig. 3 shows additionally the OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982; Wetzel, 1983; Forsberg and Ryding, 1980) limits of nutrient concentration between trophic classes as well as the limits between the classes of ecological quality included for shallow lakes by Sondergaard et al. (2005b). For the measures located in open water, regressions with TN were also significant for seasonal productivity (model 1, Table 6, \( r^2 = 0.937, p = 1.68e-05 \)). The stepwise procedure even improves the model by including the mean turbidity as second predictor (model 2 Table 6). Without the upper value of productivity (pond P6), the regressions are less strong but the predictors remain the same.

Discussion 4.1. Reliability and limitations of the method for ponds The rates of productivity measured for each pseudo-replicate for a given point and sampling occasion were similar even if the variance between the boxes increased for high means (see Table 3 and Fig. 4). Despite this uncontrolled effect, the method is sensitive and allows classifying ponds of this dataset by trophic states characterized by TN as a higher variance between pseudo-replicates occurs in systems already hypertrophic. However as the data material is small and restricted to a limited geographic area, these results need to be confirmed on a broader scale to generalize this outcome for ponds in the area. Observed rates (Table 3) were low compared with other studies (for instance see Chase (2003) with measured productivity ranging between 6.12 and 56.2 g/m²/day). This could be due to the smaller net mesh size used to cover the open face of boxes, which could have limited the colonization by algae. On the other hand this net allowed inter-sites comparisons by strongly reducing and homogenising the residual grazing factor. The nature of the artificial substrate can also be involved. Actually, the review of Cattaneo and Amireault (1992) suggested that the type of artificial substrate is not crucial but Danilov and Ekelund (2001) observed no growth of periphyton on PVC substrate and the formation of a slim layer of bacteria covering the artificial substrate. No such layer was observed in the current study and the poly-styrene plastic often employed in biology, notably for the Petri dishes, is more likely to have played an inhibitory effect as it seems to be the case with PVC. 4.2. Periphytic productivity and nutrients The significant positive regression observed between TN and mean periphytic growth rate is consistent with other studies, for instance Luttenton and Lowe (2006) found significant correlation between nitrogen concentration on nutrient-diffusive substrata (NDS) and total biovolume of periphyton growing on this substrate. Similarly Chase and Ryberg (2004) found positive correlations between primary productivity measured with a method similar to this study and TP and TN in order of importance. Kahlert and Pettersson (2002) also measured an increase in the biomass of benthic algae with trophic levels even if it was not correlated with the nutrient status of the algae itself. Moreover, rooted plants can obtain phosphorus from the sediment and in this way act as a source for the water column (Carignan and Kalff, 1982) while nitrogen on the other hand tends to be lost through denitrification within plant stands (Weisner et al., 1994). Peretyatko et al. (2007) observed notably that dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) tends to decrease in pond water during the warmer month, especially in sites without submerged species and abundant phytoplankton. Therefore, in shallow lakes with macrophyte stands, algal populations can be nitrogen limited during summer (Moss et al., 2005) even if, as in this study, the winter TN/TP ratio does not indicate a nitrogen limitation in most of the ponds. Additionally, on NDS spanning a large range of molar N/P ratios and nutrient concentrations, Luttenton and Lowe (2006) showed that nitrogen concentration is a significant predictor of the algal biovolume growing on the substrate and that neither the N/P ratio nor the phosphorus concentration of the NDS were significantly correlated with this biovolume. These results suggest that the TP concentration measured in winter is an underestimation of the available phosphorus during the growing season. As all the ponds were icy at the time of the winter sampling, the absence of turbulence under the ice cover should have limited the suspension of fine particles in the water column. During warm months with a high water temperature and a low concentration of dissolved oxygen, ponds with organic P-saturated sediment can be net source of P by release of the iron-bound P (Søndergaard et al., 1999; Fairchild and Velinsky, 2006). Conversely the winter concentrations of TN could be an over estimation of the available nutrient in summer as a significant part can be lost through denitrification. This could explain the relatively high concentrations of TN and the corresponding trophic levels attributed to the ponds when compared to the TP concentrations and corresponding trophic classes (Fig. 3). It is therefore likely that the trophic status of the ponds is overestimated when the limits of Wetzel (1983) or Forsberg and Ryding (1980) set for large lakes are directly applied to the winter concentration of TN as in Fig. 3. On the other hand the limits of nutrient concentration proposed by Søndergaard et al. (2005b) to set ecological quality classes for shallow lakes (Fig. 3, dashed lines) seems to be more appropriate for ponds. In particular, it reassigned the sites classified as eutrophic following the TP or TN scales of Vollenweider and Kerekes (1982), Forsberg and Ryding (1980) and Wetzel (1983) into moderate to good quality, and the mesotrophic sites into high quality while keeping the hypertrophic ponds in poor to bad quality classes. These scales, even if not giving a trophic status, rely directly on water quality and distribute the gradient of nutrient concentrations observed in ponds in all the quality classes based either on TP or TN. 4.3. Roles and effects of submerged macrophytes The observed lower rates of periphytic productivity within boxes placed in the submerged macrophyte stands of two truly stagnant sites harboring continuously submerged species show the influences of submerged plants on nutrient cycling. Notably, macrophytes and their associated epiphytes mobilize and store nutrients prior to releasing it during their senescence. This competitive storage involves a reduced nutrient availability for phytoplankton (Kufel and Ozimek, 1994) and for the periphyton colonizing the artificial substrate. These results are concordant with the observation of Takamura et al. (2003) who found at a similar nutrient level a significantly lower concentration of planktonic chlorophyll within submerged macrophytes than in lakes without submerged species. Similarly, Liboriussen and Jeppesen (2003) and Vadeboncoeur et al. (2001) observed lower gross primary productivity in clear water compared to turbid one. When measuring biomass of phytoplankton, Peretyatko et al. (2007) reported lower amount in ponds supporting submerged plants when compared to unvegetated ponds or those with floating-leaved species only. With a measure of the total lake net primary production, Blindow et al. (2006) observed higher level in a clear lake compared to a turbid one but the two lakes considered in that study were deeper than the ponds considered here, and their water column, if turbid, experienced more self-shading and higher rates of community respiration than shallower sites. In fact, Blindow et al. (2006) pointed out that this difference of total net primary productivity between clear and turbid water tends to decrease with the mean depth by reducing the water volume below the compensation depth. As the artificial substrates used in our study were set 2–3 cm below the water surface, the measured growths of periphyton are less influenced by phytoplankton shading. The contrasting conditions of turbidity and transparency observed between macrophyte stands and open water were previously described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes. Other factors could also explain the lower periphytic productivity rates often measured within plant stands, for example shading by the macrophytes canopy (Ozimek et al., 1990), strong evidence of release of allelopathic substances by macrophytes (Gross et al., 2007) or increased rates of sedimentation (Carpenter, 1981; Petticrew et al., 1991) accompanied by a reduced resuspension within macrophyte stands (Scheffer et al., 1993). A lower or a negative net production of the epiphyte communities colonizing the artificial substrate placed within submerged species, as seasonally observed on natural substrate by Vis et al. (2006), can also explain the difference between open water and macrophyte stands. If the respiration process is more important than in open water, the amount of carbon measured after two weeks underestimates primary production. Conversely, the refuge effect of submerged macrophyte for grazers (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997) must be here less important as the experimental design that we used strongly limit the influence of large macroinvertebrates grazers. On one of the four sites harboring submerged species (P5), the early senescence of Myriophyllum spicatum (represented by the upward arrow in Fig. 4) during the second part of June was accompanied by a strong increase in the rate of productivity at the corresponding location that even surpasses the rate measured in open water. This is probably due to the direct recycling of nutrients released by macrophytes as periphyton can directly exploit this resource (Cattaneo and Kalff, 1979; Carignan and Kalff, 1982; Rooney and Kalff, 2003). Moreover, Carpenter (1980) but also Smith and Adams (1986) showed that the importance of macrophyte-derived nutrients for epiphyton increases with the degree of senescence of the plant. Additionally, Carignan and Kalff (1982) have specifically measured that M. spicatum is a significant source of highly available P for the surrounding epiphyton and phytoplankton. Interestingly, the water transparency remains inversely correlated to the rate of primary productivity and became simultaneously lower within macrophytes than in open water (data not shown). This peak of productivity was follow by a rapid growth of dense beds of Ceratophyllum demersum in early July along with a reduction of the rate measured in the box even if transparency remained low (downward arrow in Fig. 4). During this period, the rate of productivity continued to increase in open water to reach the seasonal peak during the first fortnight of July (Fig. 4). This delayed growth in open water compared to the growth measured in senescing beds during the previous two weeks can be linked to the horizontal diffusion from beds to open water of the available nutrients, similarly to what was observed by Rooney and Kalff (2003) studying active cycling from the sediment mediated by macrophytes. During the last fortnight of July, open water was progressively colonized by stands of C. demersum generating a net reduction in the productivity rate and resulting in similar values between the two sampling points becoming gradually both vegetated. The site P9 is a bit different as it has a flow-through regime, which is not the case in the other sites. In this case the mean rates of productivity were higher in macrophyte stands than in open water (118.7%–226.5% of the rates measured in open water). As already mentioned, measured rates as well as absolute differences were very low and the values were even overlapping between pseudo-replicates of the two sampling points (Fig. 4). Nevertheless, this trend differs notably from the other sites characterized by well-marked differences in periphytic productivity measured in the boxes between plant stands and open water. This difference can be due to different factors, notably a lower current speed through the dense macrophyte stands (Gessner, 1950; Stephan and Gutknecht, 2002) increasing the water retention time and potentially enhancing both sedimentation and the use of dissolved nutrients. Other factors could be involved, notably a release of nutrients by macrophytes, as mentioned earlier. Actually, this pond exhibits low concentration of dissolved nutrients (Table 4) and the nutritive contribution of healthy plants to periphyton, even if little, is known to be more important in oligotrophic water (Eminson and Moss, 1980; Burkholder and Wetzel, 1990). Additionally, nutrient diffusion may be facilitated and mixing of the water mediated by the current tends to also homogenize the conditions across the site. In this pond, transparency was always at the maximum value at the two sampling points and the turbidity remained low in value and range (inferior to four NTU among all measurements). 5. Conclusions and perspectives Firstly, the method of periphytic productivity measurement adapted in this study operates well with this dataset of ponds and gives repeatable measures except for the hypertrophic sites that showed an increase of the variance between pseudo-replicates. Secondly the results indicated that for the study area considered, the winter concentration of total nitrogen was a significant predictor of the summer rates of periphytic productivity measured in open water or averaged by ponds. When beds of submerged macrophytes were present, the periphytic productivity within the plant stands was generally lower and the transparency higher. In that case, the winter concentration of TP was a stronger and better predictor of the productivity. This limited growth of periphyton within the boxes placed in submerged macrophyte beds puts in evidence for the positive effects of submerged plants on water quality and emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds. Extending these results for assessing pond water quality in other region of Switzerland would require a similar study on a broader scale notably with sites located at higher altitudes, as the range of environmental parameters of particular concern for primary productivity differs broadly between Alps and lowlands (Hinden et al., 2005).
