Data from 13 biomanipulated ponds averaged per pond per year and plotted on log–log scale The negative effect of submerged vegetation on phytoplankton biomass through associated mechanisms, such as increased grazing by large zooplankters finding refuge in plant beds, competition for nutrients, stabilisation of the water column and allelopathy, is well established (Jeppesen et al., 1997; Sondergaard & Moss, 1998; van Donk & van de Bund, 2002; Irfanullah & Moss, 2005). This is supported by the results obtained in this study as indicated by generally lower Chl \( a \) yields per unit of TP in the presence of extensive submerged vegetation as compared to the situation when submerged vegetation was lacking (Fig. 1). It should be noted that the effect of extensive submerged vegetation cover on the Chl \( a \) yield does not seem to depend on the size of large cladocerans suggesting that, when submerged vegetation is restored, phytoplankton can also be controlled by mechanisms other than large zooplankton grazing. The effect of large cladocerans on phytoplankton biomass is less well elucidated. Some controversy exists as to the edibility/grazing resistance of phytoplankton in general and cyanobacteria in particular (e.g. Gliwicz, 1990b; Benndorf et al., 2002). The majority of the studies, however, use number or biomass of large Cladocera or *Daphnia* to assess their effect on phytoplankton. The results of this study indicate that density of large cladocerans has a less straightforward effect on phytoplankton biomass than their size. The non-vegetated ponds, where phytoplankton was mostly controlled by nutrients and zooplankton grazing, often showed markedly lower Chl \( a \) concentrations in association with smaller numbers of large-bodied daphniids than in association with high numbers of small-bodied daphniids. This is clearly reflected on the Chl \( a \) yield per unit of TP that has visibly stronger negative relationship with size than density (Fig. 2). The stronger effect of larger cladocerans on the Chl \( a \) yield is consistent with the idea that smaller individuals have narrower food size spectrum (Burns, 1968); therefore, they rather shift phytoplankton community towards grazing resistant species than effectively control phytoplankton biomass (Cottingham & Schindler, 2000; Benndorf et al., 2002; Steiner, 2002). Apparent biomanipulation success, however, is not necessarily caused by large zooplankton grazing or submerged vegetation presence, but can be caused by a number of other factors related to fish presence (DeMelo et al., 1992). Fish presence contributes to the nutrient pool through excretion, bioturbation, and sediment resuspension (Brabrand et al., 1990; Breukelaar et al., 1994; Vanni, 2002). Changes in zooplankton community structure caused by fish removal can also alter the N/P ratio in a way that would inhibit phytoplankton growth (Sterner et al., 1992). Therefore, fish removal may result in substantial decrease in nutrient availability and subsequently in phytoplankton biomass reduction. The marked increase in SRP and the insignificant change in DIN concentrations after biomanipulation in the ponds where it resulted in phytoplankton biomass decrease show, however, that fish removal did not result in a decrease in nutrient availability in the ponds studied. There are also many reasons why biomanipulation might not work. Insufficient fish removal, phytoplankton composition shift to grazing resistant species, the presence of predator macroinvertebrates and high nutrient concentrations are generally considered as the main reasons of biomanipulation failures to reduce phytoplankton biomass (Meijer et al., 1999; Sierp et al., 2009). The drawdown of the biomanipulated ponds suggests that insufficient fish removal cannot be considered as the cause of the failure. Besides, ponds that were rapidly recolonised by fish could maintain low phytoplankton biomass in the presence of extensive submerged vegetation. When submerged vegetation was lacking, fish recolonisation was often associated with relatively smaller large cladocerans and phytoplankton assemblage bias towards bloom forming cyanobacteria. In the absence of fish, however, large cladocerans alone could control phytoplankton (Fig. 5; Peretyatko et al., 2009) suggesting that when released from predation pressure, large cladocerans can grow big enough (in the fishless ponds the length of large cladocerans exceeded at times 3 mm) to be capable of efficient control of phytoplankton, including bloom-forming cyanobacteria, and thus can prevent bloom formation. This is consistent with the report of Gliwicz (1990b) stating that Daphnia can control bloom-forming cyanobacteria below critical filament concentration. Despite the removal of fish, no marked evidence of large Cladocera control by macroinvertebrates, as reported by Benndorf et al. (2000) and Hosper & Meijer (1993), was observed during the study period. The fluctuations of large Cladocera densities in the three completely fishless ponds seemed to be related to food availability rather than predation. It is possible that macroinvertebrates preyed preferentially on smaller cladocerans and thus biased their size structure towards bigger individuals (Pinel-Alloul, 1995) as cladocerans in these two ponds were the biggest in size. This, however, can also be attributed to the absence of predation by fish as well as low food availability that gives larger filter-feeders a competitive advantage (Gliwicz, 1990a). The significant positive relationship between Chl \( a \) and TP in the biomanipulated ponds with extensive submerged vegetation and large-bodied cladocerans confirmed that the success of biomanipulation depends to a certain degree on nutrient level. Indeed, the capacity of submerged vegetation and large cladocerans to buffer the effects of eutrophication diminished at higher nutrient levels as indicated by the markedly higher Chl \( a \) values corresponding to elevated TP concentrations. This is consistent with the idea that the clear-water state becomes less stable as nutrient levels increase (Scheffer et al., 2001). Therefore, to ensure biomanipulation success in ponds excessively polluted with nutrients, reduction of nutrient loading might be indispensable. In the ponds that are not excessively polluted by nutrients, trophic (large zooplankton) and competitive (submerged vegetation) interactions seem to be more important predictors of phytoplankton biomass than nutrient availability. In the absence of fish, low phytoplankton biomass could be maintained by large Cladocera grazing alone. Because large zooplankters are very susceptible to fish recolonisation, such situation is very unstable and not sustainable in the longer term, except for ponds with recurrent anoxic conditions unsuitable for fish. Conversely, extensive submerged vegetation can withstand some degree of fish recolonisation and thus buffer, to certain extent, the effects of eutrophication. Therefore, submerged vegetation restoration seems to be crucial for the maintenance of low phytoplankton biomass on the longer term. This has important implications for the restoration of ponds affected by eutrophication, as it shows that considerable degree of their ecological quality can be restored by biomanipulation even when nutrient loading reduction is not feasible in the short term, as is often the case because of considerable phosphorus accumulation in the sediment (Jeppesen et al., 2005; Sondergaard et al., 2005a) and surface and ground water contamination by urban pollution. The slopes of the regression lines obtained by the analysis of the data from the Brussels ponds are within the range of the slopes based on the data from temperate lakes (Phillips et al., 2008), suggesting that the ponds studied function in a similar way. Therefore, these results can also be used to get insights into the Chl \( a \)-TP relationship in lakes. Conclusions In ponds lacking submerged vegetation and large-bodied cladocerans, phytoplankton biomass is mainly nutrient driven and therefore the Chl \( a \)-TP relationship is strong. The presence of extensive submerged vegetation and/or intense grazing by large-bodied cladocerans can considerably weaken the Chl \( a \)-TP relationship by inhibiting phytoplankton growth despite high nutrient availability. As biomanipulation of ponds leads to the restoration of submerged vegetation and enhances large zooplankton grazing, it can be used to restore a considerable degree of their ecological quality even when nutrient loading reduction is not feasible. The capacity of submerged vegetation and large zooplankton grazing to buffer eutrophication effects diminishes at higher nutrients levels; therefore, to ensure biomanipulation success in ponds excessively polluted with nutrients, reduction of nutrient loading might be indispensable. submerged_macrophytes_as_refuges.full_text:
Submerged macrophytes as refuges for grazing Cladocera against fish predation: observations on seasonal changes in relation to macrophyte cover and predation pressure Julia H. Stansfield¹, Martin R. Perrow²*, Louise D. Tench¹, Adrian J. D. Jowitt² & Ayesha A. L. Taylor¹ ¹National Rivers Authority, Biology Laboratory, Station Road, St Olaves, Great Yarmouth, NR31 9JA, UK ²ECON, School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich NR4 7TJ, UK (*author for correspondence) Key words: zooplankton, zooplanktivorous fish, macrophyte, refugia, predator/prey interactions, lake restoration Abstract The provision of a refuge from fish predation for large-bodied Cladocera among stands of submerged macrophytes is thought to be an important stabilising mechanism against nutrient-induced phytoplankton increases in clear water shallow lakes. The occurrence of any refuge effect in relation to the seasonal impact of both macrophyte development and recruitment of zooplanktivorous fish was monitored over the summer months (May to September) in three lakes (Cromes Broad, Hoveton Little Broad/Pound End, and Upton Broad) of variable trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover, in the Norfolk Broads in Eastern England. At all sites, Daphnia spp. exhibited a early summer peak of abundance but had declined rapidly by July probably as a result of predation from underyearling fish. In extensive macrophyte stands (Cromes Broad) Daphnia spp. persisted after its elimination in open water, indicating some refuge effect. At sites with macrophyte cover and/or low fish predation pressure, Daphnia spp. was replaced by Ceriodaphnia spp., both with and without Simocephalus sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera, apparently capable of exerting a high grazing pressure on phytoplankton. This occurred, even under high predation pressure from a relatively high density of zooplanktivorous 0+ fish (Cromes Broad), consistent with the refuge hypothesis. In addition, at this site, significant positive associations of cladoceran abundance with increasing macrophyte cover were apparent throughout the summer. From information on the distribution of fish it is suggested that dense macrophytes offer the most suitable refuge through provision of predator-free space. Introduction Eutrophication of shallow freshwater lakes frequently results in increased standing crops of phytoplankton or perhaps filamentous algae. This in turn leads to the decline or loss of submerged macrophytes, typically through shading (Phillips et al., 1978; Scheffer, 1990), with consequent gross changes in biotic structure and function (Moss, 1983; De Nie, 1987; Bronmark & Weisner, 1992). However, there is growing empirical and experimental evidence that stabilising mechanisms associated with the presence of stands of macrophytes, may prevent or reduce increases in algal growth up to a threshold level of nutrient loading (Howard-Williams, 1981; Timms & Moss, 1984; Mitchell et al., 1988; Balls et al., 1989; Andersson et al., 1990; Blindlow et al., 1993; Van Donk et al., 1993; Schriver et al., 1995). Consequently, within a range of nutrient concentration, either macrophytes or phytoplankton may dominate; the alternative stable state hypothesis (Irvine et al., 1989; Scheffer et al., 1993). Several stabilising mechanisms which perpetuate the macrophyte-dominated state have been suggested. These include: allelopathy, the production of com- pounds limiting algal growth by the macrophytes themselves (Wium-Anderson et al., 1982); competition for N, with macrophytes maintaining a competitive advantage over algae through luxury uptake (Balls et al., 1989) and acting as a sink for available nutrients (in both water column and sediments) (Ozimek et al., 1990; Van Donk et al., 1993); prevention of resuspension of sediment and recirculation of fast sinking algae by wind and wave action through calming of the water column (James & Barko, 1990); provision of refuges for grazing zooplankton (Timms & Moss, 1984) and refuges for piscivorous fish acting upon the production (Spencer & King, 1984; Grimm & Backx, 1990) or the distribution (Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) of zooplanktivorous fish thereby reducing predation pressure upon the zooplankton (Hambright et al., 1986, Turner & Mittelbach, 1990). Detailed knowledge of the mechanisms responsible for maintaining clear water and low algal populations in lakes dominated by macrophytes is critical for those lake managers concerned with the sustainable restoration (i.e. reversal of anthropogenic eutrophication) of shallow lakes, particularly if this is to be achieved in a predictable and cost-effective manner (Shapiro, 1990). In restoration programmes, the refuge effect for zooplankton is particularly appealing (Shapiro, 1990). This is due to two reasons. First, after nutrient loading has been reduced to the range where macrophyte dominance is likely to be stable (TP<0.15 mg l\(^{-1}\) or higher if N is strongly limiting-Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990), the removal of zooplanktivorous fish, often termed biomanipulation (Lammens et al., 1990), is often required to enhance populations of grazing zooplankton to reduce algal crops to provide a suitable light climate for macrophyte growth. If this mechanism operates, then it is likely that grazing has some importance in maintaining clear water within macrophyte beds. Second, during the development of macrophyte stands following biomanipulation which may or may not be rapid (Meijer et al., 1994; Perrow et al., 1994, Moss et al., 1996), any stabilising mechanism is of increased value if it also preserves water clarity in the open water surrounding macrophyte stands. The diel migration of large-bodied Cladocera from macrophyte stands to open water to feed provides such a mechanism (Timms & Moss, 1984). Although macrophyte stands have been demonstrated to provide refuges for zooplankton (Schriver et al., 1995; Phillips et al., 1996) the timing of such effects relative to the seasonal development of macrophytes and recruitment of 0+ fish is poorly understood. The aim of this study was to describe the seasonal pattern of use of submerged macrophytes by grazing Cladocera in relation to potential predation pressure from fish and to determine whether the refuge effect is plausible as a mechanism in promoting clear water in beds of macrophytes. This adopted a comparative approach by monitoring zooplankton abundance and community structure, fish abundance and biomass, chlorophyll a concentration (as a index of algal abundance) and macrophyte cover during the macrophyte growing season (May–September) in three lakes of varying trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover. Description of study sites The three lakes studied (Hoveton Little/Pound End, Crones and Upton Broads) are among the Norfolk Broads, a series (around 50) of small (1–124 ha), shallow (0.5–2 m) lakes in eastern England, formed from flooded medieval peat diggings. Most may now be classed as hypertrophic and only four retain their original macrophyte populations (Moss, 1983). The study sites represent a continuum from phytoplankton to macrophyte dominance. The first, Hoveton Little Broad, has been divided into two sections as part of a long term management strategy aimed at evaluating the effects of different restorative actions (Table 1). For the purposes of this study, Hoveton Little Broad, acts as a control section with turbid phytoplankton dominated water and few submerged macrophytes, whereas the other biomanipulated section, Pound End, has clear water and some macrophytes, although these are restricted to bird exclosures. The second, Crones Broad, retains a relatively high nutrient loading but has recently developed an extensive cover of Ceratophyllum demersum L. with Potamogeton freisii Rupr. (Perrow et al., 1997). The third, Upton Broad, being isolated from riverine inputs and surrounded by wet woodland, has largely retained its original character and has a large cover of macrophytes, particularly Najas marina L., with Chara spp., P. pectinatus L. and Zannichellia palustris L. (Perrow et al., 1997). The physical characteristics, management measures employed and relevant biological data are shown in Table 1. Table 1. Characteristics of the study sites.

Materials and methods Zooplankton, macrophytes and chlorophyll \( a \) Sampling for zooplankton, macrophytes, and chlorophyll \( a \) was carried out monthly from May to September 1994. At each site, ten zooplankton samples were taken from both open water and from amongst submerged macrophytes, where present. Where macrophytes occurred the density in a 0.25 m\(^2\) quadrat centred on each sampling point was expressed as PVI (per cent volume infested-Canfield et al., 1984). This was estimated by multiplying the estimated % cover by the height of the stand and dividing by the depth of water. At Pound End, five samples were taken from each of the two large (a. 500–1000 m\(^2\)) bird exclosures. In the open water and when macrophyte stands reached the water surface, a tube sampler was used (length 90 cm, diameter 10 cm) in order to sample the whole water column. When macrophyte stands did not reach the water surface a Patalas sampler (10 litre capacity) was used to obtain a sample from among the macrophyte stand. Water was strained through a 64 \( \mu \)m net and the animals retained were preserved in 70% alcohol. Samples were counted under a stereo microscope using 25 \( \times \) magnification. Differences between mean abundance of important cladoceran zooplankton between open water and macrophytes were tested using Mann-Whitney U-tests on each sampling occasion. In addition, the relationships between abundance of particular cladoceran species and % macrophyte cover were explored using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (\( r_s \)). Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations were determined according to the methods of Moss et al. (1986). Fish Fish populations were sampled on two occasions, in May and September. This corresponded to the period prior to the recruitment of cyprinids and after the late summer period in which 0+ fish are likely to exert a depressive effect on zooplankton (Townsend & Perrow, 1989), respectively. In addition, sampling in May provided a baseline of the adult fish stock prior to the recruitment of underyearlings, whereas sampling in September allowed the relative recruitment strength of the 0+ fish to be estimated. Point abundance sampling (PAS) (Copp & Penáz, 1988) conducted with high frequency (600 Hz) pulsed DC electrofishing equipment was used to sample all habitats in proportion to their abundance. During sampling the 3 m fibreglass dinghy, with one electrofishing operator and one person controlling the boat using ‘push’ (facing the direction of travel) rowing, was rowed systematically along transect lines (8–10 oar strokes apart). At the equivalent distance along the transect line, a point was sampled by rapidly immers- ing the large (45 cm diameter) anode and swinging it through a 2 m arc in one motion. Any stunned fish were removed and transferred to individual buckets. The area sampled was quantified as 2.4 m\(^2\). This was achieved by using a voltmeter to determine the distance at which the voltage gradient was reduced to 0.12 V which may be used as the threshold limit for effective electrofishing (Copp & Penáz, 1988). At the end of each transect all fish were identified, counted, measured to the nearest mm fork length and weighed to the nearest gram, before being returned to a stretch of water that had been sampled previously. In addition, the % of the water column occupied by submerged macrophytes was estimated visually at each sampling point. The entire area of Pound End, Upton and Cromes Broads were sampled, whereas only part of Hoveton Little Broad (c. 6 ha-comparable to the size of Pound End) was covered. Results Fish The spring biomass of adult cyprinid and percid fishes was variable but low (up to 110 kg ha\(^{-1}\) but typically <15 kg ha\(^{-1}\)) (Table 2). The increase in biomass and especially, density, of potentially zooplanktivorous fish (all except pike, *Esox lucius* L. and eel, *Anguilla anguilla* (L.)) over the sampling period underlines the important contribution the recruitment of 0+ fish makes to fish production in the study lakes (Table 2). The relative recruitment strength of the different species in the different lakes is illustrated in Figure 1. Zooplankton Three genera of large-bodied grazing Cladocera zooplankton were found at significant density (>50 l\(^{-1}\)) in some or all of the study sites. These were *Daphnia hyalina/longispina* (Leydig/O.F.M.) *Ceriodaphnia reticulata/quadrangula* (Jurine/O.F. M.) and *Simocephalus vetulus* (O.F.M.). *Daphnia* spp. had an early summer peak of abundance, albeit of varying magnitude, at all sites, but had declined to low populations by July. At Cromes Broad, where extensive macrophyte stands developed from June onwards (Figure 1), *Daphnia* spp. persisted amongst the macrophytes after its elimination in open water (Figure 2). At Cromes and Pound End *Daphnia* spp. was replaced by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. both with (Cromes and Pound End) and without (Upton) *Simocephalus* sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera. This was not the case in Hoveton Little Broad, where cladoceran populations remained extremely low throughout the summer. The patterns of habitat use by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. varied between the different sites (Figure 2). At Pound End, macrophyte beds were favoured in early season, although once populations had built up by mid-summer, significant numbers (>100 l\(^{-1}\)) were found in open water. At Upton, prior to the peak in macrophyte populations, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was more abundant in open water, thereafter there was no significant difference between the different habitats. In contrast, in Cromes, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds compared to open water on all occasions (Figure 2). A similar pattern was shown by *Simocephalus* sp. where it occurred, as it was virtually always significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds (Figure 2). For sites with macrophytes, the relationships between PVI and the abundance of the different genera as well as all grazing Cladocera combined are shown in Table 3. At Cromes, there is a consistent pattern of increasing abundance of all genera, including *Daphnia* spp. while it was still present, with increasing PVI. At Upton no such pattern was found, with either no significant relationships, or in July, a significant negative relationship with *Ceriodaphnia* spp. Pound End represented an intermediate situation, with different species exerting different preferences: *Daphnia* spp. tended to be negatively associated with macrophytes; *Ceriodaphnia* spp. displayed positive associations early in the summer but no relationship in subsequent samples and *Simocephalus* sp. showed significant positive correlations with PVI on all occasions. Discussion Seasonal interactions between macrophytes, fish, zooplankton and phytoplankton There is clearly some interaction between extent of macrophyte development, intensity of predation by 0+ fish measured simply as a function of density and the structure and abundance of the cladoceran community and its potential impact on algal abundance (measured as chlorophyll *a*) (Figure 1). Indeed, where fish recruitment is poor or absent, *Daphnia* spp. populations typically persist throughout the summer months (Perrow et al., 1994). Conversely, it is clear that the relatively low overwintering stock of older fish exerted little influence on the development of the *Daphnia* spp. population. Second, in all sites, *Daphnia* spp. was quickly replaced by high densities of other species which is not consistent with food limitation and indeed at no site was the abundance of edible algae (expressed as chlorophyll *a*) apparently limiting. It therefore seems reasonable to conclude that predation by 0+ fish is responsible for the decline in *Daphnia* spp. Moreover, this appears to be readily achieved by a relatively low number of 0+ fish in Upton (prior to the development of macrophytes) and relatively moderate recruitment in Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads. However, *Daphnia* spp. persisted in Cromes Broad for a further month even in the presence of a suite of zooplanktivorous fish at relatively high density. This seems related to the early development of an extensive cover of macrophytes at this site. *Daphnia* spp. showed a positive association with macrophytes (Figure 2) and increasing macrophyte cover (Table 3) at this time, quite unlike the situation in any other site. Such use of macrophytes is consistent with the refuge hypothesis. However, *Daphnia* spp. appeared unable to exploit macrophytes as a refuge over an extensive period. This is in keeping with the behavioural ecology of the group which are typically pelagic and have been shown to avoid macrophytes (Pennak, 1973; Dorgelo & Heykoop, 1985). Recent experiments in the laboratory have shown that a clear trade-off exists, *Daphnia magna* Straus preferring to stay in open water until exposed to the risk of predation from zooplanktivorous fish whereupon it migrates to macrophytes, predation risk clearly outweighing repellency (Lauridsen & Lodge, 1996). However, many common fish species, particularly 0+ cyprinids, are capable of feeding in darkness (Townsend & Risebrow, 1982) and so the risk of predation, although reduced, is still evident. In addition, Daphnia spp. populations may suffer some predation from the fish concentrated in a low density of macrophytes (Figure 3). Therefore, in the face of intense predation pressure from a high density of zooplanktivorous fish, as at Cromes Broad, Daphnia spp. may not be able to persist through time, even with the provision of suitable refuges. Following the decline of Daphnia spp., at those sites retaining at least some macrophyte cover Ceriodaphnia spp. dominated, both with (Pound End) and without Simocephalus sp. (Upton). At Pound End, there was even some partial recovery of Daphnia populations in late summer. In contrast, the connected Hoveton Little Broad, with relatively high numbers of 0+ roach, displayed no replacement of Daphnia spp. with other species or any recovery of populations. The consequence of the presence of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus was the maintenance of large populations (typically >50 l\(^{-1}\), Figure 1) of grazing Cladocera throughout the summer months in Cromes and Pound End. The patterns of habitat use of these species also appeared to be related to the potential predation pressure from fish, thus also consistent with the refuge hypothesis. For example, where predation pressure was presumably low from a low density of 0+ perch as in Upton, Ceriodaphnia spp. was present in both open water and macrophyte beds (Figure 2). Under moderate fish predation pressure in Pound End (0.45 m\(^{-2}\) of 0+ perch and roach), Ceriodaphnia spp. and particularly Simocephalus sp. were more abundant in macrophytes, although Ceriodaphnia spp. also occurred at high density in open water (Figure 2). In contrast, where predation pressure was likely to be intense from a suite of 0+ fish at high density (0.8 m\(^{-2}\)) in Cromes, large populations of both Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. were only maintained through association with macrophytes. Furthermore, under intense predation pressure the abundance of cladocerans was almost always positively correlated with increasing PVI suggesting that increasing cover offered a better refuge (Table 3). What is the mechanism behind the refuge effect? Schriver et al. (1995) demonstrate that a refuge effect may exist at low macrophyte density (15–20% of volume) but that this is dependent on fish density. In the current study, it is suggested that macrophytes may act as refuges for zooplankton at relatively high fish ![Bar chart showing the relative distribution of all fish species in different levels of macrophyte PVI in Cromes Broad in September.](page_320_370_1047_482.png) Figure 3. Relative distribution of all fish species in different levels of macrophyte PVI in Cromes Broad in September. density (Cromes) where macrophyte coverage is extensive and the density of macrophytes is high (Table 1). However, the situation at Pound End suggests that even where the distribution of macrophytes is limited, providing patches of dense macrophytes are available (Table 1), a refuge against moderate predation pressure may be provided. The reasons for this may be that dense macrophyte stands contain relatively few fish (Figure 3). By implication, this suggests that predation risk for Cladocera declines with increasing macrophyte cover. Evidence for this is provided by Phillips et al. (1996), who demonstrated that predation pressure, derived from known numbers of fish with known diet, upon zooplankton declined with increasing macrophyte cover. It is therefore suggested that the formation of predator-free space is the mechanism responsible for the refuge effect. The question is, why do zooplanktivorous fish avoid dense macrophytes? (Engel, 1988). Several plausible mechanisms exist. First, oxygen concentrations (Davis, 1975) and pH (Beklioglu & Moss, 1995) may be unsuitable in macrophyte stands, although there is no evidence that either was limiting in the samples collected during routine monitoring of the study sites. Second, and perhaps more applicable, the foraging efficiency of some fish may decline with increasing habitat complexity (Winfield, 1986; Diehl, 1988). However, when foraging on zooplankton, this is clearly species and size dependent. For example, 0+ perch (Perca fluviatilis L.) may show high feeding efficiency in structured environments unlike 0+ roach (Rutilus rutilus (L.)) (Winfield, 1986), and vegetation may serve as a competitive refuge for perch (Persson, 1993). In support of this, several authors (Hall & Werner 1977; Carpenter et al., 1987; Venugopal & Winfield, 1993) have demonstrated that small fish may associate with macrophytes. However, this is typically a behavioural response to potential predation risk (Savino & Stein, 1982; Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) and not because of enhanced foraging opportunity. Whether small fish take refuge in macrophytes in response to predation risk is dependent on a number of factors including the functional type of predator and prey (Jacobsen et al., 1997). It is perhaps significant that in this study the relative proportion of piscivorous pike increased with increasing macrophyte cover (Figure 3). In addition, the individuals present in these habitats were 0+, the size class most likely to consume 0+ zooplanktivores (Van Densen, 1994). Therefore, a third explanation for the avoidance of dense macrophytes by fish in this study may be that they were exposed to a greater risk of predation in these habitats. This in turn may have led to a reduced predation risk for zooplankton (Turner & Mittelbach, 1990) thereby enhancing the refuge effect. Are refuging Cladocera able to control phytoplankton populations? The presence of large numbers of cladoceran grazers exerting an influence on phytoplankton populations is essential to the value of any refuge effect in explaining the presence of clear water in macrophyte-dominated lakes. Particularly to species other than Daphnia spp.? The relationship between grazing rate and body length are very similar for Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. compared to Daphnia spp. (Peters & Downing, 1984; Knoechel & Holtby, 1986; Bern, 1987; Mourelatos & Lacroix, 1990) and if at high enough density it seems reasonable to conclude that these species may be able to graze out phytoplankton crops, as observed by Turner & Mittelbach (1992). The interconnected Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads, with the same nutrient concentration, but radically different chlorophyll \(a\) values, appear to provide a convincing example of the grazing potential of these Cladocera (Figure 1). Moreover, in Cromes Broad, the filtering capacity of Simocephalus spp. and Ceriodaphnia spp., which are maintained at densities in excess of 50 l\(^{-1}\) throughout the summer months, appears to more than compensate for that of Daphnia spp. (Table 4). In Upton, the situation is less clear, where Simocephalus sp. is absent and the filtering rate of Ceriodaphnia spp. in midsummer does not compensate the loss of Daphnia spp. However, it is still comparable with that of Daphnia spp. at Cromes in early season, before the development of macrophytes when the only likely explanation for the control of phytoplankton populations is grazing. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that grazing by Ceriodaphnia spp. is at least a contributory factor in limiting phytoplankton development in Upton in mid- to late summer. From the patterns of habitat use of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp., it is likely that only Ceriodaphnia spp. may have the potential to graze in the open water between stands of macrophytes, Simocephalus sp. always being limited to the macrophytes themselves (Lauridsen et al., in press). Thus in developing macrophyte populations at the beginning of the growing season or following a restoration attempt using control of zooplanktivorous fish, it seems that large populations of Daphnia spp. are required to provide the clear water necessary for macrophyte development. Following the establishment of macrophyte cover and/or recruitment of 0+ fish, Daphnia may be expected to decline, with Ceriodaphnia assuming the role of grazing in open water between as well as within macrophyte stands, with Simocephalus contributing to control of phytoplankton standing crop in the macrophyte beds themselves (Table 4). Conclusions Several results of the study are consistent with the refuge hypothesis: • The elimination of Daphnia spp. by 0+ fish is delayed where extensive stands of macrophytes are present in early summer. • Large populations (\(>50\ l^{-1}\)) of grazing Cladocera may be maintained throughout the summer at relatively high fish density. • The level of use of macrophyte stands is linked to fish predation pressure. • Cladoceran abundance is positively associated with increasing macrophyte cover. Essential to the value of the refuge effect as a mechanism promoting the stability of submerged macrophyte populations in shallow lakes, the presence of significant populations of grazing Cladocera seems to contribute to the maintenance of a low phytoplankton standing crop and the attainment of clear water. Moreover, macrophyte-associated species such as Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. appear to make an important contribution to this effect where Daphnia spp. is reduced by fish predation and/or disfavoured by extensive macrophyte cover. The mechanism for the refuge effect in this study appears to be the provision of predator-free space as zooplanktivorous fish appear to avoid dense macrophytes. Submerged macrophytes as refuges for grazing Cladocera against fish predation: observations on seasonal changes in relation to macrophyte cover and predation pressure Julia H. Stansfield¹, Martin R. Perrow²*, Louise D. Tench¹, Adrian J. D. Jowitt² & Ayesha A. L. Taylor¹ ¹National Rivers Authority, Biology Laboratory, Station Road, St Olaves, Great Yarmouth, NR31 9JA, UK ²ECON, School of Biological Sciences, University of East Anglia, Norwich NR4 7TJ, UK (*author for correspondence) Key words: zooplankton, zooplanktivorous fish, macrophyte, refugia, predator/prey interactions, lake restoration Abstract The provision of a refuge from fish predation for large-bodied Cladocera among stands of submerged macrophytes is thought to be an important stabilising mechanism against nutrient-induced phytoplankton increases in clear water shallow lakes. The occurrence of any refuge effect in relation to the seasonal impact of both macrophyte development and recruitment of zooplanktivorous fish was monitored over the summer months (May to September) in three lakes (Cromes Broad, Hoveton Little Broad/Pound End, and Upton Broad) of variable trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover, in the Norfolk Broads in Eastern England. At all sites, Daphnia spp. exhibited a early summer peak of abundance but had declined rapidly by July probably as a result of predation from underyearling fish. In extensive macrophyte stands (Cromes Broad) Daphnia spp. persisted after its elimination in open water, indicating some refuge effect. At sites with macrophyte cover and/or low fish predation pressure, Daphnia spp. was replaced by Ceriodaphnia spp., both with and without Simocephalus sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera, apparently capable of exerting a high grazing pressure on phytoplankton. This occurred, even under high predation pressure from a relatively high density of zooplanktivorous 0+ fish (Cromes Broad), consistent with the refuge hypothesis. In addition, at this site, significant positive associations of cladoceran abundance with increasing macrophyte cover were apparent throughout the summer. From information on the distribution of fish it is suggested that dense macrophytes offer the most suitable refuge through provision of predator-free space. Introduction Eutrophication of shallow freshwater lakes frequently results in increased standing crops of phytoplankton or perhaps filamentous algae. This in turn leads to the decline or loss of submerged macrophytes, typically through shading (Phillips et al., 1978; Scheffer, 1990), with consequent gross changes in biotic structure and function (Moss, 1983; De Nie, 1987; Bronmark & Weisner, 1992). However, there is growing empirical and experimental evidence that stabilising mechanisms associated with the presence of stands of macrophytes, may prevent or reduce increases in algal growth up to a threshold level of nutrient loading (Howard-Williams, 1981; Timms & Moss, 1984; Mitchell et al., 1988; Balls et al., 1989; Andersson et al., 1990; Blindlow et al., 1993; Van Donk et al., 1993; Schriver et al., 1995). Consequently, within a range of nutrient concentration, either macrophytes or phytoplankton may dominate; the alternative stable state hypothesis (Irvine et al., 1989; Scheffer et al., 1993). Several stabilising mechanisms which perpetuate the macrophyte-dominated state have been suggested. These include: allelopathy, the production of com- pounds limiting algal growth by the macrophytes themselves (Wium-Anderson et al., 1982); competition for N, with macrophytes maintaining a competitive advantage over algae through luxury uptake (Balls et al., 1989) and acting as a sink for available nutrients (in both water column and sediments) (Ozimek et al., 1990; Van Donk et al., 1993); prevention of resuspension of sediment and recirculation of fast sinking algae by wind and wave action through calming of the water column (James & Barko, 1990); provision of refuges for grazing zooplankton (Timms & Moss, 1984) and refuges for piscivorous fish acting upon the production (Spencer & King, 1984; Grimm & Backx, 1990) or the distribution (Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) of zooplanktivorous fish thereby reducing predation pressure upon the zooplankton (Hambright et al., 1986, Turner & Mittelbach, 1990). Detailed knowledge of the mechanisms responsible for maintaining clear water and low algal populations in lakes dominated by macrophytes is critical for those lake managers concerned with the sustainable restoration (i.e. reversal of anthropogenic eutrophication) of shallow lakes, particularly if this is to be achieved in a predictable and cost-effective manner (Shapiro, 1990). In restoration programmes, the refuge effect for zooplankton is particularly appealing (Shapiro, 1990). This is due to two reasons. First, after nutrient loading has been reduced to the range where macrophyte dominance is likely to be stable (TP<0.15 mg l\(^{-1}\) or higher if N is strongly limiting-Hosper & Jagtman, 1990; Jeppesen et al., 1990), the removal of zooplanktivorous fish, often termed biomanipulation (Lammens et al., 1990), is often required to enhance populations of grazing zooplankton to reduce algal crops to provide a suitable light climate for macrophyte growth. If this mechanism operates, then it is likely that grazing has some importance in maintaining clear water within macrophyte beds. Second, during the development of macrophyte stands following biomanipulation which may or may not be rapid (Meijer et al., 1994; Perrow et al., 1994, Moss et al., 1996), any stabilising mechanism is of increased value if it also preserves water clarity in the open water surrounding macrophyte stands. The diel migration of large-bodied Cladocera from macrophyte stands to open water to feed provides such a mechanism (Timms & Moss, 1984). Although macrophyte stands have been demonstrated to provide refuges for zooplankton (Schriver et al., 1995; Phillips et al., 1996) the timing of such effects relative to the seasonal development of macrophytes and recruitment of 0+ fish is poorly understood. The aim of this study was to describe the seasonal pattern of use of submerged macrophytes by grazing Cladocera in relation to potential predation pressure from fish and to determine whether the refuge effect is plausible as a mechanism in promoting clear water in beds of macrophytes. This adopted a comparative approach by monitoring zooplankton abundance and community structure, fish abundance and biomass, chlorophyll a concentration (as a index of algal abundance) and macrophyte cover during the macrophyte growing season (May–September) in three lakes of varying trophic status, fish community structure and nature and extent of macrophyte cover. Description of study sites The three lakes studied (Hoveton Little/Pound End, Crones and Upton Broads) are among the Norfolk Broads, a series (around 50) of small (1–124 ha), shallow (0.5–2 m) lakes in eastern England, formed from flooded medieval peat diggings. Most may now be classed as hypertrophic and only four retain their original macrophyte populations (Moss, 1983). The study sites represent a continuum from phytoplankton to macrophyte dominance. The first, Hoveton Little Broad, has been divided into two sections as part of a long term management strategy aimed at evaluating the effects of different restorative actions (Table 1). For the purposes of this study, Hoveton Little Broad, acts as a control section with turbid phytoplankton dominated water and few submerged macrophytes, whereas the other biomanipulated section, Pound End, has clear water and some macrophytes, although these are restricted to bird exclosures. The second, Crones Broad, retains a relatively high nutrient loading but has recently developed an extensive cover of Ceratophyllum demersum L. with Potamogeton freisii Rupr. (Perrow et al., 1997). The third, Upton Broad, being isolated from riverine inputs and surrounded by wet woodland, has largely retained its original character and has a large cover of macrophytes, particularly Najas marina L., with Chara spp., P. pectinatus L. and Zannichellia palustris L. Materials and methods Zooplankton, macrophytes and chlorophyll \( a \) Sampling for zooplankton, macrophytes, and chlorophyll \( a \) was carried out monthly from May to September 1994. At each site, ten zooplankton samples were taken from both open water and from amongst submerged macrophytes, where present. Where macrophytes occurred the density in a 0.25 m\(^2\) quadrat centred on each sampling point was expressed as PVI (per cent volume infested-Canfield et al., 1984). This was estimated by multiplying the estimated % cover by the height of the stand and dividing by the depth of water. At Pound End, five samples were taken from each of the two large (a. 500–1000 m\(^2\)) bird exclosures. In the open water and when macrophyte stands reached the water surface, a tube sampler was used (length 90 cm, diameter 10 cm) in order to sample the whole water column. When macrophyte stands did not reach the water surface a Patalas sampler (10 litre capacity) was used to obtain a sample from among the macrophyte stand. Water was strained through a 64 \( \mu \)m net and the animals retained were preserved in 70% alcohol. Samples were counted under a stereo microscope using 25 \( \times \) magnification. Differences between mean abundance of important cladoceran zooplankton between open water and macrophytes were tested using Mann-Whitney U-tests on each sampling occasion. In addition, the relationships between abundance of particular cladoceran species and % macrophyte cover were explored using the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (\( r_s \)). Chlorophyll \( a \) concentrations were determined according to the methods of Moss et al. (1986). Fish Fish populations were sampled on two occasions, in May and September. This corresponded to the period prior to the recruitment of cyprinids and after the late summer period in which 0+ fish are likely to exert a depressive effect on zooplankton (Townsend & Perrow, 1989), respectively. In addition, sampling in May provided a baseline of the adult fish stock prior to the recruitment of underyearlings, whereas sampling in September allowed the relative recruitment strength of the 0+ fish to be estimated. Point abundance sampling (PAS) (Copp & Penáz, 1988) conducted with high frequency (600 Hz) pulsed DC electrofishing equipment was used to sample all habitats in proportion to their abundance. During sampling the 3 m fibreglass dinghy, with one electrofishing operator and one person controlling the boat using ‘push’ (facing the direction of travel) rowing, was rowed systematically along transect lines (8–10 oar strokes apart). At the equivalent distance along the transect line, a point was sampled by rapidly immers- ing the large (45 cm diameter) anode and swinging it through a 2 m arc in one motion. Any stunned fish were removed and transferred to individual buckets. The area sampled was quantified as 2.4 m\(^2\). This was achieved by using a voltmeter to determine the distance at which the voltage gradient was reduced to 0.12 V which may be used as the threshold limit for effective electrofishing (Copp & Penáz, 1988). At the end of each transect all fish were identified, counted, measured to the nearest mm fork length and weighed to the nearest gram, before being returned to a stretch of water that had been sampled previously. In addition, the % of the water column occupied by submerged macrophytes was estimated visually at each sampling point. The entire area of Pound End, Upton and Cromes Broads were sampled, whereas only part of Hoveton Little Broad (c. 6 ha-comparable to the size of Pound End) was covered. Results Fish The spring biomass of adult cyprinid and percid fishes was variable but low (up to 110 kg ha\(^{-1}\) but typically <15 kg ha\(^{-1}\)) (Table 2). The increase in biomass and especially, density, of potentially zooplanktivorous fish (all except pike, *Esox lucius* L. and eel, *Anguilla anguilla* (L.)) over the sampling period underlines the important contribution the recruitment of 0+ fish makes to fish production in the study lakes (Table 2). The relative recruitment strength of the different species in the different lakes is illustrated in Figure 1. Zooplankton Three genera of large-bodied grazing Cladocera zooplankton were found at significant density (>50 l\(^{-1}\)) in some or all of the study sites. These were *Daphnia hyalina/longispina* (Leydig/O.F.M.) *Ceriodaphnia reticulata/quadrangula* (Jurine/O.F. M.) and *Simocephalus vetulus* (O.F.M.). *Daphnia* spp. had an early summer peak of abundance, albeit of varying magnitude, at all sites, but had declined to low populations by July. At Cromes Broad, where extensive macrophyte stands developed from June onwards (Figure 1), *Daphnia* spp. persisted amongst the macrophytes after its elimination in open water (Figure 2). At Cromes and Pound End *Daphnia* spp. was replaced by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. both with (Cromes and Pound End) and without (Upton) *Simocephalus* sp., thus maintaining large populations of grazing Cladocera. This was not the case in Hoveton Little Broad, where cladoceran populations remained extremely low throughout the summer. The patterns of habitat use by *Ceriodaphnia* spp. varied between the different sites (Figure 2). At Pound End, macrophyte beds were favoured in early season, although once populations had built up by mid-summer, significant numbers (>100 l\(^{-1}\)) were found in open water. At Upton, prior to the peak in macrophyte populations, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was more abundant in open water, thereafter there was no significant difference between the different habitats. In contrast, in Cromes, *Ceriodaphnia* spp. was significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds compared to open water on all occasions (Figure 2). A similar pattern was shown by *Simocephalus* sp. where it occurred, as it was virtually always significantly more abundant in macrophyte beds (Figure 2). For sites with macrophytes, the relationships between PVI and the abundance of the different genera as well as all grazing Cladocera combined are shown in Table 3. At Cromes, there is a consistent pattern of increasing abundance of all genera, including *Daphnia* spp. while it was still present, with increasing PVI. At Upton no such pattern was found, with either no significant relationships, or in July, a significant negative relationship with *Ceriodaphnia* spp. Pound End represented an intermediate situation, with different species exerting different preferences: *Daphnia* spp. tended to be negatively associated with macrophytes; *Ceriodaphnia* spp. displayed positive associations early in the summer but no relationship in subsequent samples and *Simocephalus* sp. showed significant positive correlations with PVI on all occasions. Indeed, where fish recruitment is poor or absent, *Daphnia* spp. populations typically persist throughout the summer months (Perrow et al., 1994). Conversely, it is clear that the relatively low overwintering stock of older fish exerted little influence on the development of the *Daphnia* spp. population. Second, in all sites, *Daphnia* spp. was quickly replaced by high densities of other species which is not consistent with food limitation and indeed at no site was the abundance of edible algae (expressed as chlorophyll *a*) apparently limiting. It therefore seems reasonable to conclude that predation by 0+ fish is responsible for the decline in *Daphnia* spp. Moreover, this appears to be readily achieved by a relatively low number of 0+ fish in Upton (prior to the development of macrophytes) and relatively moderate recruitment in Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads. However, *Daphnia* spp. persisted in Cromes Broad for a further month even in the presence of a suite of zooplanktivorous fish at relatively high density. This seems related to the early development of an extensive cover of macrophytes at this site. *Daphnia* spp. showed a positive association with macrophytes (Figure 2) and increasing macrophyte cover (Table 3) at this time, quite unlike the situation in any other site. Such use of macrophytes is consistent with the refuge hypothesis. However, *Daphnia* spp. appeared unable to exploit macrophytes as a refuge over an extensive period. This is in keeping with the behavioural ecology of the group which are typically pelagic and have been shown to avoid macrophytes (Pennak, 1973; Dorgelo & Heykoop, 1985). Recent experiments in the laboratory have shown that a clear trade-off exists, *Daphnia magna* Straus preferring to stay in open water until exposed to the risk of predation from zooplanktivorous fish whereupon it migrates to macrophytes, predation risk clearly outweighing repellency (Lauridsen & Lodge, 1996). However, many common fish species, particularly 0+ cyprinids, are capable of feeding in darkness (Townsend & Risebrow, 1982) and so the risk of predation, although reduced, is still evident. In addition, Daphnia spp. populations may suffer some predation from the fish concentrated in a low density of macrophytes (Figure 3). Therefore, in the face of intense predation pressure from a high density of zooplanktivorous fish, as at Cromes Broad, Daphnia spp. may not be able to persist through time, even with the provision of suitable refuges. Following the decline of Daphnia spp., at those sites retaining at least some macrophyte cover Ceriodaphnia spp. dominated, both with (Pound End) and without Simocephalus sp. (Upton). At Pound End, there was even some partial recovery of Daphnia populations in late summer. In contrast, the connected Hoveton Little Broad, with relatively high numbers of 0+ roach, displayed no replacement of Daphnia spp. with other species or any recovery of populations. The consequence of the presence of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus was the maintenance of large populations (typically >50 l\(^{-1}\), Figure 1) of grazing Cladocera throughout the summer months in Cromes and Pound End. The patterns of habitat use of these species also appeared to be related to the potential predation pressure from fish, thus also consistent with the refuge hypothesis. For example, where predation pressure was presumably low from a low density of 0+ perch as in Upton, Ceriodaphnia spp. was present in both open water and macrophyte beds (Figure 2). Under moderate fish predation pressure in Pound End (0.45 m\(^{-2}\) of 0+ perch and roach), Ceriodaphnia spp. and particularly Simocephalus sp. were more abundant in macrophytes, although Ceriodaphnia spp. also occurred at high density in open water (Figure 2). In contrast, where predation pressure was likely to be intense from a suite of 0+ fish at high density (0.8 m\(^{-2}\)) in Cromes, large populations of both Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. were only maintained through association with macrophytes. Furthermore, under intense predation pressure the abundance of cladocerans was almost always positively correlated with increasing PVI suggesting that increasing cover offered a better refuge (Table 3). What is the mechanism behind the refuge effect? Schriver et al. (1995) demonstrate that a refuge effect may exist at low macrophyte density (15–20% of volume) but that this is dependent on fish density. However, the situation at Pound End suggests that even where the distribution of macrophytes is limited, providing patches of dense macrophytes are available (Table 1), a refuge against moderate predation pressure may be provided. The reasons for this may be that dense macrophyte stands contain relatively few fish (Figure 3). By implication, this suggests that predation risk for Cladocera declines with increasing macrophyte cover. Evidence for this is provided by Phillips et al. (1996), who demonstrated that predation pressure, derived from known numbers of fish with known diet, upon zooplankton declined with increasing macrophyte cover. It is therefore suggested that the formation of predator-free space is the mechanism responsible for the refuge effect. The question is, why do zooplanktivorous fish avoid dense macrophytes? (Engel, 1988). Several plausible mechanisms exist. First, oxygen concentrations (Davis, 1975) and pH (Beklioglu & Moss, 1995) may be unsuitable in macrophyte stands, although there is no evidence that either was limiting in the samples collected during routine monitoring of the study sites. Second, and perhaps more applicable, the foraging efficiency of some fish may decline with increasing habitat complexity (Winfield, 1986; Diehl, 1988). However, when foraging on zooplankton, this is clearly species and size dependent. For example, 0+ perch (Perca fluviatilis L.) may show high feeding efficiency in structured environments unlike 0+ roach (Rutilus rutilus (L.)) (Winfield, 1986), and vegetation may serve as a competitive refuge for perch (Persson, 1993). In support of this, several authors (Hall & Werner 1977; Carpenter et al., 1987; Venugopal & Winfield, 1993) have demonstrated that small fish may associate with macrophytes. However, this is typically a behavioural response to potential predation risk (Savino & Stein, 1982; Werner et al., 1983; Persson & Eklov, 1995) and not because of enhanced foraging opportunity. Whether small fish take refuge in macrophytes in response to predation risk is dependent on a number of factors including the functional type of predator and prey (Jacobsen et al., 1997). It is perhaps significant that in this study the relative proportion of piscivorous pike increased with increasing macrophyte cover (Figure 3). In addition, the individuals present in these habitats were 0+, the size class most likely to consume 0+ zooplanktivores (Van Densen, 1994). Therefore, a third explanation for the avoidance of dense macrophytes by fish in this study may be that they were exposed to a greater risk of predation in these habitats. This in turn may have led to a reduced predation risk for zooplankton (Turner & Mittelbach, 1990) thereby enhancing the refuge effect. Are refuging Cladocera able to control phytoplankton populations? The presence of large numbers of cladoceran grazers exerting an influence on phytoplankton populations is essential to the value of any refuge effect in explaining the presence of clear water in macrophyte-dominated lakes. Particularly to species other than Daphnia spp.? The relationship between grazing rate and body length are very similar for Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. compared to Daphnia spp. (Peters & Downing, 1984; Knoechel & Holtby, 1986; Bern, 1987; Mourelatos & Lacroix, 1990) and if at high enough density it seems reasonable to conclude that these species may be able to graze out phytoplankton crops, as observed by Turner & Mittelbach (1992). The interconnected Pound End and Hoveton Little Broads, with the same nutrient concentration, but radically different chlorophyll \(a\) values, appear to provide a convincing example of the grazing potential of these Cladocera (Figure 1). Moreover, in Cromes Broad, the filtering capacity of Simocephalus spp. and Ceriodaphnia spp., which are maintained at densities in excess of 50 l\(^{-1}\) throughout the summer months, appears to more than compensate for that of Daphnia spp. (Table 4). In Upton, the situation is less clear, where Simocephalus sp. is absent and the filtering rate of Ceriodaphnia spp. in midsummer does not compensate the loss of Daphnia spp. However, it is still comparable with that of Daphnia spp. at Cromes in early season, before the development of macrophytes when the only likely explanation for the control of phytoplankton populations is grazing. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that grazing by Ceriodaphnia spp. is at least a contributory factor in limiting phytoplankton development in Upton in mid- to late summer. From the patterns of habitat use of Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp., it is likely that only Ceriodaphnia spp. may have the potential to graze in the open water between stands of macrophytes, Simocephalus sp. always being limited to the macrophytes themselves (Lauridsen et al., in press). Thus in developing macrophyte populations at the beginning of the growing season or following a restoration attempt using control of zooplanktivorous fish, it seems that large populations of Daphnia spp. are required to provide the clear water necessary for macrophyte development. Following the establishment of macrophyte cover and/or recruitment of 0+ fish, Daphnia may be expected to decline, with Ceriodaphnia assuming the role of grazing in open water between as well as within macrophyte stands, with Simocephalus contributing to control of phytoplankton standing crop in the macrophyte beds themselves (Table 4). Conclusions Several results of the study are consistent with the refuge hypothesis: • The elimination of Daphnia spp. by 0+ fish is delayed where extensive stands of macrophytes are present in early summer. • Large populations (\(>50\ l^{-1}\)) of grazing Cladocera may be maintained throughout the summer at relatively high fish density. • The level of use of macrophyte stands is linked to fish predation pressure. • Cladoceran abundance is positively associated with increasing macrophyte cover. Essential to the value of the refuge effect as a mechanism promoting the stability of submerged macrophyte populations in shallow lakes, the presence of significant populations of grazing Cladocera seems to contribute to the maintenance of a low phytoplankton standing crop and the attainment of clear water. Moreover, macrophyte-associated species such as Ceriodaphnia spp. and Simocephalus sp. appear to make an important contribution to this effect where Daphnia spp. is reduced by fish predation and/or disfavoured by extensive macrophyte cover. The mechanism for the refuge effect in this study appears to be the provision of predator-free space as zooplanktivorous fish appear to avoid dense macrophytes. The diversity of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte communities in ponds LAURIE E. FRIDAY Department of Biological Sciences, University of Exeter SUMMARY. 1. The range of factors which may influence the wide variation in the structure of pond communities is reviewed. 2. Factors explaining the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate and macrophyte taxa are investigated, using multiple regression analysis, for a group of ponds in which biogeographical effects are likely to be minimal. 3. Numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa in these ponds are highly correlated with pH and probably, therefore, with other associated aspects of water chemistry. 4. Many invertebrate taxa, from species to entire phyla, were not found below pH 5.5, but few characteristically 'acidophilic' taxa were apparent. 5. Details of species composition of the macroinvertebrate fauna differ widely even between ponds of similar pH. 6. The diversity and composition of macrophyte communities are not adequately predicted by any of the factors investigated. Introduction Ponds and other small water bodies are highly individual habitats: the fauna and flora usually vary widely, and often unpredictably, between ponds even within a small geographical area. While it is sometimes possible to find correlations between observed faunal or floral diversity and various factors, it is rarely possible, except by rigorous experimental treatment, to establish the causes of inter-pond variation. A wide variety of explanatory factors has been put forward, as a result of field studies of small water bodies or on theoretical grounds, as possible influences on the diversity and composition of pond communities. These factors may be grouped together under two broad headings: 'biogeographical' factors, operating via the dispersal of organisms to essentially insular habitats, and 'habitat' characteristics, both physico-chemical and biotic, influencing the establishment and persistence of colonizing species. These categories are not mutually exclusive, but form a useful basis for reviewing the wide range of factors which might explain inter-pond variation in the number and identities of species. Correspondence: Dr L. E. Friday, Department of Applied Biology, Pembroke Street, Cambridge CB2 3DX. (i) Biogeographical factors (a) Pond age. Studies of the initial colonization of newly created ponds show a general increase in the numbers of species of invertebrates and macrophytes (Gates, 1927; Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). Where dispersal distances are short, the rate of acquisition of new species has been observed to decline within a few years (Barnes, 1983), suggesting an approach to an 'equilibrium number of species', as predicted by MacArthur & Wilson's (1967) theory of island biogeography. However, Godwin's (1923) observations on the flora of much older ponds suggest that numbers of less vagile species (i.e. those with weak or passive dispersal) may continue to rise over many decades. As a pond ages, so the habitat it presents to colonists changes, partly due to increases in the extent and diversity of aquatic vegetation and in the production of autochthonous detritus. These changes are accompanied by changes in the identity of the dominant invertebrate taxa (Street & Titmus, 1979; Barnes, 1983). While it is possible to fit a model to the observed rise in numbers of taxa with age, the order in which individual colonists establish is not easy to predict. Invasion by an individual species depends on the availability of suitable propagules in 'source' habitats, the species' dispersal mechanisms, and the distance over which it has to disperse, but is also subject to chance (Talling, 1951). (b) Isolation. MacArthur & Wilson's model predicts a decrease in the equilibrium number of species on an island, and changes in the species represented, with increasing isolation from the source of colonists. Aho (1978a) found a significant correlation between isolation of small, productive Finnish lakes and the diversity of their molluscan faunas. Several authors have suggested that changes in isolation over historical or geological time (due to flooding, changes in river courses, creation or destruction of source habitats) have influenced the diversity of less vagile organisms in lakes (e.g. Boycott, 1919; Godwin, 1923; Aho, 1978b; Barbour & Brown, 1974). The immediate surroundings of ponds may also influence their chances of discovery by actively dispersing organisms, but surrounding vegetation and land use are likely to be of greater importance in their effect on aspects of the pond habitat, namely hydrology, water chemistry and allochthonous organic inputs. (c) Pond area. Connor & McCoy (1979), in their review of the species–area relationship, point out that the possible effects of area on community diversity have both biogeographical and biotic elements: as area increases, so the number of habitat types, with their associated species, is likely to increase; population sizes should also increase with area, thus reducing the extinction rate of resident species (MacArthur & Wilson, 1967); and large 'target' areas may simply receive a larger number of colonizing propagules, and therefore a chance of a greater variety of species, than smaller ones. Lassen (1975), Aho (1978a), Driver (1977) and Fryer (1985) found correlations between area (or log area) and the numbers of species of molluscs, chironomids and crustaceans respectively. Which of these aspects may account for the observed relationships is not possible to determine from diversity data alone, but Fryer (1985) suggests that the types of habitats found in different sized water bodies ('pond' as opposed to 'lake' habitats) may partly explain the composition of the crustacean faunas in his study area. Area, as an expression of the size of a water body, is also related to its persistence. Small ponds tend to be less permanent than larger ones, may show greater fluctuations in physical and chemical conditions, and so present quite a different type of habitat. Macan (1954, 1962) discusses the probable influence of habitat stability on the identity, and possibly on the diversity, of corixid species in a water body. (ii) Characteristics of the habitat (a) Habitat diversity. Factors contributing to the diversity of habitat for pond macrophytes include details of the bank topography and changes in substratum associated with irregularities in the shoreline. For the macroinvertebrate fauna, the diversity of macrophytic vegetation and local changes in substratum may be major factors. Observations by several authors on invertebrate communities associated with different species of macrophytes (e.g. Soszka, 1975; Dvorak & Best, 1982; Lodge, 1985), suggest that a correlation might be expected between macrophyte and macroinvertebrate numbers of species. Palmer (1981) found a close relationship between macrophyte species diversity and the number of species of Coleoptera and Hemiptera in a survey of base-rich ponds in Norfolk. (b) Competition and predation. Little direct evidence has been put forward to show that biotic interactions are major determinants of pond biotic diversity. However, changes in fish populations are often accompanied by changes in the plant and invertebrate communities (Macan, 1965, 1977b; Korinkova, 1967; Henrickson & Oscarson, 1985) and the effect of fish predation on zooplankton community structure is well documented (see Zaret, 1980). Biotic interactions might possibly be a major influence from the very earliest stages of pond colonization. In new ponds, extensive pure stands of emergent or floating-leaved macrophytes may establish within a few years (Barnes, 1983) and preclude other species by competition for light or space. They may constitute very distinctive habitats for invertebrates and if, by chance, different aggressive species colonize neighbouring ponds, then quite different communities may result. (c) Water chemistry. Many workers have found a correlation between pond biotic diversity and water chemistry. Scandinavian studies of molluscan communities (e.g. Aho, 1987a; Økland, 1980) link species diversity to a combination of pH and calcium levels. Strong positive correlations between pH and numbers of species of Crustacea have been reported from acidic, low-calcium ponds and lakes in Northern Britain (Fryer, 1980) and Norway (Økland & Økland, 1980). The composition of macrophytic communities may also be changed during lake acidification (Grahn, 1975). Green (1986) found a non-linear relationship between conductivity and zooplankton diversity in crater lakes. Several authors stress the importance of the general level of productivity of a water body (usually gauged by concentrations of nutrient ions) in determining the assortment of species found there, e.g. Saether (1975). In the present study, the distribution of littoral macroinvertebrates and macrophytes in a group of ponds within a small geographical area were investigated to discover which factors best predict the numbers of taxa and the types of communities found in each pond. In view of the difficulties inherent in distinguishing the confounding effects of different types of variables, the ponds were chosen to minimize the possible influence of pond age and isolation. Sites Sixteen ponds were chosen from among the large number of water bodies created by open-cast extraction of ball-clay in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, U.K. The study ponds all lie within an area of heath, woodland and pasture, 5×2 km, centred on National Grid Reference SY935835, just north of the chalk escarpment (Fig. 1). The ponds were chosen to represent as wide a range of physico-chemical and habitat conditions (as judged from terrestrial and aquatic vegetation) as possible. The exact ages of individual ponds are not known, but all date from the nineteenth century, with the exception of pond Q, which was formed in the eighteenth century (English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd, pers. comm.). From a study of the rate of colonization of newly created ball-clay ponds in the area (Barnes, 1983), it appears that the equilibrium number of macroinvertebrate taxa for small ponds is approached within 20 years of the first appearance of the water body. It is expected, therefore, that the ponds chosen for this study have attained the colonization asymptote, at least as far as macroinvertebrates are concerned, and any differences in age between them are not likely to be of importance. Dispersal distances between the ponds are small, the greatest nearest-neighbour distance being <1 km. No discrete source of colonizing propagules is recognizable, there being numerous small water bodies (ball-clay ponds, bomb craters and streams) in the area as well as the Corfe River to the east and the River Stour to the north-west. It is therefore assumed that the source pool of colonists is diffuse, so that no pond is substantially more isolated than any other. All the ponds contain at least 1 m depth of water throughout the year and none is connected, at any time, to any other water body. Methods (i) Morphometry Pond areas and shore lengths were estimated from large-scale maps produced by English China Clays (Ball Clays) Ltd surveyors. For the larger ponds, maximum depths and basin profiles were obtained from depth measure- FIG. 1. Location of the study site and map of the sixteen ball-clay ponds, labelled A–R. ments taken at 5 m intervals along transects; depths of smaller ponds were measured using a lead line from the bank. (ii) Chemistry Water samples were taken from 20 cm below the surface, 2 m from the shore, away from dense vegetation. All ponds were sampled within 2 h around noon on 12 April 1979 and again on 8 August 1979. Temperature and dissolved oxygen were recorded in situ and samples were analysed the same day by the Wessex Water Authority chemical laboratory, Poole, using standard methods (see Barnes, 1981; for details). For each sample, pH, electrical conductivity, turbidity, total hardness, alkalinity, nitrate, ammonium, orthophosphate, and 5-day B.O.D. were determined. Seven samples were later analysed for calcium and two for total aluminium, using an atomic absorption spectrophotometer at the University of Exeter. (iii) Macrophytes All ponds were surveyed during a 2-week period in August 1979 to determine the total area vegetated, the number of species, and their relative abundance, expressed as cover abundance scores as follows: 1 = 0.1–5% of vegetated area 2 = 6–25% of vegetated area 3 = 26–50% of vegetated area 4 = 51–75% of vegetated area 5 = 76–100% of vegetated area (iv) Macroinvertebrates The macroinvertebrate communities of the shallow littoral were sampled using standard sampling units, each consisting of five separate 2 m sweeps with an F.B.A. pond net (mesh aperture 1 mm). Trials showed that five sweeps obtained at least 85% of the species to be discovered by repeated sweeping within a given weed bed. Pond nets tend to under-sample certain elements of the fauna (see Macan, 1977a, for a critique), and the species lists obtained from one period of sampling will not be complete. However, such samples, taken in a standard manner and within a short space of time, may be used to compare communities between ponds. All sixteen ponds were sampled in a 3-day period in early April 1979. All were sampled with equal intensity, that is the number of sampling units employed in each pond was proportional to the extent of the shallow littoral habitat. An increase in the number of samples as pond size increased was deemed necessary to incorporate the apparent greater diversity of littoral habitats in larger ponds. The shoreline of each pond was divided arbitrarily into 100 m stretches and one sampling unit was taken in each 100 m stretch. The positions of the five individual sweeps in each sampling unit were determined by possibility of access to the water. Identification was taken to species wherever possible, but chironomid larvae were identified only to genus, and some members of other groups could be identified only to family. The relative numerical abundance of taxa were expressed as abundance scores as follows: 1 = present, but a mean of <1 individual per sampling unit 2 = 1–10 individuals per sampling unit 3 = 11–100 individuals per sampling unit 4 = >100 individuals per sampling unit The use of approximately logarithmic abundance categories to some extent overcomes the problem of comparing relative abundance of taxa of very different body size and reduces the dominating effect of seasonal swarms of small individuals. Results Numbers of taxa The numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa and macrophyte species found in each pond are shown in Table 1, together with values for selected physical and chemical parameters. The wide range of all these parameters over the sixteen ponds is apparent: for example, the number of macroinvertebrate taxa ranges from twenty-four to eighty-eight; pH from 3.8 to 7.5; and pond area from 0.023 to 2.0 ha. The total number of macroinvertebrate taxa found was 174 and the total number of macrophyte species thirty-one. The relationships between numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa (INVERTS) and macrophyte species (PLANTS) and physical and chemical characteristics of the ponds were investigated by correlation and regression analyses carried out using the statistical package MINITAB 81.1 (Ryan, 1981). Regression analyses were used to discover which, if any, of the biotic, physical and chemical factors might adequately explain the variation in numbers of macroinvertebrate taxa or macrophyte species found in these ponds. Preliminary analyses suggested that regression analysis would not be inappropriate, since the measurement errors in the y-variables (INVERTS or PLANTS) are great relative to those in the x-variables (predictors), and the individual variables are approximately normally distributed. Bivariate plots suggested the need to log-transform INVERTS, PLANTS, area and vegetated area for regression analysis (i.e. LINVERTS, LPLANTS, LAREA, LVAREA); this gave an acceptable degree of homoscedasticity in the residuals (Draper & Smith, 1981). Regression analyses proceeded by using predicator variables in turn, and, for multiple regression, adding them one at a time, using a correlation matrix as a guide and inspecting residuals and coefficients at each stage. The effectiveness of the various regression equations for predicting numbers of taxa in individual ponds was assessed by plotting the number of taxa predicted v. the number observed for each pond ('predicted-y v. observed-y' plots). Points falling above the line of equality indicate an over-estimation by the equation, those below an under-estimation (see Fig. 3). As a first step, Pearson correlation coefficients were computed between all pairs of the fourteen variables given in Table 1, log-transformed as appropriate. Sixteen pairs of observations were used in each case, except those involving calcium, for which only seven pairs could be used. Table 2, the correlation half-matrix, shows a number of distinct patterns: (i) LINVERTS is positively correlated with calcium and pH (\( P < 0.01 \)) and with LPLANTS, alkalinity, and LVAREA (\( P < 0.05 \)). (ii) All pairwise correlations between pH, conductivity, B.O.D., total hardness, alkalinity and calcium are significant at the 1% level. (iii) LAREA and LVAREA are correlated (\( P < 0.05 \)), depth is correlated with LAREA (\( P < 0.01 \)), and LVAREA with LINVERTS (\( P < 0.05 \)) but none of these morphometric variables is correlated with any chemical factor.
